pages.blurb: The Night League's club in Space's old Platja d'en Bossa building, opened May 2017; voted world number one by DJ Mag readers from 2022 to 2025.

pages.title: UNVRS
pages.blurb: The Night League's 'hyperclub' on the old Ku and Privilege site near Sant Rafel, opened May 2025 with a different residency every night of the week.

pages.title: Pikes
pages.blurb: Tony Pike's farmhouse hotel outside Sant Antoni, opened 1980: Wham!'s pool, Freddie Mercury's party, and since the Ibiza Rocks takeover a DJs' retreat.

pages.title: Manumission
pages.blurb: The McKays' theatrical Monday at Ku, then Privilege: 8,000–10,000 people, stage shows and the Motel, from 1994 until it ended at Amnesia in 2008.

pages.title: Circoloco
pages.blurb: Antonio Carbonaro and Andrea Pelino's Monday at DC10 since 1999: a free morning after-party that grew into a global brand with its own label.

pages.title: We Love… Sundays at Space
pages.blurb: Space's Sunday party, grown from Darren Hughes's Home and programmed by Mark and Sarah Broadbent: terrace and club, until it left for Sankeys in 2015.

pages.title: Enter.
pages.blurb: Richie Hawtin's Thursday at Space, 2012–15: his first solo Ibiza residency, with themed rooms, a sake bar and new lighting in the main room.

pages.title: Music On
pages.blurb: Marco Carola's long-set tech-house night: Fridays at Amnesia from 2012 to 2018, then at Pacha from 2019, where it still runs on Fridays.

pages.title: Paradise
pages.blurb: Jamie Jones's Hot Creations party: eight seasons at DC10 from 2012, Wednesdays at Amnesia from 2022 and at UNVRS since 2025.

pages.title: Glitterbox
pages.blurb: Defected's disco-and-house party with performers, conceived by Simon Dunmore and launched at Space in 2014; on Sundays at Hï Ibiza since 2017.

pages.title: Afterlife
pages.blurb: Tale Of Us's melodic-techno party and label: Space in 2016, Privilege in 2017, then Thursdays at Hï Ibiza from 2018, built around big-screen visuals.

pages.title: Solomun +1
pages.blurb: Solomun's Sunday at Pacha since 2013: one invited guest each week, long sets and a back-to-back finish, with the DJ booth moved down to the floor.

pages.title: Cream Ibiza
pages.blurb: The Liverpool promoters' summer night at Amnesia from 1995, on Thursdays in later years, until RA reported its departure after 22 years in 2018.

pages.title: Ibiza Uncovered
pages.blurb: Sky One's 1997 documentary series on young Britons in San Antonio; it began the Uncovered franchise (to 2002) and the Brits-abroad TV template.

pages.title: Ricardo Urgell
pages.blurb: Founder of Pacha, with his brother Piti: Sitges in 1967 (some say 1966), Ibiza's farmhouse club from 1973; sold the group in 2017.

pages.title: Pepe Roselló
pages.blurb: Ibiza club owner since 1963 (Capri/Playboy, Sant Antoni) who ran Space at Platja d'en Bossa from 1989 until its closure in 2016.

pages.title: Tony Pike
pages.blurb: Hertfordshire-born, naturalised Australian hotelier who built Pikes near Sant Antoni from 1978; Wham!, Freddie Mercury and after-hours DJs.

pages.title: Marco Carola
pages.blurb: Neapolitan techno DJ and producer; founder of Zenit and other labels and of Music On, at Amnesia 2012–18 and at Pacha since 2019.

pages.title: Jamie Jones
pages.blurb: Welsh house DJ and producer behind Hot Creations and Hot Natured; RA's top DJ of 2011; Paradise at DC10 from 2012, at Amnesia since 2022.

pages.title: Solomun
pages.blurb: Bosnian-born Hamburg DJ and producer; co-founded Diynamic in 2005; Mixmag DJ of the Year 2012; Solomun +1, Pacha's Sunday night, from the mid-2010s.

pages.title: Tale Of Us
pages.blurb: Carmine Conte and Matteo Milleri, a duo formed in Milan in 2008; founders of Afterlife, in Ibiza at Space (2016), Privilege (2017) and Hï from 2018.

pages.title: Loco Dice
pages.blurb: Düsseldorf DJ and producer, ex-hip hop, on the Ibiza circuit since 2002: Circoloco at DC10, then Space, Ushuaïa, Pacha and Hï.

pages.title: Luciano
pages.blurb: Swiss-born, Chile-raised DJ and producer; Cadenza founder; Cocoon at Amnesia 2001–06, DC10 from 2006, Vagabundos at Pacha 2010–12.

pages.title: Brandon Block
pages.blurb: London DJ: co-founded Flying with Dean Thatcher in 1989; with Alex P, an early resident of Space's Sunday terrace; two Blockster hits in 1999.

pages.title: Erick Morillo
pages.blurb: New York house DJ and producer: Reel 2 Real's "I Like to Move It" (1993), Subliminal Records (1997) and Subliminal Sessions at Pacha.

pages.title: Sueño Latino — Sueño Latino
pages.blurb: Italian house of 1989 built on the opening of Manuel Göttsching's "E2-E4"; a Balearic staple, remixed in 1992 by Derrick May.

pages.title: Faithless — Insomnia
pages.blurb: Faithless's 1995 single: a minor hit at first, then a German smash, Pete Tong's Ibiza favourite and a UK number three on its 1996 reissue.

pages.title: Spiller — Groovejet (If This Ain't Love)
pages.blurb: Spiller and Sophie Ellis-Bextor's disco-house single, named after a Miami club, that beat Victoria Beckham to UK number one in August 2000.

pages.title: Art of Noise — Moments in Love
pages.blurb: Art of Noise's slow 1983 ZTT piece; Alfredo played it at dawn in a near-empty Amnesia in 1984, and it became a founding Balearic record.

pages.title: Hilltop
pages.blurb: Open-air palm-grove party ground behind Little Vagator: Sunday trance until 10pm, a festival since at least 2008, and still running in 2024.

pages.title: Nine Bar
pages.blurb: Clifftop bar at Ozran above Little Vagator that began as a tea shack; its sunset-to-10pm trance sessions drew 1,000-plus in the 1990s.

pages.title: Shiva Valley
pages.blurb: Beach shack beside Curlies at the south end of Anjuna, known for its Tuesday sundown psytrance party; opening date undocumented.

pages.title: Disco Valley
pages.blurb: Open ground at Vagator beach where some of the first organised Goa trance parties ran, c.1991–93; later used only at Christmas and New Year.

pages.title: Paradiso (Anjuna)
pages.blurb: Multi-level nightclub on the Anjuna cliffs, once billed as Goa's most popular club; Fodor's now lists the site as Nyex Beach Club.

pages.title: Curlies
pages.blurb: Beach shack at Anjuna's southern end grown into a bar, restaurant and club, known for its sunsets; in a coastal-zone demolition case since 2016.

pages.title: Goa full-moon parties
pages.blurb: Dusk-to-dawn parties on north Goa's beaches and in its woods, timed to the full moon and Christmas–New Year: bands in the 1970s, DJs from the 1980s.

pages.title: Sunburn
pages.blurb: Percept's EDM festival, first held on Candolim beach in December 2007; Vagator from 2013, Pune 2016–18, Goa again 2019–24, Mumbai in 2025.

pages.title: Ozora
pages.blurb: Week-long psytrance and arts festival at Dádpuszta near Ozora, Hungary, grown from the Solipse eclipse gathering of August 1999; annual since 2004.

pages.title: Universo Paralello
pages.blurb: New Year psytrance festival started by DJ Swarup (Juarez Petrillo) in Goiás in 2000; on Pratigi beach, Bahia, since 2003, roughly every two years.

pages.title: Rainbow Serpent
pages.blurb: Psytrance-rooted festival on open land near Lexton, Victoria, held on the Australia Day weekend from 1998; renamed Rainbow Spirit Festival in 2023.

pages.title: Laurent
pages.blurb: French DJ who, with Fred Disko, turned Goa's parties electronic around 1983, cutting European synth records into all-night cassette sets.

pages.title: Fred Disko
pages.blurb: French DJ whom Laurent credits as the first to play electronic music at Goa's parties, working from cassettes around 1983.

pages.title: Eight Finger Eddie
pages.blurb: Boston-born traveller Yertward Mazamanian, who settled at Anjuna in the mid-1960s, ran a soup kitchen and in 1975 started the Anjuna flea market.

pages.title: Man With No Name
pages.blurb: Martin Freeland's Goa trance alias: "Teleport" on Dragonfly in 1994, then UK hits for Perfecto with "Floor-Essence" and "Paint a Picture".

pages.title: Doof
pages.blurb: Nick Barber's Goa trance project, from a 1993 NovaMute EP to Dragonfly and TIP Records; his 1996 album Let's Turn On is an early psytrance touchstone.

pages.title: Tsuyoshi Suzuki
pages.blurb: Tokyo-born DJ who co-founded London's Matsuri Productions in 1994, played Return to the Source and recorded in Prana; Matsuri Digital since 2009.

pages.title: Flying Rhino
pages.blurb: London Goa and psytrance label founded in August 1994 by James Monro, Dominic Lamb and George Barker; closed 2002, back online in 2007.

pages.title: Blue Room Released
pages.blurb: London label run by Simon Ghahary from 1994 to 2002: Juno Reactor, Total Eclipse, Koxbox and X-Dream, often on lavish multi-vinyl gatefold sets.

pages.title: Matsuri Productions
pages.blurb: London Goa trance label founded in 1994 by Tsuyoshi Suzuki and John Perloff: Prana, Transwave, Koxbox.

pages.title: The Goa noise ban
pages.blurb: India's Noise Pollution Rules of 2000: loud outdoor music stops at 10pm.

pages.title: Juno Reactor — Jungle High
pages.blurb: Juno Reactor track by Ben Watkins and Johann Bley, issued as a 1997 Perfecto single with an Our House remix and an Oakenfold edit.

pages.title: Man With No Name — Teleport
pages.blurb: Martin Freeland's 1994 Goa trance track, out on Dragonfly and TIP's first compilation; Perfecto's 1996 reissue reached No. 55 in the UK.

pages.title: Astral Projection — People Can Fly
pages.blurb: Astral Projection track from the 1996 album Trust in Trance, by Tel Aviv's Avi Nissim and Lior Perlmutter; a games studio later took its name.

pages.title: Infected Mushroom — Bust a Move
pages.blurb: Opening track of Infected Mushroom's 2000 album Classical Mushroom; the Haifa duo say it was the track that introduced them to Europe's trance scene.

pages.title: Back to the Future
pages.blurb: Dave Roberts's 1989 party series, run alongside Sunrise: grain silos in Hampshire that April, then a joint festival with Sunrise at Longwick in August.

pages.title: Freedom to Party
pages.blurb: The orbital promoters' campaign against the rave crackdown and Graham Bright's bill: launched October 1989, rallies in London in January and March 1990.

pages.title: Paul Staines
pages.blurb: Libertarian who handled publicity for Tony Colston-Hayter's Sunrise parties and helped launch the Freedom to Party campaign in 1989.

pages.title: Ken Tappenden
pages.blurb: Kent Police chief superintendent who set up the Pay Party Unit and by 1989 co-ordinated the national police response to the orbital raves.

pages.title: Graham Bright
pages.blurb: Conservative MP for Luton South (1983–97) whose private member's bill became the Entertainments (Increased Penalties) Act 1990.

pages.title: Wayne Anthony
pages.blurb: Co-founder of the Genesis warehouse parties (1988–90), Freedom to Party speaker and author of the memoir Class of 88.

pages.title: The tabloids and acid house, 1988–89
pages.blurb: How the Sun went from selling smiley T-shirts in October 1988 to 'Evils of Ecstasy' a week later, and led the press campaign against the raves until 1990.

pages.title: Lil Louis — French Kiss
pages.blurb: Lil Louis's Chicago record that slows to a stop and restarts over one note; a UK No. 2 in August 1989, at the height of the orbital summer.

pages.title: D Mob — We Call It Acieed
pages.blurb: Danny D's October 1988 hit with Gary Haisman's chant: UK No. 3, on Top of the Pops on 20 October, then dropped from BBC playlists in the tabloid backlash.

pages.title: Apocalypse Now
pages.blurb: Tony Colston-Hayter's 1988 studio parties in London, sold as private events and filmed by TV news; the commercial model that became Sunrise.

pages.title: Black Box — Ride On Time
pages.blurb: Italian piano-house record on a sampled Loleatta Holloway vocal; a rave favourite before six weeks at No. 1 and the UK's best-selling single of 1989.

pages.title: WestBam
pages.blurb: Münster-born Berlin DJ and producer, co-founder of Low Spirit and Mayday, who played every Love Parade 1989–2008 and co-wrote its anthems with Dr. Motte.

pages.title: Danielle de Picciotto
pages.blurb: American-born Berlin artist and musician who co-founded the Love Parade with Dr. Motte in 1989, handling its visual side, and left it within a few years.

pages.title: Low Spirit
pages.blurb: Berlin label founded in 1985 by Westbam and four partners: home of Marusha, Members of Mayday and the Love Parade anthems, and the team behind Mayday.

pages.title: Fuckparade
pages.blurb: Berlin's yearly counter-demonstration to the Love Parade, started as the Hateparade in 1997 for gabber and hardcore; a court confirmed it as a demo in 2007.

pages.title: Rave The Planet
pages.blurb: Dr. Motte's yearly Berlin techno demonstration since 2022, run by a non-profit company, whose campaign won techno heritage status in 2024.

pages.title: Love Parade disaster, Duisburg 2010
pages.blurb: The crowd crush at the Love Parade in Duisburg on 24 July 2010 that killed 21 and ended the parade; the trial closed in 2020 without a verdict.

pages.title: Rainer Schaller
pages.blurb: Founder of the McFit gym chain, whose company Lopavent owned and ran the Love Parade from 2006, took it to the Ruhr and organised Duisburg 2010.

pages.title: Dr. Motte & Westbam — Sunshine
pages.blurb: The official anthem of the 1997 Love Parade, Dr. Motte and Westbam's first and most successful: No. 5 in Germany, on Low Spirit.

pages.title: Dr. Motte & Westbam — One World One Future
pages.blurb: The 1998 Love Parade anthem, issued as Love Parade 1998 (One World One Future) on Low Spirit/BMG; No. 6 in Germany, 14 weeks on the chart.

pages.title: Love Parades abroad
pages.blurb: The Love Parade's copies and spin-offs outside Germany, 1994–2009: Melbourne, Buenos Aires, Radio 1's Leeds parade of 2000, San Francisco, Santiago.

pages.title: 3 Phase feat. Dr. Motte — Der Klang der Familie
pages.blurb: Sven Röhrig's 1992 Tresor record with Dr. Motte, the sixth Tresor release, an early Berlin club hit listed as the 1992 Love Parade anthem.

pages.title: Pete Tong
pages.blurb: Radio 1's Friday-night dance presenter since 1991 and host of the Essential Mix since 1993; earlier a London Records A&R man who compiled early Chicago house.

pages.title: Kenny Ken
pages.blurb: London jungle DJ: original AWOL resident at the Paradise Club from 1992, winner of the first Jungle Sound Clash (1994), "Everyman", Kiss 100 show 1994–97.

pages.title: Ron Trent
pages.blurb: Chicago DJ and producer: "Altered States" (1990), made as a teenager; Prescription with Chez Damier from 1993; Future Vision; the live band WARM (2022).

pages.title: John Acquaviva
pages.blurb: Italian-born Ontario DJ who co-founded Plus 8 with Richie Hawtin (first release 1990), ran Definitive, championed Final Scratch and helped found Beatport.

pages.title: Theo Parrish
pages.blurb: Washington-born, Chicago-raised Detroit DJ and producer: trained as a sound sculptor, founded Sound Signature in 1997, known for long, EQ-heavy sets.

pages.title: Delano Smith
pages.blurb: One of Detroit's first club DJs, playing from 1978 beside Ken Collier; he left the booth in the mid-1980s and came back to make deep house on Mixmode and Sushitech.

pages.title: Claude Young
pages.blurb: Detroit second-wave DJ and producer: Dow and Utensil labels (1993), a DJ-Kicks mix, Soft Thru on Elypsia (1997), Different World; retired from DJing in 2023.

pages.title: Ian St Paul
pages.blurb: Trevor Fung's cousin and Paul Oakenfold's partner: on the 1987 Ibiza trip, then the promoter who started Future and Spectrum; later in Goa trance with TIP.

pages.title: David Morales
pages.blurb: Brooklyn DJ and remixer: the Paradise Garage at 21, the Red Zone from 1989, Def Mix with Frankie Knuckles, Grammy Remixer of the Year 1998, The Face.

pages.title: Tony Humphries
pages.blurb: Brooklyn-born DJ of the Jersey garage sound: Club Zanzibar in Newark from 1982, Kiss FM mix shows until 1994, then the first Ministry of Sound Sessions mix.

pages.title: Roger Sanchez
pages.blurb: Queens-raised house DJ and producer: Strictly Rhythm records from 1990, a Grammy-winning remix, the UK number one "Another Chance" (2001) and Release Yourself.

pages.title: Chez Damier
pages.blurb: Chicago-born deep house DJ and producer: co-founder of Detroit's Music Institute (1988), KMS label manager, then Prescription and Balance with Ron Trent.

pages.title: Kid Paul
pages.blurb: Berlin DJ Paul Schmitz-Moormann: at UFO aged thirteen, Dubmission resident with Paul van Dyk, co-producer of Energy 52's "Café del Mar" (1993).

pages.title: Simon Reynolds
pages.blurb: London-born critic whose Energy Flash (1998) is a history of rave and its offshoots, and who framed British dance music as the hardcore continuum.

pages.title: Essential Mix
pages.blurb: BBC Radio 1's weekly two-hour guest mix, devised by producer Eddie Gordon and presented by Pete Tong since the first show on 30 October 1993.

pages.title: Amsterdam Dance Event
pages.blurb: Amsterdam's five-day October conference and club festival, begun in 1996 as a trade meeting; in 2025 it drew a record 600,000 visitors to 300 venues.

pages.title: Sandwell District
pages.blurb: Techno label and collective founded in Birmingham in 2002 by Regis and Female; joined by Function and Silent Servant, it ended in 2011 and returned in 2023.

pages.title: XL Recordings
pages.blurb: London label begun in 1989 as an imprint of Beggars Banquet's Citybeat: The Prodigy, SL2 and T99 first, then Dizzee Rascal, Adele and Radiohead.

pages.title: Chain Reaction
pages.blurb: Basic Channel's Berlin sister label, 1995–2003: dub techno from Porter Ricks, Monolake, Fluxion and Vladislav Delay, its CDs packed in metal cans.

pages.title: 2 Bad Mice
pages.blurb: 2 Bad Mice: Hertford breakbeat hardcore act of Sean O'Keeffe, Simon Colebrooke and Rob Playford on Moving Shadow; "Bombscare" (1992) charted again in 1996.

pages.title: British Murder Boys
pages.blurb: Regis and Surgeon's duo, formed in 2002: industrial techno 12-inches, a staged Tokyo farewell in 2013, a 2016 return and a first studio album in 2024.

pages.title: Sound Factory
pages.blurb: Chelsea warehouse club at 530 West 27th Street (1989–95) where Junior Vasquez played all-morning sets to a ballroom crowd; the building became Twilo.

pages.title: Astroworld Festival, 2021
pages.blurb: Travis Scott's Houston festival, where a crowd surge killed ten on 5 November 2021; no indictments, and the wrongful-death suits settled by May 2024.

pages.title: Atlas Electronic
pages.blurb: Karim Mrabti's festival at Villa Janna outside Marrakech, capped at 2,000 a day, putting club DJs beside gnawa musicians; no edition after its fourth, in 2019, has been reported.

pages.title: Audioriver
pages.blurb: Poland's electronic music festival, free on the Płock beach in 2006; it moved to the Błonia in Łódź in 2024 and held its twentieth edition in 2026.

pages.title: AVA Festival
pages.blurb: Sarah McBriar's Audio Visual Arts festival and conference in Belfast, begun as a one-day event in 2014; on the Titanic Slipways in 2024 and 2026.

pages.title: Azimuth
pages.blurb: Desert festival at AlUla that began inside Winter at Tantora in March 2020 with Jean-Michel Jarre; co-organised with MDLBeast for its September 2025 edition.

pages.title: Balad Beast
pages.blurb: MDLBeast's festival in Al-Balad, Jeddah's old town and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, first held in December 2022 with a 12,000 daily cap.

pages.title: Baum Festival
pages.blurb: Bogotá techno and house festival at Corferias, begun in 2015; more than 50,000 at its eleventh edition in May 2026.

pages.title: Bestival
pages.blurb: Rob and Josie da Bank's festival at Robin Hill on the Isle of Wight from 2004, then Lulworth; Bestival Ltd went into administration in October 2018.

pages.title: The Big Chill
pages.blurb: Pete Lawrence and Katrina Larkin's ambient all-dayer of 1994 that became an August festival at Eastnor Castle; Festival Republic called off 2012 and it never returned.

pages.title: Big Day Out
pages.blurb: Ken West and Vivian Lees's touring Australian festival, whose Boiler Room was its dance stage from 1994; it was last held in 2014.

pages.title: Black & Blue
pages.blurb: Montreal's AIDS-benefit circuit festival, begun in 1991 with about 800 people, 17,000 at the Olympic Stadium in 1999; the 2023 edition was called off over funding cuts.

pages.title: Boomtown
pages.blurb: Theatrical festival-town on the Matterley Estate near Winchester since 2011; about 75,000 in 2026 and permitted to run until 2030.

pages.title: The BPM Festival
pages.blurb: Ten-day January festival in Playa del Carmen from 2008 until the shooting of 16 January 2017; then Portugal from September 2017, and later Costa Rica.

pages.title: Brave! Factory
pages.blurb: Closer's late-August festival in Kyiv, first held at the disused Metrobud train works in 2017; back from 2023, at the Dovzhenko film studios from 2024.

pages.title: Circuit Festival
pages.blurb: Barcelona's nine-day August festival of gay circuit parties, launched by Matinée Group in 2008; its seventeenth edition in 2026 expected more than 60,000.

pages.title: Coachella's Sahara and Yuma tents
pages.blurb: Coachella's dance tents in Indio: the Sahara, as old as the festival and rebuilt for 2024, and the air-conditioned Yuma, opened in 2013.

pages.title: Creamfields Buenos Aires
pages.blurb: Cream's Argentine festival, from San Isidro in 2001 to Puerto Madero and the Costanera Sur; back at Parque de la Ciudad from 2024, its eighteenth edition in November 2026.

pages.title: Cape Town Electronic Music Festival
pages.blurb: City festival of workshops and music days founded in 2012; Richie Hawtin, Black Coffee and Shangaan Electro played in 2013, and by 2017 it was held in City Hall.

pages.title: Dance Valley
pages.blurb: Daytime dance festival at Spaarnwoude near Velsen since 1995; its 2001 edition for 90,000 ended in rain and hypothermia.

pages.title: Defqon.1
pages.blurb: Q-dance's hardstyle festival, at Almere from 2003 and Biddinghuizen from 2011; over 72,000 a day; cancelled for heat in 2026, with 2027 announced.

pages.title: Distant Heat
pages.blurb: Annual electronic dance festival in Jordan's Wadi Rum desert, 2003 to 2010, drawing several thousand under a peace-through-music banner before foundering on permits.

pages.title: Djakarta Warehouse Project
pages.blurb: Ismaya Live's festival, from Jakarta's clubs in 2008 to Ancol, the Jakarta International Expo and, for 2023 and 2025, Bali.

pages.title: Electric Daisy Carnival
pages.blurb: Insomniac's carnival-themed festival: the Los Angeles Coliseum until 2010, the Las Vegas Motor Speedway from 2011, about 525,000 in 2024 by DJ Mag's count.

pages.title: Electric Forest
pages.blurb: Insomniac and Madison House's woodland festival at Rothbury, Michigan, grown from the Rothbury Festival of 2008, where jam bands share the bill with EDM.

pages.title: Electric Picnic
pages.blurb: John Reynolds's festival at Stradbally Hall, County Laois, from 2004; run by Festival Republic since 2009 and licensed for 80,000 a day by 2026.

pages.title: Electric Zoo
pages.blurb: Made Event's Labor Day festival on Randall's Island; final day cancelled after two deaths in 2013; ended after the oversold, gate-rushed weekend of 2023.

pages.title: Festival Estéreo Picnic
pages.blurb: Páramo Presenta's Bogotá festival each March, 2,300 or 2,800 in Zona F in 2010, by different counts, and 152,000 over four days in Parque Simón Bolívar in 2025.

pages.title: Field Day
pages.blurb: London park festival begun in 2007 by Tom Baker and club promoters; Broadwick-owned from 2017, it faced a KKR boycott and a Brockwell Park court case in 2025.

pages.title: Forbidden Forest
pages.blurb: Dance festival at Belvoir Castle since 2016, licensed by Melton in 2022 after bass complaints; the Arcadia Spider played its tenth edition in 2026.

pages.title: Fuji Rock Festival
pages.blurb: Smash's summer festival, at Naeba from 1999, whose covered Red Marquee ran all night with bands and DJs; 123,500 visits counted in 2026.

pages.title: Fusion Festival
pages.blurb: Kulturkosmos Müritz's sponsor-free festival on a former Soviet airfield at Lärz, tickets by lottery since 2012; about 79,000 on site in 2024, no edition in 2027.

pages.title: Glade Festival
pages.blurb: Glastonbury's Glade turned festival: Wasing Estate from 2004, the Matterley Bowl in 2009, cancelled over police costs in 2010, Houghton Hall in 2011 and 2012.

pages.title: Glastonbury Festival
pages.blurb: The festival at Worthy Farm, where dance music moved from market stalls and travellers' fields to the Pyramid Stage between 1989 and 1997; fallow in 2026.

pages.title: Global Gathering
pages.blurb: Angel Music Group's airfield festival at Long Marston, sister to Godskitchen, which toured from Miami to Malaysia; after four deaths in three years it stopped in 2015.

pages.title: HARD Summer
pages.blurb: Gary Richards's Los Angeles festival, Live Nation majority-owned from 2012; two deaths at Pomona in 2015 led to county review of large events; at Hollywood Park since 2024.

pages.title: Homelands
pages.blurb: Mean Fiddler's dance festival in the Matterley Bowl near Winchester, 1999–2005, with arenas run by club brands and more than 50,000 at its height.

pages.title: Homelands Ireland
pages.blurb: Mean Fiddler and the Pod's dance festival at Mosney, County Meath: Orbital and Underworld in September 1999, Leftfield and 35,000 in the mud in April 2000.

pages.title: Kala
pages.blurb: Week-long beach festival at Dhërmi on Albania's Ionian coast, run by the Snowboxx team since 2018, pairing long house and techno sets with live bands.

pages.title: Kappa FuturFestival
pages.blurb: Turin's July daytime techno and house festival at Parco Dora, a park on a former Michelin site; 125,000 came in 2026, and Monterrey was next.

pages.title: Kilifi New Year (Beneath the Baobabs)
pages.blurb: New Year festival on a baobab plateau near Takaungu Creek on the Kenyan coast; 4,000 tickets for its fourth edition, 2019–20, and five stages by 2024–25.

pages.title: Les Dunes Électroniques
pages.blurb: Desert festival on the Star Wars Mos Espa set near Nefta, Tunisia; more than 7,000 came in 2014, Mixmag reported, and it returned in 2019 after the 2015 attacks.

pages.title: Life Festival
pages.blurb: Irish techno and house camping festival first held in 2006, at Belvedere House outside Mullingar from 2010; it did not run there in 2024.

pages.title: Lightning in a Bottle
pages.blurb: Do LaB's California festival, grown from a birthday party into a five-day event at Buena Vista Lake in Kern County.

pages.title: Lovebox
pages.blurb: Groove Armada's festival, in Victoria Park from 2005 and Gunnersbury Park in 2018–19; a return at Dreamland, Margate, was scheduled for 29–30 May 2026.

pages.title: Magnetic Fields
pages.blurb: Wild City's festival at Alsisar Mahal in Rajasthan, December 2013 to December 2024; it moved to Khetri as Nomads in February 2026.

pages.title: Medusa Festival
pages.blurb: Beach dance festival at Cullera, south of Valencia, suspended after winds brought down part of a stage on 13 August 2022; about 185,000 in 2026.

pages.title: Melt
pages.blurb: Techno-and-indie festival held from 1999 among the mining excavators of Ferropolis; its organisers ended it after the July 2024 edition, citing rising costs.

pages.title: Moga Festival
pages.blurb: Matthieu Corosine's house festival, begun in Essaouira in 2016; from 2021 its main edition moved to Costa da Caparica, near Lisbon, with Essaouira editions alongside.

pages.title: Monegros Desert Festival
pages.blurb: The Arnau family's 22-hour desert rave outside Fraga, cancelled in 2015 over a land dispute among heirs, revived in 2022; more than 60,000 in 2026.

pages.title: Movement Torino
pages.blurb: Turin's Halloween-week techno festival, begun in 2006 by Maurizio Vitale and Luigi Mazzoleni as a cousin of Detroit's festival, mostly at Lingotto Fiere.

pages.title: Mutek
pages.blurb: Alain Mongeau's Montreal festival of electronic music and digital art, begun at Ex-Centris in 2000, with editions on four continents.

pages.title: Mysteryland
pages.blurb: ID&T's open-air festival, a roving rave from 1993 and at the former Floriade grounds in Haarlemmermeer from 2003; paused in 2026, with a new concept promised for 2027.

pages.title: Neversea
pages.blurb: Untold's beach festival on Plaja Modern in Constanța from 2017; it lost its beach in 2025 and its team moved to Kapital in Bucharest.

pages.title: Oasis Festival
pages.blurb: Marjana Jaidi's house and techno festival in Marrakech, first announced for the Fellah Hotel in September 2015; paused after its 2024 edition for a planned permanent venue.

pages.title: Parklife
pages.blurb: Sacha Lord and Sam Kandel's Manchester weekend festival, from Platt Fields in 2010 to Heaton Park in 2013; majority-owned by LN-Gaiety since 2016.

pages.title: Rhythm and Vines
pages.blurb: New Year festival at Waiohika Estate near Gisborne from 2003, a 25,000 sell-out in 2010; its December 2026 edition was billed as its last there.

pages.title: Rural
pages.blurb: Atsushi Maeda's open-air techno festival in the Japanese mountains, at Naeba Green Land in 2023 and Camp Nowhere in Fukushima from 2024.

pages.title: Sandbox Festival
pages.blurb: Red Sea house and techno festival at El Gouna, Egypt, begun by Tito El Khachab's Nacelle in 2012; about 7,000 by 2026.

pages.title: Sex Garage raid
pages.blurb: Police raid on a Montreal after-hours loft party in July 1990, called the city's Stonewall; the city and police apologised in 2017.

pages.title: Shambala Festival
pages.blurb: Independent, sponsor-free Northamptonshire festival begun in 2000 by friends with a sound system; meat and fish free since 2016; moving to employee ownership from 2026.

pages.title: Shambhala Music Festival
pages.blurb: Family-run, sponsor-free festival on the Salmo River Ranch in British Columbia, with crew-run stages, PK Sound rigs and drug checking on site since 2003.

pages.title: Skol Beats
pages.blurb: Beer-sponsored São Paulo festival at and beside the Anhembi; 59,000 came in 2006, O Globo reported.

pages.title: Soundstorm
pages.blurb: MDLBeast's government-approved December festival at Banban, north of Riyadh, first held as MDL Beast in 2019; the 2026 edition was called off in the autumn.

pages.title: Stereosonic
pages.blurb: Summer EDM festival touring Australia's capitals from Melbourne in 2007; bought by SFX in 2013, it was cancelled in 2016 after SFX's bankruptcy and never returned.

pages.title: Strichka
pages.blurb: Closer's spring festival in Kyiv's ribbon factory, begun around Nastia's birthday in 2014; a daytime festival under the wartime curfew from 2023.

pages.title: Sunwaves
pages.blurb: Minimal techno and house festival on the Romanian coast from 2007; left Romania after its 35th edition in May 2025, with a Bulgarian edition scheduled for 2026.

pages.title: Symbiosis Gathering
pages.blurb: Bosque Hrbek's Californian festival from 2005, at Woodward Reservoir near Oakdale from 2013; its team led the Oregon Eclipse Gathering in August 2017.

pages.title: The Glade (Glastonbury)
pages.blurb: Glastonbury's dance area among the trees, grown out of the Avalon field and opened in 2000; it gave its name to the Glade Festival, first held in 2004.

pages.title: The Mother
pages.blurb: Free festival planned for Corby on 7 July 1995 in defiance of the Criminal Justice Act; police scattered it, and Black Moon lost its rig under section 63.

pages.title: Time Warp Argentina, April 2016
pages.blurb: Five people died after the festival's first night at Costa Salguero; the city stopped festival permits, a judge ordered nightclubs shut, and the criminal case ran into 2020.

pages.title: Tomorrowland
pages.blurb: The Beers brothers' festival at De Schorre in Boom since 2005, about 400,000 over two weekends; its main stage burned in 2025 and was rebuilt for 2026.

pages.title: Tomorrowland Around the World
pages.blurb: Tomorrowland's online festival of 25–26 July 2020: green-screen studios on four continents, eight virtual stages and over a million viewers; repeated in July 2021.

pages.title: Tribe
pages.blurb: Du Serena's psytrance festival from São Paulo state, begun with about 50 people at New Year 2000–01; 25,000 by 2005, later at Parque Maeda in Itu.

pages.title: Ultra Music Festival
pages.blurb: Miami's March festival since 1999: Collins Park, Bayfront and Bicentennial Parks, Virginia Key in 2019, then Bayfront under a 55,000 daily cap.

pages.title: Unsound
pages.blurb: Kraków's themed festival of experimental and club music, begun in 2003 by Mat Schulz and Stephen Berkley; in 2026 split between Warsaw and Kraków for the first time.

pages.title: Untold
pages.blurb: Cluj-Napoca's August festival, opened at Cluj Arena in 2015; its organisers counted more than 500,000 people in 2026.

pages.title: UNUM
pages.blurb: Five-day, round-the-clock house, techno and minimal festival near Shëngjin on Albania's north-west coast, first held in 2019.

pages.title: Warrior's Dance
pages.blurb: The Prodigy's own festival: about 65,000 at Milton Keynes Bowl on 24 July 2010, revived in August 2026 as four shows in Dublin, Milton Keynes, Edinburgh and Manchester.

pages.title: Wonderfruit
pages.blurb: Five-day December festival of music, art and food on the Fields at Siam Country Club, Chonburi, begun in 2014; capped at about 25,000 a day by 2025.

pages.title: XXXperience
pages.blurb: Independent Brazilian festival begun by the DJs Feio and Rica Amaral in 1996 as a psytrance rave for up to 400; a multi-stage festival from 2008–09.

pages.title: YinYang Music Festival
pages.blurb: Rainbow Gao and Tommy Hendriks's festival on the Great Wall, at Huangyaguan from 2014 and Jinshanling in 2019; about 1,000 strong in 2017, announced again for 2025.

pages.title: ZoukOut
pages.blurb: Zouk's dusk-to-dawn December festival on Siloso Beach, Sentosa, from about 9,000 at the first (2000 or 2001) to around 40,000 over two days by the late 2010s.

pages.title: Afrika Bambaataa
pages.blurb: Bronx DJ, founder of the Universal Zulu Nation (1973), whose "Planet Rock" (1982) put Kraftwerk on an 808 and fixed electro.

pages.title: Alton Miller
pages.blurb: Detroit DJ and producer who co-founded the Music Institute in 1988, played its Saturday Back to Basics, and launched a Music Institute label in 2019.

pages.title: Armand Van Helden
pages.blurb: Strictly Rhythm producer whose "Professional Widow" remix and speed-garage mixes made his name; UK number one with "You Don't Know Me" (1999).

pages.title: Arthur Baker
pages.blurb: Boston-born producer of "Planet Rock" (1982), "Walking on Sunshine" and "Confusion", records made for New York's Garage and Fun House.

pages.title: London Astoria
pages.blurb: Charing Cross Road cinema turned club: The Trip's acid house in 1988, pirate and jungle raves in the 1990s, G-A-Y, then demolition for Crossrail in 2009.

pages.title: BBC Radio 1
pages.blurb: The BBC's national pop station since 1967: Peel's sessions, Pete Tong's Essential Mix, One in the Jungle, Ibiza weekends and, from 2020, a separate Radio 1 Dance service.

pages.title: Beyoncé
pages.blurb: Her house and ballroom album Renaissance (2022), with "Break My Soul" built on Big Freedia and Robin S, won the 2023 Grammy for Best Dance/Electronic Album.

pages.title: Björk
pages.blurb: Icelandic singer and producer who sang on 808 State's ex:el, made Debut with Nellee Hooper, worked with LFO's Mark Bell, and later with Arca and Jlin.

pages.title: Black Box
pages.blurb: Daniele Davoli's Italian house project: 'Ride On Time', Britain's best-selling single of 1989, and the uncredited voices of Loleatta Holloway and Martha Wash.

pages.title: BMG
pages.blurb: Bertelsmann's music arm: the 1987–2008 major behind Deconstruction, Logic and Low Spirit releases, then the rights company that bought Strictly Rhythm, RAM and Mute's catalogue.

pages.title: Boy George
pages.blurb: Culture Club's singer, who turned house DJ and producer around 1990: Jesus Loves You on More Protein, Ministry's The Annual, Angels, Café Mambo and Homelands.

pages.title: Cabaret Voltaire
pages.blurb: Sheffield industrial pioneers who moved to electro and Chicago house; Richard H. Kirk's Sweet Exorcist helped define bleep on Warp.

pages.title: Calvin Harris
pages.blurb: Dumfries-born producer: I Created Disco (2007) made on an Amiga, Rihanna's "We Found Love", 18 Months' nine top-ten singles, Las Vegas residencies, Creamfields headliner.

pages.title: Chaka Khan
pages.blurb: Singer whose "I'm Every Woman" and "Ain't Nobody" Frankie Knuckles re-edited at the Warehouse; her 1989 remix album brought in Knuckles, Morales and Humphries.

pages.title: Danny Tenaglia
pages.blurb: New York's Twilo star and Be Yourself host, a Garage-schooled marathon DJ and remixer who brought his own STAX sound system back in 2023.

pages.title: Darren Hughes
pages.blurb: Liverpool promoter who co-founded Cream in 1992, then built Home on Leicester Square and Home's Sundays at Space, the party that became We Love…

pages.title: Dave Roberts
pages.blurb: Tony Colston-Hayter's partner in Apocalypse Now and Sunrise, promoter of Back to the Future, and head of Sunrise's failed 1990 relaunch.

pages.title: Dave Seaman
pages.blurb: Leeds-born DJ and producer: Mixmag editor in the late 1980s, Shelley's in Stoke, Brothers in Rhythm with Steve Anderson, Renaissance and Global Underground mixes.

pages.title: David Guetta
pages.blurb: Paris DJ of Le Palace, Queen and Pacha's F*** Me I'm Famous whose 2009 work with the Black Eyed Peas took club sound into American pop.

pages.title: Deconstruction
pages.blurb: British dance label founded in 1987 with Mike Pickering: Black Box's "Ride on Time", M People, Robert Miles, Kylie Minogue, Dave Clarke and the Cream compilations.

pages.title: Defected
pages.blurb: Simon Dunmore's London house label (1999): Soulsearcher, Roger Sanchez, Glitterbox, Defected Croatia, and keeper of Strictly Rhythm and Classic Music.

pages.title: Depeche Mode
pages.blurb: Mute's synth band, heard by the Belleville three and Berlin techno DJs, whose songs have gone to club remixers from Kevorkian and Hardfloor to Chris Liebing.

pages.title: DJ Hell
pages.blurb: Bavarian DJ Helmut Geier, Tresor resident from 1992 and founder of International DeeJay Gigolo Records (Munich, 1996), home of electroclash.

pages.title: DJ Sneak
pages.blurb: Carlos Sosa, Puerto Rican-born Chicago house DJ: Gramaphone counter, Cajmere's Cajual and Relief labels, lyrics on Daft Punk's "Digital Love", Magnetic Recordings from 2001.

pages.title: Dubfire
pages.blurb: Ali Shirazinia: Deep Dish's Grammy-winning half, then a minimal techno DJ of SCI+TEC, Desolat, Minus and the Cocoon Heroes.

pages.title: Energy 52
pages.blurb: Berlin duo of Kid Paul and Cosmic Baby whose "Café del Mar" (Eye Q, 1993), remixed for two decades, became the template of the trance anthem.

pages.title: FFRR
pages.blurb: London Records' dance label, run by Pete Tong: Balearic Beats, 'French Kiss', Orbital's 'Chime', Goldie's Timeless; revived by Warner in 2011.

pages.title: Forgemasters
pages.blurb: Sheffield trio of Robert Gordon, Winston Hazel and Sean Maher whose "Track With No Name" (1989) was Warp's first record and the blueprint of bleep.

pages.title: Gary Numan
pages.blurb: Synthesiser pop star of 1979's "Are 'Friends' Electric?" and "Cars": played on Detroit radio, cited by Bambaataa, sampled by Basement Jaxx and Armand Van Helden.

pages.title: Gilles Peterson
pages.blurb: London DJ and broadcaster behind Acid Jazz, Talkin' Loud, Brownswood, Worldwide FM and We Out Here, on Kiss, Radio 1 and BBC 6 Music.

pages.title: Giorgio Moroder
pages.blurb: South Tyrolean producer whose Munich records with Donna Summer, above all "I Feel Love" (1977), set the sequenced template for electronic dance music.

pages.title: Grace Jones
pages.blurb: Disco singer with Tom Moulton, then the Compass Point records with Sly and Robbie; on stage at the Gallery, Le Palace, the Fridge and Amnesia.

pages.title: Happy Mondays
pages.blurb: Salford band on Factory whose Haçienda crowd, Oakenfold-produced Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches and remixes made Madchester.

pages.title: Hart Plaza
pages.blurb: Isamu Noguchi's riverfront plaza in downtown Detroit, home since May 2000 of the Detroit Electronic Music Festival, now Movement, each Memorial Day weekend.

pages.title: The Infinity Project
pages.blurb: Raja Ram and Graham Wood's Goa trance group, whose initials named TIP Records and whose "Stimuli" was its first release (1994).

pages.title: James Brown
pages.blurb: Singer and bandleader who made funk and put the groove on "the one"; his breaks, above all "Funky Drummer", fed disco, hip hop, house and rave.

pages.title: Jazzy M
pages.blurb: London DJ Michael Schiniou: Spin Offs and Vinyl Zone counters, LWR's Jacking Zone house show, the Oh-Zone label that first pressed Orbital's "Chime", Ministry of Sound resident.

pages.title: Jean-Michel Jarre
pages.blurb: French composer of Oxygène (1976) and million-strong open-air shows; a model for trance and house producers and later their collaborator.

pages.title: John Peel
pages.blurb: Radio 1 presenter from 1967 to 2004 whose sessions and late-night shows gave acid house, techno, hardcore and acid techno a national hearing.

pages.title: Josh Wink
pages.blurb: Philadelphia DJ and producer whose "Higher State of Consciousness" (1995) put a distorted 303 line in the UK top ten; co-founded Ovum Recordings with King Britt in 1994.

pages.title: Kerri Chandler
pages.blurb: New Jersey deep house producer and DJ from the Zanzibar years: the Atmosphere EP, Madhouse and Kaoz Theory, and a touring rotary mixer.

pages.title: KKR
pages.blurb: American private-equity firm: owner of Pioneer DJ in 2015–20, and from 2024 of Superstruct, whose festivals faced a 2025 artist boycott over KKR's investments.

pages.title: Kool Kat
pages.blurb: Neil Rushton's Midlands licensing label (1987), which brought Derrick May's Detroit records to Britain and turned into Network Records.

pages.title: Kraftwerk
pages.blurb: Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider's Düsseldorf group, whose machine-made records from Autobahn to Computer World fed electro in New York and techno in Detroit.

pages.title: Kylie Minogue
pages.blurb: The pop singer club producers kept remaking: Deconstruction with Brothers in Rhythm, 'Can't Get You Out of My Head', 'Slow', Disco and 'Padam Padam'.

pages.title: Larry Sherman
pages.blurb: Jukebox collector whose Bridgeport pressing plant became Trax Records, pressing much of Chicago house's first wave; the label's owner from 1984 to 2007; died in 2020.

pages.title: Lemon D
pages.blurb: Kevin King, the Brixton drum and bass producer who founded Valve Recordings with Dillinja in 1997 and built the Valve Sound System with him.

pages.title: Len Faki
pages.blurb: Stuttgart-born Berghain resident from the club's first months and founder of Figure (2003); his Rainbow Delta and Berghain 03 helped define the Berghain sound.

pages.title: Lil Louis
pages.blurb: Marvin Burns, the Chicago party DJ whose "French Kiss" (1989) stopped dead and restarted, a UK No. 2 in the orbital summer; later "Club Lonely" with Joi Cardwell.

pages.title: Madonna
pages.blurb: The pop singer who came out of Danceteria and the Funhouse, took vogue from the ballroom floor and kept hiring house, trance and electronic producers.

pages.title: Mark Broom
pages.blurb: London techno producer from the Fat Cat years: Pure Plastic with Dave Hill, records for Baby Ford's Ifach, hardgroove with Ben Sims, and Beard Man.

pages.title: Martin Garrix
pages.blurb: Dutch big-room producer of "Animals" (2013), five times DJ Mag's number one, and a headliner at Ultra, Tomorrowland, Ushuaïa and Creamfields.

pages.title: Matthias Hoffmann
pages.blurb: Frankfurt producer who co-founded Eye Q and Harthouse with Sven Väth and Heinz Roth, and was half of Cygnus X.

pages.title: Michael Jackson
pages.blurb: The Motown-bred pop singer whose Off the Wall and Thriller filled dance floors and whose 1990s singles were remixed by Knuckles, Morales, Sanchez and Masters at Work.

pages.title: Moby
pages.blurb: New York producer whose "Go" (Instinct, 1991), built on a Twin Peaks sample, reached the UK top ten; his Lomax-sampling Play (1999) sold more than 12 million.

pages.title: Moodymann
pages.blurb: Kenny Dixon Jr, Detroit DJ and producer of sample-built soulful house; founded KDJ Records in 1994 and Mahogani Music in 2002, and plays in 3 Chairs.

pages.title: Motown
pages.blurb: Berry Gordy's Detroit label (1959): Hitsville, the Funk Brothers and the soul records that fed disco, northern soul, Chicago house and Detroit techno's first generation.

pages.title: Mute Records
pages.blurb: Daniel Miller's London label (1978): Depeche Mode, Yazoo and Erasure, the post-punk line Birmingham techno grew from, and the NovaMute techno imprint.

pages.title: New Order
pages.blurb: Manchester band formed from Joy Division in 1980: "Blue Monday", Arthur Baker's New York, Technique in Ibiza, and the money behind the Haçienda.

pages.title: Nick Höppner
pages.blurb: Former Groove editor and Panorama Bar resident who conceived Berghain's label Ostgut Ton in 2005 and ran it until 2012; debut album Folk (2015).

pages.title: Nicky Siano
pages.blurb: Opened the Gallery in 1972, where Larry Levan and Frankie Knuckles learned by watching him; Studio 54 resident and co-writer of Dinosaur's 'Kiss Me Again'.

pages.title: Nightmares on Wax
pages.blurb: George Evelyn's Leeds project: "Dextrous" (1989) and "Aftermath" in Warp's bleep run, then Smokers Delight (1995); Warp's longest-serving signing, by Mixmag's account.

pages.title: NovaMute
pages.blurb: Mute Records' techno imprint (1992): Plus 8 and Tresor licences, Juno Reactor's Transmissions, Luke Slater's Freek Funk, Speedy J and Hawtin's DE9 mixes.

pages.title: Objekt
pages.blurb: TJ Hertz, Berlin-based producer and DJ: Hessle Audio and PAN records, the Dopplereffekt split Hypnagogia, Mixmag's DJ of the Year in 2018.

pages.title: Peacefrog
pages.blurb: London label of Pete Hutchison: Luke Slater, Theo Parrish's First Floor and Detroit and Chicago in the 1990s, then José González.

pages.title: Peshay
pages.blurb: London drum and bass producer Paul Pesce: "Piano Tune" on Good Looking, Metalheadz at the Blue Note and the live-jazz album Miles From Home (1999).

pages.title: Pet Shop Boys
pages.blurb: Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe's London duo: Bobby Orlando's first "West End Girls", Introspective's long house-era mixes with Frankie Knuckles, the Fridge and Flesh, Creamfields…

pages.title: Pink Floyd
pages.blurb: London rock band in dance music's prehistory: the More score that drew people to Ibiza, Alfredo's and Goa's record boxes, touring rigs, and acid house's chill-out rooms.

pages.title: Pioneer
pages.blurb: Tokyo electronics firm whose DJ division made the CDJ-500 (1994), DJM mixers and CDJ-1000 booth standards; sold to KKR in 2014–15, renamed AlphaTheta in 2020.

pages.title: Primal Scream
pages.blurb: Glasgow band whose "Loaded" (1990) and Screamadelica (1991), made with Andrew Weatherall, joined rock and acid house in the charts.

pages.title: Prince
pages.blurb: Never made house or techno, but Mojo played him in Detroit, Knuckles and Hardy in Chicago, and techno's founders took his one-man studio as their model.

pages.title: Ralphi Rosario
pages.blurb: Youngest of WBMX's Hot Mix 5 (1981), maker of "You Used to Hold Me" (1987) and, in Rosabel, a remixer with a run of US dance No. 1s.

pages.title: Red Bull Music Academy
pages.blurb: Red Bull's travelling school for producers and DJs, run by Yadastar from Berlin in 1998 until 2019, whose lectures and RBMA Daily oral histories documented dance music's founders.

pages.title: Renaat Vandepapeliere
pages.blurb: Ghent DJ and A&R man, the R of R&S Records: brought Joey Beltram to Belgium in 1989, released "Energy Flash", "Mentasm" and Aphex Twin, later signed James Blake.

pages.title: Rephlex
pages.blurb: Aphex Twin and Grant Wilson-Claridge's label, founded in Cornwall in 1991, which called its music braindance and released Squarepusher, µ-Ziq, Drexciya and Leila.

pages.title: Rob Mitchell
pages.blurb: Co-founder of Warp with Steve Beckett and Robert Gordon, first as a Division Street record shop and from 1989 as a label; died in 2001.

pages.title: Robert Armani
pages.blurb: South Side Chicago acid techno producer on Djax-Up-Beats, Dance Mania and Tresor; Hardfloor's 1993 remix of his "Circus Bells" carried him across Europe.

pages.title: Robert Owens
pages.blurb: Ohio-born singer and DJ of Fingers Inc.

pages.title: Roland
pages.blurb: Japanese instrument maker founded by Ikutaro Kakehashi in Osaka in 1972: the TR-808, TB-303 and TR-909, then Aira, Boutique and the TR-1000.

pages.title: Salsoul
pages.blurb: The Cayre brothers' New York disco label: the Salsoul Orchestra, Walter Gibbons's 1976 twelve-inch of "Ten Percent", Loleatta Holloway, and records Chicago house was built on.

pages.title: Seth Troxler
pages.blurb: Michigan-raised DJ of the Visionquest crew, first in Resident Advisor's 2012 poll, and a regular at fabric, DC10's Circoloco and festivals worldwide.

pages.title: Skrillex
pages.blurb: Sonny Moore, the Los Angeles producer who made brostep the sound of America's EDM boom, then returned to the club with Fred again.., Four Tet and Flowdan.

pages.title: Smartbar
pages.blurb: Joe Shanahan's basement club under Metro in Wrigleyville, opened in 1982 with Frankie Knuckles; home of Derrick Carter's residency and Queen!

pages.title: Sony
pages.blurb: The electronics maker whose Walkmans and DATs ran raves and Goa beaches, and the major that licensed techno in Japan, fought UR and bought Ministry of Sound.

pages.title: Soul II Soul
pages.blurb: Jazzie B's London sound system turned group: the Africa Centre and the Fridge, "Keep On Movin'" and "Back to Life" (1989), and a slower beat against acid house.

pages.title: Stardust
pages.blurb: Thomas Bangalter, Alan Braxe and Benjamin Diamond's one-off trio, and its only single, 'Music Sounds Better with You'.

pages.title: Suv
pages.blurb: Paul Southey, the fourth member of the Full Cycle crew with Roni Size, Krust and DJ Die, and a credited producer on New Forms.

pages.title: Swedish House Mafia
pages.blurb: Axwell, Steve Angello and Sebastian Ingrosso: Pacha 2010, 'Don't You Worry Child', the farewell at Ultra in 2013 and the reunion of 2018.

pages.title: Tall Paul
pages.blurb: London DJ Paul Newman: first slot at Trade, The Gallery at Turnmills, "Rock da House" (1997) and Camisra's "Let Me Show You" (1998).

pages.title: DJ Trace
pages.blurb: Duncan Hutchison, London jungle and drum and bass producer: Lucky Spin, Don FM and Kool FM, No U-Turn with Nico and Ed Rush, and co-namer of techstep.

pages.title: Vince Lawrence
pages.blurb: Comiskey Park usher on Disco Demolition Night, co-writer of 'On and On', Trax's first A&R and lyricist of 'Love Can't Turn Around'.

pages.title: Virgin Records
pages.blurb: Branson's London label: its 10 Records imprint named techno with the 1988 Detroit compilation, and it later signed Daft Punk, Photek and Frankie Knuckles.

pages.title: Warner
pages.blurb: The American major behind Eye Q's distribution, Perfecto, the Strictly Rhythm venture and FFRR's revival, later Spinnin' Records' owner and a party to the Suno suits.

pages.title: The Woodentops
pages.blurb: Rolo McGinty's London band whose "Why" Alfredo played at Amnesia, putting them into the Balearic canon.

pages.title: Yamaha
pages.blurb: The Hamamatsu instrument maker whose FM synths (the DX7, the DX100), QX and QY sequencers and SPX effects filled house and techno studios; Steinberg's owner since 2004.

pages.title: David A. Hardy
pages.blurb: Space artist who painted the first panoramic effects wheel, Space Panorama, for Orion Lighting in 1974, then wheels such as Space Ritual for Optikinetics.

pages.title: Krishna Lights
pages.blurb: Light-show firm in a Goodge Street basement that converted Rank Tutor 2 projectors to turn wheels; its staff went on to found Optikinetics and Pluto Electronics.

pages.title: The liquid wheel
pages.blurb: Slow-turning disc of sealed coloured oils, or printed or painted art, in a projector's gate: the British light show made into a product for clubs and mobile discos.

pages.title: Optikinetics
pages.blurb: British maker of the Solar 100 and Solar 250 effects projectors and their wheels, founded near Hatfield in 1970 and based in Luton; now trading as Opti.

pages.title: Orion Lighting
pages.blurb: Larry Wooden's Essex light-show firm, whose panoramic wheels began with David A. Hardy's Space Panorama in 1974; it went under in 1981.

pages.title: Pluto Electronics
pages.blurb: Effects projector and wheel maker started by Richard Millington, Rick Westlake and Micky Thompson after Krishna Lights; moved from Penge to Andover in 1976, collapsed in 1982.

pages.title: Solar 250
pages.blurb: Optikinetics' multi-effect wheel projector, launched in mid-1974; 10,000 sold by 1977 and about 70,000 by estimate; still made, now with an LED source.

pages.title: Wayne Shires
pages.blurb: London promoter and club operator: Substation in Soho, Substation South in Brixton, Crash and Area in the Vauxhall arches, East Bloc, Bloc South and Summer Rites.

pages.title: Crash, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: Wayne Shires's club in Arch 66 Goding Street, Vauxhall, modelled on New York's Tunnel; it helped draw gay clubbing south of the river.

pages.title: Area, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: Three-room club in the Vauxhall arches, opened by Wayne Shires beside Crash; later a Vauxhall weekend room and a home for Lost, it closed in the 2010s.

pages.title: Substation
pages.blurb: Wayne Shires's Soho basement club on Falconberg Court, later on Dean Street, and its Brixton sister Substation South (c. 1997–2005), home of Queer Nation.

pages.title: East Bloc
pages.blurb: Late-licence basement club at 217 City Road, Shoreditch, run by Wayne Shires and Tom Stephan; home of Dish, War and Gutterslut, later renamed Sedition.

pages.title: Roland TR-606 Drumatix
pages.blurb: Drum machine — The 303's companion, a cheap analogue drum box with a sync socket; its hi-hats are the sound of early Chicago and of acid.

pages.title: Roland TR-707
pages.blurb: Drum machine — Sampled drums in a plastic box, and the clap and snare of a hundred Chicago jack tracks, Mr. Fingers and Farley among them.

pages.title: Roland Juno-60 / Juno-106
pages.blurb: Polysynth — The warm, cheap polysynth with the chorus button, behind the pads of deep house and, per Roland, the bassline of "Can You Feel It".

pages.title: Roland Alpha Juno
pages.blurb: Polysynth — An unloved budget synth until its "WhatThe" patch of detuned saws, chorus and pitch sweep became the hoover on "Mentasm", the loudest sound in rave.

pages.title: Roland SH-101
pages.blurb: Monosynth — Arpeggiator and sequencer in a body that could be slung round the neck; a cheap bassline machine for hardcore and techno once the 303 got expensive.

pages.title: Roland Jupiter-8
pages.blurb: Polysynth — The expensive one, Duran Duran's and Frankie Goes to Hollywood's synth, sampled into house from records rather than played.

pages.title: Roland MC-202 / MC-4
pages.blurb: Sequencer — Roland's step sequencers, with notes, gates and accents typed in one at a time, the way the boxes were programmed before the computer.

pages.title: Korg MS-10 / MS-20
pages.blurb: Monosynth — The semi-modular Korg whose filter screams; Juan Atkins's first synthesiser, bought for him by his grandmother in 1979.

pages.title: Korg M1
pages.blurb: Workstation — The M1, house's piano and organ: Organ 2 is the bassline of "Show Me Love" and a decade of Italian and UK house, Piano 16' the 1990s garage piano.

pages.title: Yamaha DX7 / DX100
pages.blurb: FM synth — Digital electric piano and bells of the 80s.

pages.title: Casio CZ-5000 / CZ-101
pages.blurb: Phase-distortion synth — A Casio home keyboard whose detuned patch became the "reese": Kevin Saunderson's "Just Want Another Chance" bassline, later jungle's and drum & bass's…

pages.title: Minimoog
pages.blurb: Monosynth — Bob Moog's portable; the bass of Parliament and the lead of Kraftwerk's "Autobahn", the sound Detroit grew up on.

pages.title: ARP 2600 / Odyssey
pages.blurb: Semi-modular — The other American synth: Herbie Hancock, Stevie Wonder, and the sawtooth leads of early electro.

pages.title: E-mu Emulator / Fairlight CMI
pages.blurb: Sampler — The first samplers, priced like houses.

pages.title: E-mu SP-1200
pages.blurb: Sampling drum machine — Ten seconds of 12-bit sampling; hip-hop's machine, and the grit under early hardcore and Todd Terry's house.

pages.title: Akai S900 / S950
pages.blurb: Sampler — The first affordable rack sampler: S900s and S950s cut "Voodoo Ray" and much breakbeat hardcore after it; the S950 had the first, crude timestretch.

pages.title: Akai S1000
pages.blurb: Sampler — Stereo, CD-quality, and a timestretch that could slow a vocal without lowering it: the smear that became jungle's signature.

pages.title: Akai MPC60 / MPC3000
pages.blurb: Sampling sequencer — Roger Linn's pads and swing; hip-hop's instrument, and the swing setting that house and later UK garage borrowed for their shuffle.

pages.title: Atari ST + Cubase / Notator
pages.blurb: Computer sequencer — A home computer with MIDI sockets built in: the bedroom studio's brain from 1988 to the mid-90s, running Steinberg Cubase or C-Lab Notator with every machine…

pages.title: Funktion-One
pages.blurb: Sound system — Tony Andrews's horn-loaded system, from Turbosound: Berghain, Space, fabric's rooms, Glastonbury's stages; the sound of the 2000s and 2010s club.

pages.title: Roland JP-8000
pages.blurb: Virtual-analogue synth — The supersaw: seven detuned saws in one oscillator, and trance's lead from the late 1990s on.

pages.title: Clavia Nord Lead
pages.blurb: Virtual-analogue synth — The red keyboard from Clavia, who coined "virtual analogue": digital models of analogue circuits, the lead and stab of the late 1990s.

pages.title: Access Virus
pages.blurb: Virtual-analogue synth — A German virtual-analogue that became a studio workhorse of trance and techno from the late 1990s.

pages.title: Novation Bass Station
pages.blurb: Monosynth — Novation's first synth (1993): a cheap analogue bass box with a Wasp filter, sold as a way round the scarce TB-303 and a fixture of 1990s acid.

pages.title: Cubase VST / Logic / Pro Tools
pages.blurb: Software — Audio inside the computer: from 1996 the whole track could live on a PC or Mac, with plug-ins instead of boxes.

pages.title: FruityLoops / FL Studio
pages.blurb: Software — Image-Line's Belgian step sequencer (1997): cheap, pirated and quick, the first DAW of grime, early dubstep and EDM's bedroom stars.

pages.title: Propellerhead Reason / ReBirth
pages.blurb: Software — ReBirth (1996) put two 303s and an 808, later a 909, on a screen; Reason (2000) became a patchable rack of virtual hardware.

pages.title: Pioneer CDJ-1000
pages.blurb: CD deck — Pioneer's 2001 deck with a turntable-sized platter and Vinyl Mode became the booth standard; USB came in 2007, the networked CDJ-2000 in 2009.

pages.title: Allen & Heath Xone:92
pages.blurb: DJ mixer — Allen & Heath's four-band, twin-filter mixer (2003), grown from Richie Hawtin's MIDI-modded Xone:62; the techno booth standard before his Model 1.

pages.title: MP3, Beatport, SoundCloud
pages.blurb: Format — The record shop goes online: Discogs (2000) for the past, Beatport (2004) for new tracks as MP3s, SoundCloud (2007) for everyone's uploads.

pages.title: Elektron Machinedrum / Octatrack
pages.blurb: Hardware groovebox — Elektron's Machinedrum (2001) and Octatrack (2011): Swedish sequencer-led boxes at the heart of the 2010s hardware live set.

pages.title: Eurorack modular
pages.blurb: Modular synth — Doepfer's A-100 (1995) set the Eurorack standard; hundreds of makers later, patch cables went on stage in sets by Surgeon and Karenn.

pages.title: Roland TR-8 / TR-8S
pages.blurb: Drum machine — Roland's 2014 Aira TR-8 modelled the 808 and 909 circuits digitally for £399; the TR-8S (2018) added samples, the Boutique TR-08 shrank it.

pages.title: Behringer clones
pages.blurb: Drum machine — The RD-8, TD-3 and Model D copy the 808, 303 and Minimoog exactly for less than a night out.

pages.title: PLAYdifferently Model 1
pages.blurb: DJ mixer — Hawtin and Andy Rigby-Jones's 2016 analogue mixer: no fixed channel EQ, but Contour filters, a Sculpt band and drive.

pages.title: Boiler Room and the stream
pages.blurb: Format — Boiler Room's webcam livestream (London, 2010) made the filmed DJ set a release in itself: Dekmantel's stages, Sherelle's 2019 set, HÖR's hard techno.

pages.title: Web Audio and the browser
pages.blurb: Software — The W3C's browser audio standard (drafted 2011, Recommendation 2021).

pages.title: Daphne Oram
pages.blurb: BBC Radiophonic Workshop's first studio manager (1958) and inventor of Oramics, a machine that read sound drawn on 35mm film.

pages.title: Delia Derbyshire
pages.blurb: BBC Radiophonic Workshop composer who realised the Doctor Who theme in 1963 and co-made White Noise's An Electric Storm.

pages.title: BBC Radiophonic Workshop
pages.blurb: The BBC's electronic sound unit at Maida Vale, opened in 1958 with Daphne Oram as its first studio manager.

pages.title: Suzanne Ciani
pages.blurb: Buchla player who turned to advertising and pinball sound design, then released Seven Waves (1982).

pages.title: Laurie Spiegel
pages.blurb: Composer who made The Expanding Universe (1980) on Bell Labs' GROOVE system and wrote the Music Mouse software.

pages.title: Pauline Oliveros
pages.blurb: Tape-music pioneer and co-founder of the San Francisco Tape Music Center, who coined deep listening in 1988.

pages.title: Éliane Radigue
pages.blurb: French composer of long drone pieces on the ARP 2500 synthesiser, who died in February 2026.

pages.title: Bebe Barron
pages.blurb: With Louis Barron, scored Forbidden Planet (1956); union rules meant the film credited 'electronic tonalities' rather than music.

pages.title: Wendy Carlos — Switched-On Bach
pages.blurb: Moog album co-produced by Rachel Elkind that won three Grammys in 1970 and became a platinum seller.

pages.title: Pink Noises (Tara Rodgers)
pages.blurb: Duke University Press book of twenty-four interviews with women in electronic music and sound.

pages.title: Martha Wash
pages.blurb: Weather Girls singer whose uncredited vocals on Black Box and C+C Music Factory records led to lawsuits and settlements.

pages.title: Loleatta Holloway
pages.blurb: Gospel-trained Salsoul singer whose vocal on Love Sensation (1980) was sampled for Black Box's Ride On Time.

pages.title: Jocelyn Brown
pages.blurb: Singer of Inner Life, Incognito and Todd Terry records, and co-writer of Somebody Else's Guy (1984).

pages.title: Kym Mazelle
pages.blurb: Chicago singer credited as the First Lady of House Music; sang with Marshall Jefferson and on Soul II Soul's Missing You.

pages.title: Donna Summer
pages.blurb: Singer of Love to Love You Baby and I Feel Love, recorded in Munich with Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte.

pages.title: C+C Music Factory — Gonna Make You Sweat (Everybody Dance Now)
pages.blurb: Hot 100 No. 1 whose lead vocal was Martha Wash's, mimed in the video by Zelma Davis.

pages.title: Robin S.
pages.blurb: Singer of 'Show Me Love'; the StoneBridge remix reached No. 1 on the US dance chart in 1993.

pages.title: Robin S. — Show Me Love
pages.blurb: Failed in 1990; StoneBridge's remix reached UK No. 6 and US Hot 100 No. 5 in 1993.

pages.title: Crystal Waters
pages.blurb: Writer and singer of 'Gypsy Woman (She's Homeless)', made with the Basement Boys in 1991.

pages.title: Crystal Waters — Gypsy Woman (She's Homeless)
pages.blurb: Basement Boys production released 3 April 1991; US Hot 100 No. 8, UK No. 2.

pages.title: Adeva
pages.blurb: Church-trained singer on Cooltempo whose album Adeva!

pages.title: Ultra Naté
pages.blurb: Basement Boys singer and DJ whose 'Free' (1997) reached UK No. 4.

pages.title: Diane Charlemagne
pages.blurb: Urban Cookie Collective singer and the voice of Goldie's 'Inner City Life'.

pages.title: Liz Torres (singer)
pages.blurb: Puerto Rico-born Chicago house singer whose 'Mind Games' (1986) was played at the Paradise Garage.

pages.title: Sharon White
pages.blurb: New York DJ who became the second DJ at the Saint in 1981 and played Sahara, Studio 54 and the Paradise Garage.

pages.title: Judy Weinstein
pages.blurb: Founder of the For the Record pool (1978) and the Def Mix production and management company.

pages.title: For the Record
pages.blurb: Record pool founded by Judy Weinstein in 1978; it grew to almost 100 DJs in six months and closed in 2008.

pages.title: Def Mix Productions
pages.blurb: Weinstein's production and management company, home to Frankie Knuckles, David Morales and Satoshi Tomiie, with a Pacha residency.

pages.title: Screamin' Rachael
pages.blurb: Chicago punk vocalist who sang on Z Factor's 'Fantasy', later president of Trax Records.

pages.title: Teri Bristol
pages.blurb: Chicago house DJ and producer who, with Psycho-Bitch, ran queer nights at Crobar, Medusa and Smartbar.

pages.title: Stacey 'Hotwaxx' Hale
pages.blurb: Detroit DJ called the Godmother of House; early woman on the city's radio and founder of the Sheometry festival.

pages.title: K-Hand
pages.blurb: Kelli Hand, Detroit producer and founder of Acacia Records, named 'The First Lady of Detroit' by the city in 2017.

pages.title: DJ Minx
pages.blurb: Detroit DJ who founded Women on Wax in 1996 and made 'A Walk in the Park' (2001).

pages.title: Superjane
pages.blurb: Chicago collective of DJ Heather, Colette, Lady D and Dayhota, who say they were America's first all-woman DJ group.

pages.title: Your Sisters' House
pages.blurb: Women-led Thursday rave benefit founded by Liz Roberts in 1993, combining a dinner, a forum and a dance.

pages.title: Lisa Loud
pages.blurb: Ibiza regular and Future DJ who co-ran Loud Noise, then founded the promotions company Loud & Clear in 1991.

pages.title: Nancy Noise
pages.blurb: Co-resident with Paul Oakenfold at Future in 1988 and Lisa Loud's partner at the Loud Noise night.

pages.title: Jenni Rampling
pages.blurb: Co-founder and manager of Shoom, known for running its strict door.

pages.title: Smokin Jo
pages.blurb: Trade resident named top DJ in DJ Magazine's 1992 poll; Mixmag calls her the only woman to win it.

pages.title: Sheryl Garratt
pages.blurb: Writer at The Face, editor 1989–95 and author of Adventures in Wonderland (1999).

pages.title: Helen Mead
pages.blurb: NME and i-D writer who brought acid house into the NME and introduced Primal Scream to Andrew Weatherall.

pages.title: Mrs Wood
pages.blurb: Hardbag and hard house DJ and producer from Barnsley; 'Joanna' (1995) reached UK No. 40.

pages.title: Rachel Auburn
pages.blurb: One of the first women DJs on the London circuit; played Heaven, the Garage and Trade and later made hard house.

pages.title: Princess Julia
pages.blurb: Blitz-era club figure, DJ, stylist and writer, who played the Garage room at Heaven.

pages.title: Dread Broadcasting Corporation
pages.blurb: Ladbroke Grove pirate station from 1981, with The Ranking Miss P and DJ Camilla among its presenters.

pages.title: Dream FM (Leeds)
pages.blurb: Leeds pirate station where Rachel Fox presented as Daisy & Havoc and a good share of the DJs were women.

pages.title: DJ Flight
pages.blurb: Drum and bass DJ who began on Flex FM in 1997 and was among the first women on Rinse FM.

pages.title: Kemistry & Storm — DJ-Kicks
pages.blurb: The !K7 mix released on 25 January 1999; the first drum and bass instalment in the series.

pages.title: Mrs Wood — Joanna
pages.blurb: React Music hardbag record remixed by Tony De Vit; UK No. 40.

pages.title: Regina Baer
pages.blurb: Co-founder of Tresor and of the Kraftwerk power station, who oversaw the vault's renovation and managed Tresor from 1991 to 2005.

pages.title: Electric Indigo
pages.blurb: Susanne Kirchmayr, Vienna DJ and producer who worked at Hard Wax in Berlin and founded female:pressure in 1998.

pages.title: female:pressure
pages.blurb: International network and database of women, trans and non-binary artists in electronic music, publisher of the facts reports from 2013.

pages.title: Gudrun Gut
pages.blurb: West Berlin musician from Malaria!

pages.title: Monika Kruse
pages.blurb: DJ who began at Munich's Babalu in 1991, moved to Berlin in 1997 and founded Terminal M in 2000.

pages.title: Marusha
pages.blurb: Nuremberg-born rave DJ and presenter of Rave Satellite on Fritz, whose 1994 Somewhere Over the Rainbow was a German hit.

pages.title: Le Pulp
pages.blurb: Small lesbian-run club on the Grands Boulevards with free entry, residencies for Chloé and Jennifer Cardini, and the Kill the DJ party.

pages.title: Miss Kittin
pages.blurb: Caroline Hervé, whose records with The Hacker and Golden Boy made her an electroclash name; founded Nobody's Bizzness in 2004.

pages.title: Cassy
pages.blurb: Vienna-born DJ who moved to Berlin in 2003 and became a Panorama Bar resident with an Ostgut Ton mix.

pages.title: Annie Nightingale
pages.blurb: In 1970 the first woman to present on BBC Radio 1, a champion of acid house and rave until late 2023.

pages.title: Mary Anne Hobbs
pages.blurb: Radio 1 presenter of The Breezeblock and the 2006 Dubstep Warz special, who left the station in July 2010.

pages.title: Sister Bliss
pages.blurb: Keyboardist, producer and DJ, co-founder of Faithless and co-writer of Insomnia.

pages.title: Sonique
pages.blurb: Singer and DJ whose It Feels So Good went to UK number one in 2000 after a US breakthrough.

pages.title: Lisa Lashes
pages.blurb: Hard house and trance DJ, one of the Tidy Girls, with Ibiza residencies and a place in DJ Mag's 2000 Top 100.

pages.title: Tidy Trax
pages.blurb: Hard house and trance label of the Tidy Boys, home to the Tidy Girls and the Tidy Weekender from 2002.

pages.title: The Breezeblock
pages.blurb: Mary Anne Hobbs's BBC Radio 1 programme of experimental electronic music, begun on 17 February 1997 and renamed in 2006.

pages.title: Sarah Lockhart
pages.blurb: Founder of the FWD>> night, a driving force behind Tempa and Rinse FM's licence, and from 2020 head of A&R at Sony Music Publishing UK.

pages.title: Tempa Records
pages.blurb: Dubstep label created by Ammunition around 2000–01 that released Skream's Midnight Request Line and the Dubstep Allstars compilations.

pages.title: Naja Orashvili
pages.blurb: Georgian producer and activist, co-founder of Bassiani and Horoom, and a founding member of the White Noise Movement.

pages.title: Lynn Cosgrave
pages.blurb: Ran Ministry of Sound's club and started its label, founded TrusttheDJ, and runs the management company Safehouse.

pages.title: Mandy Parnell
pages.blurb: Mastering engineer and founder of Black Saloon Studios who has mastered Björk, Aphex Twin's Syro, Feist and The xx.

pages.title: Georgia Taglietti
pages.blurb: Joined Sónar as a volunteer in 1995, later handling press and booking; managing director of shesaid.so since 2017.

pages.title: Almudena Heredero
pages.blurb: Built Primavera Pro, directs Primavera Sound Madrid and is vice-president of MIM, the association of women in the music industry.

pages.title: Megan Perez-Carpenter
pages.blurb: Lead talent buyer for Lightning in a Bottle and the Do LaB stage at Coachella; tracks the gender mix of her bookings.

pages.title: Stephanie LaFera
pages.blurb: Head of electronic music at the talent agency WME from March 2020; founded the management company Little Empire Music.

pages.title: Andrea Parker
pages.blurb: Cellist turned producer whose Kiss My Arp (1999) came out on Mo' Wax and who later founded the electro label Touchin' Bass.

pages.title: Mira Calix
pages.blurb: Durban-born Warp artist who worked in the label's press office before releasing records and installation pieces such as an insect-sound work for the London Sinfonietta.

pages.title: Cooly G
pages.blurb: Brixton-raised producer and singer who signed to Hyperdub in 2009 and released the album Playin' Me in 2012.

pages.title: Jlin
pages.blurb: Producer from Gary, Indiana, whose Planet Mu albums Dark Energy (2015) and Black Origami (2017) took footwork into ballet and orchestral work.

pages.title: Holly Herndon
pages.blurb: Producer and Stanford PhD whose album PROTO (2019) featured an AI named Spawn trained on a Berlin choir, and who launched Holly+ in 2021.

pages.title: SOPHIE
pages.blurb: Glasgow producer whose Oil of Every Pearl's Un-Insides (2018) was Grammy-nominated and who worked with Charli XCX, Vince Staples and Madonna.

pages.title: Leila
pages.blurb: Producer born in Tehran, Björk's live mixer and sound engineer from 1994, with albums on Rephlex, XL and Warp.

pages.title: Arca
pages.blurb: Venezuelan-born producer who worked on Yeezus and Björk's Vulnicura and whose Kick series began in 2020.

pages.title: Avalon Emerson
pages.blurb: San Francisco-born DJ and producer who moved to Berlin in 2014 and now records as Avalon Emerson & the Charm.

pages.title: Saffron
pages.blurb: Bristol label and training project founded by Laura Lewis-Paul, teaching production and DJing to women and gender non-conforming people.

pages.title: Noise Manifesto
pages.blurb: Paula Temple's label, which aims for half its artists to be women or trans and released her album Edge of Everything in 2019.

pages.title: Return to Disorder
pages.blurb: Helena Hauff's label, named after her 2014 EP, whose first releases came from Children of Leir and Morah.

pages.title: FACTS (female:pressure survey)
pages.blurb: Count of women, non-binary and male acts at electronic festivals: 9.2% female in 2012, 30.0% in 2023.

pages.title: Discwoman
pages.blurb: Bushwick collective, booking agency and events platform for women, trans and genderqueer artists, founded by Hutchinson, Burgess-Olson and McCharen-Tran.

pages.title: Keychange
pages.blurb: PRS Foundation scheme launched in 2017 with a 50:50 line-up pledge for 2022; later run from Reeperbahn Festival and Brussels.

pages.title: Progressing Gender Representation in UK Dance Music
pages.blurb: Jaguar Foundation report of 3 August 2022: 5% of dance chart tracks and under 1% of top radio airplay by women or non-binary artists.

pages.title: The Konstantin interview row
pages.blurb: June 2017 Groove interview remarks by Giegling's Konstantin led to Sunfall cancelling a Giegling session and a 2018 ADE petition.

pages.title: #ForTheMusic
pages.blurb: Open letter and petition launched by the DJ Rebekah on 25 September 2020 against sexual harassment in dance music.

pages.title: SISTER
pages.blurb: Network of women and gender non-conforming electronic music professionals, grown from a Facebook group begun by TOXE and led by Lenora Thornton.

pages.title: SIREN
pages.blurb: Five-member London collective running parties, a zine, workshops and an online platform for marginalised people in nightlife.

pages.title: KNTXT
pages.blurb: Charlotte de Witte's party series, radio show and label, a label from September 2019 with Liquid Slow, made with Chris Liebing.

pages.title: Lenske
pages.blurb: Amelie Lens's own label, started in 2018 alongside her Exhale party series that began at Labyrinth Club.

pages.title: Raving George — You're Mine
pages.blurb: Charlotte de Witte's 2015 Spinnin' Records release under her male alias, shortly before she dropped the name.

pages.title: Labyrinth Club
pages.blurb: Hasselt club where Amelie Lens won a residency in 2013 and curated the Exhale nights.

pages.title: Propaganda (Moscow)
pages.blurb: Moscow club where Nina Kraviz held a regular night from 2008.

pages.title: Honey Dijon
pages.blurb: Chicago-born DJ and producer, based in New York and Berlin, whose 2017 album The Best of Both Worlds led to work on Beyoncé's Renaissance.

pages.title: The Blessed Madonna
pages.blurb: Marea Stamper, Smart Bar talent buyer, curator of the DAPHNE series (2015) and, from July 2020, The Blessed Madonna; debut album Godspeed (2024).

pages.title: Peggy Gou
pages.blurb: Incheon-born, London-trained DJ whose 2016 EP and 2023 hit Nanana made her a festival headliner; 12th in DJ Mag's 2025 poll.

pages.title: Jayda G
pages.blurb: Canadian DJ and producer whose Both of Us was Grammy-nominated in 2020; trained in environmental toxicology.

pages.title: HAAi
pages.blurb: Australian-born DJ and producer, Phonox resident from 2016 and Mute artist from 2020; album Baby, We're Ascending (2022).

pages.title: Eris Drew
pages.blurb: Perth-born DJ who first heard the Motherbeat at a Chicago rave in 1994; Smart Bar resident and, with Octo Octa, label owner.

pages.title: Octo Octa
pages.blurb: Maya Bouldry-Morrison, producer and DJ; with Eris Drew runs the label T4T LUV NRG and toured a LUV NRG sound system in 2024.

pages.title: Sama' Abdulhadi
pages.blurb: Ramallah-raised techno DJ whose 2018 Boiler Room set was the first the platform streamed from Palestine.

pages.title: Uncle Waffles
pages.blurb: Eswatini-born DJ whose Zone 6 set in Soweto went viral in 2021; played Coachella in 2023.

pages.title: DBN Gogo
pages.blurb: Mandisa Radebe, amapiano DJ and producer; Khuza Gogo (2021) went platinum and she founded Zikode Records in 2022.

pages.title: ANNA
pages.blurb: Ana Miranda, Brazilian techno DJ from Amparo; Odd Concept (2016) and Hidden Beauties (2018) took her to Europe's main rooms.

pages.title: Indira Paganotto
pages.blurb: Psy-techno DJ and ARTCORE label owner; 36th in DJ Mag's 2025 poll.

pages.title: DJ Mag Top 100 DJs 2025
pages.blurb: Announced at UNVRS Ibiza on 30 September 2025; Charlotte de Witte placed ninth, her first top-ten place.

pages.title: T4T LUV NRG
pages.blurb: Label of Eris Drew and Octo Octa, who also tour a LUV NRG sound system.

pages.title: Sheila Henderson
pages.blurb: Lifeline researcher whose interviews with women ravers produced a 1993 report and the book Ecstasy: Case Unsolved (1997).

pages.title: Lifeline (Manchester)
pages.blurb: Drugs charity whose Peanut Pete and Claire and Jose comics took harm-reduction advice to ravers in the early 1990s.

pages.title: Club Cultures (Sarah Thornton)
pages.blurb: Sarah Thornton's study of clubs and raves from 1988 to 1992, which introduced the idea of subcultural capital.

pages.title: Club Cultures and Female Subjectivity (Maria Pini)
pages.blurb: Maria Pini's book, built on women ravers' own accounts, arguing that dance culture gave women more than critics allowed.

pages.title: Hillegonda Rietveld
pages.blurb: Programmer and player in Quando Quango, Haçienda backstage manager, then author of This Is Our House and professor at London South Bank.

pages.title: Quando Quango
pages.blurb: Factory Records dance group formed by Hillegonda Rietveld and Mike Pickering; "Love Tempo" (1983) was remixed in New York.

pages.title: Beyond the Dance Floor (Rebekah Farrugia)
pages.blurb: Ethnography of DJs and producers on the American West Coast, including the Sister SF network of 1997 to 2008.

pages.title: Fiona Measham
pages.blurb: Criminologist who has researched drugs in clubs and festivals for three decades and co-founded The Loop in 2013.

pages.title: Emma Warren
pages.blurb: Founding contributor to Jockey Slut and staff writer at The Face; author of Dance Your Way Home (2023).

pages.title: Chal Ravens
pages.blurb: Journalist who co-edited FACT's website and, with Tom Lea, launched the podcast and newsletter No Tags in 2023.

pages.title: Vinca Petersen
pages.blurb: Photographer who spent about ten years travelling Europe with free-party sound systems; her book No System appeared in 1999.

pages.title: Molly Macindoe
