pages.blurb: Photographer of raves, free parties and teknivals since 1997; her book Out of Order covers 1997 to 2006.

pages.title: Good Night Out Campaign
pages.blurb: Campaign begun by Hollaback London in March 2014 that trains and accredits venues to deal with sexual harassment.

pages.title: Ask for Angela
pages.blurb: Code-word scheme devised by Hayley Crawford at Lincolnshire County Council in 2016 and adopted by venues across Britain.

pages.title: Girls Night In boycotts
pages.blurb: Student-led one-night boycotts of clubs in around forty British towns and cities in protest at spiking.

pages.title: Honest Jon's
pages.blurb: Portobello Road shop begun in a Golborne Road butcher's; James Lavelle and Gilles Peterson worked its counter, and it has run a label since 2002.

pages.title: Dub Vendor
pages.blurb: Reggae specialist that grew from a Clapham Junction market stall to shops on Lavender Hill and Ladbroke Grove, home of the Fashion Records label.

pages.title: Section 5 Records
pages.blurb: Moving Shadow's shop at 121 King's Road, Chelsea, opened in the premises Lucky Spin left and owned by Rob Playford and Steve Lyall.

pages.title: Zoom Records
pages.blurb: Camden dance shop and progressive house label where Billy Nasty, from 1989, and Dave Wesson worked the counter and compiled Cool Cuts chart lists.

pages.title: Music Power
pages.blurb: Green Lanes shop that was Kiss FM's mailing address in 1987; Nicky Power ran the Ruff, Tuff & Wicked Stuff label and an Ilford branch.

pages.title: Big Apple Records
pages.blurb: Surrey Street, Croydon shop with Artwork's studio on its second floor; Hatcha served, and its label was first to sign Skream and Benga.

pages.title: Rhythm Division
pages.blurb: Roman Road shop in Bow tied to the growth of grime, where MCs played dubplates and Wiley filmed a video; a coffee shop replaced it.

pages.title: Supertone Records
pages.blurb: Brixton reggae shop on Acre Lane run by Wally Bryan, grown from a sound system started in 1969.

pages.title: Kristina Records
pages.blurb: Opened at 44 Stoke Newington Road by Jason Spinks, Jack Rollo and Jamie Thornington; left Dalston in August 2018, reopening on Well Street in 2019.

pages.title: Lucky Seven
pages.blurb: Second-hand shop that began on Bradbury Street, Dalston, in 2004 and moved to 127 Stoke Newington Church Street in 2009 under Jason Gore.

pages.title: Love Vinyl
pages.blurb: Hackney shop at 5 Pearson Street founded by Zafar Chwodry of Reckless with Jake Holloway, Stuart Patterson and James Manero.

pages.title: Flashback Records
pages.blurb: Second-hand chain that began on Essex Road, Islington, and added Crouch End in 2006 and Shoreditch in 2014.

pages.title: Rat Records
pages.blurb: Camberwell second-hand shop at 348 Camberwell New Road, Tom Fisher's from 1999, with a queue for new stock each Saturday; it closed in June 2022.

pages.title: Crazy Beat Records
pages.blurb: Upminster shop at 87 Corbets Tey Road, open almost forty years, with classic house and UK garage among its biggest sellers.

pages.title: Piccadilly Records
pages.blurb: Manchester shop that began as a department-store record counter in Piccadilly Plaza and has traded at 53 Oldham Street since 1997.

pages.title: Vinyl Exchange
pages.blurb: Second-hand shop at 18 Oldham Street, Manchester, whose staff have included Dave Booth and Balearic Mike.

pages.title: Manchester Underground
pages.blurb: Corn Exchange basement shop opened by three former Spin Inn staff; the 1996 bomb closed its first premises.

pages.title: 3 Beat Records
pages.blurb: Liverpool dance shop that grew from a Quiggins stall into a label with number one singles; traded as 3B Records from 2009.

pages.title: 23rd Precinct
pages.blurb: Bath Street basement that Billy Kiltie turned into Glasgow's house and techno counter, and the home of the Limbo label.

pages.title: Limbo Records
pages.blurb: House label run from the 23rd Precinct shop in Glasgow; its first record was Havana's "Schtoom".

pages.title: Rubadub
pages.blurb: Glasgow shop and distributor, begun in Paisley, that imports Detroit, Chicago and New York labels and sells synthesisers at 35 Howard Street.

pages.title: Jumbo Records
pages.blurb: Leeds shop opened by the mobile-disco DJ Hunter Smith to sell reggae and soul; now at 1–3 Merrion Centre.

pages.title: Crash Records
pages.blurb: Leeds independent that opened on Woodhouse Lane and has traded at 35 The Headrow since 1987.

pages.title: The Diskery
pages.blurb: Birmingham shop opened by Morris Hunting in 1952; at 99 Bromsgrove Street from 1972, on Bristol Street by 2024.

pages.title: Hard to Find Records
pages.blurb: Birmingham mail-order business started in Jason Kirby's bedroom around 1991 to supply dance records; it held about 1.7 million records by 2012.

pages.title: Selectadisc
pages.blurb: Brian Selby's Nottingham shop, where Graeme Park bought the singles; it began on Mansfield market and closed on Market Street.

pages.title: Rooted Records
pages.blurb: Gloucester Road dance shop managed by Tom Ford (Peverelist), from which the Idle Hands label was run; it closed in 2010.

pages.title: Rounder Records
pages.blurb: Brighton Square shop and ticket outlet where Norman Cook and Skint's Damian Harris both worked; it closed on 29 July 2012.

pages.title: Underground Solu'shn
pages.blurb: Dance shop at 9 Cockburn Street, Edinburgh, started by three DJs and still selling twelve-inches and DJ equipment in 2026.

pages.title: Rock and Soul
pages.blurb: Midtown record and DJ-equipment shop opened by Shirley and Joseph Bechor in 1975 at 462 Seventh Avenue; now on West 37th Street.

pages.title: Dance Tracks
pages.blurb: East 3rd Street deep-house shop run by Stan Hatzakis, then Joe Claussell and Stefan Prescott; closed 30 November 2007.

pages.title: A-1 Record Shop
pages.blurb: Second-hand shop at 439 East 6th Street, founded by Isaac Kosman; a hip-hop producers' digging spot whose staff included Ron Morelli and Daniel Wang.

pages.title: Satellite Records
pages.blurb: Bowery shop that stocked every dance genre on twelve-inch and moved south of Houston Street about 2001; closed later that decade.

pages.title: Halcyon
pages.blurb: Shawn Schwartz's Brooklyn dance shop: Smith Street from 1999, Dumbo from 2004, beside the club Output from 2016; shut in 2020.

pages.title: Submerge and Somewhere in Detroit
pages.blurb: Underground Resistance's distributor, founded 1992, and its basement shop at 3000 East Grand Boulevard, beside the Exhibit 3000 techno museum.

pages.title: Amoeba Music
pages.blurb: Californian record shops founded on Telegraph Avenue, Berkeley, in 1990; San Francisco opened in 1997 and Hollywood in 2001.

pages.title: Vinyl Dreams (593 Haight Street)
pages.blurb: Mike Battaglia's dance shop at 593 Haight Street, the below-ground space that was Tweekin Records in the 1990s and 2000s.

pages.title: Mike Huckaby
pages.blurb: Detroit DJ and producer who managed Record Time's dance room and did its ordering, after working at Buy-Rite.

pages.title: Joe Claussell
pages.blurb: DJ who ran Dance Tracks with Stefan Prescott until 1998, founded Spiritual Life Music and was one of Body & Soul's three DJs.

pages.title: Chip E.
pages.blurb: Importes Etc. counter hand who claims the shop's "house" signs and made the Jack Trax EP with "It's House" and "Time to Jack".

pages.title: Manny Lehman
pages.blurb: Vinylmania's counter man from 1981 to 1989, who supplied Larry Levan with imports, remixed for the shop's label and later did A&R at A&M.

pages.title: Space Hall
pages.blurb: Kreuzberg shop spread over Zossener Straße 33–35, with house and techno in a dim back room joined to the rest in 2009.

pages.title: The Record Loft
pages.blurb: Christian Pannenborg's second-hand dance shop in a courtyard at Adalbertstraße 9, selling unpriced records at the lowest Discogs listing; lease cancelled 2016.

pages.title: USA Import
pages.blurb: Frie Verhelst and José Pascual's Antwerp import shop, which added a studio and label in the new beat years.

pages.title: Music Man
pages.blurb: DJ shop at Steendam 72 that sold ten thousand records a week in the 1990s; Renaat Vandepapeliere of R&S started out there.

pages.title: Technique
pages.blurb: Shibuya dance-vinyl shop at Udagawacho 33-14, popular with travelling DJs; it moved into Parco in 2020 and shut its doors in March 2022.

pages.title: Disk Union (Shibuya Club Music Shop)
pages.blurb: The Tokyo chain's club floor in the Antenna 21 building, Udagawacho, with more than 25,000 hip hop, house and techno records.

pages.title: Cisco
pages.blurb: Shibuya importer with separate techno and house shops in Udagawacho; the slope outside is still called Cisco-zaka.

pages.title: Manhattan Records
pages.blurb: Founded behind Shibuya police station in 1980; its move to Udagawacho in 1992 or 1993 drew the import shops that made the district.

pages.title: Lighthouse Records
pages.blurb: Deep house, techno and disco shop opened in Shibuya in 2008, by 2025 in a basement in Kanda-Surugadai.

pages.title: Bandcamp
pages.blurb: Direct-sale platform founded in 2008; bought by Epic Games in March 2022 and sold to Songtradr in October 2023.

pages.title: Killasan
pages.blurb: Osaka reggae sound system crew; a quarter of its club system, shipped to Berlin about 2001, became the centre of the Wax Treatment parties.

pages.title: Ata
pages.blurb: Frankfurt DJ who founded the Delirium shop with Heiko Schäfer in 1992, co-ran Ongaku, Klang Elektronik and Playhouse, and opened Robert Johnson in 1999.

pages.title: Michael Mayer
pages.blurb: Black Forest DJ who became Delirium Köln's buyer two weeks after it opened, then a partner in Kompakt; still behind its counter in 2024.

pages.title: Drexciya — Journey of the Deep Sea Dweller
pages.blurb: Four Clone compilations that put 57 Drexciya tracks from Underground Resistance, Rephlex and Submerge EPs back in print.

pages.title: Adamski
pages.blurb: Adam Tinley, who played raves live on a synthesiser and drum machine and took "Killer", with Seal, to number one in May 1990.

pages.title: Guru Josh
pages.blurb: Paul Walden, the Jersey-born keyboard player whose "Infinity" reached number five in 1990 and number three as a 2008 remix.

pages.title: N-Joi
pages.blurb: Nigel Champion and Mark Franklin's Southend duo, fronted by the singer Saffron, whose "Anthem" reached number eight on reissue in 1991.

pages.title: The Shamen
pages.blurb: Colin Angus's Aberdeen band, who toured the Synergy club night from 1989 and reached number one with "Ebeneezer Goode" in 1992.

pages.title: Utah Saints
pages.blurb: Jez Willis and Tim Garbutt, Harrogate club promoters whose sample-built singles reached the top ten and who supported U2 in stadiums.

pages.title: Seal
pages.blurb: The singer who handed Adamski's MC a demo tape at a 1989 rave and sang and co-wrote "Killer".

pages.title: Adamski — Killer
pages.blurb: Made on one synthesiser and one drum machine with Seal singing; number one for four weeks from 12 May 1990.

pages.title: Guru Josh — Infinity (1990's...
pages.blurb: The saxophone-led rave single that entered the chart in February 1990 and peaked at number five.

pages.title: The Orb — Blue Room
pages.blurb: A single just under 40 minutes long, number eight in June 1992; Guinness World Records lists it as the longest to reach the UK chart.

pages.title: Utah Saints — Something Good
pages.blurb: Built on Akai samplers and an Atari around a line from Kate Bush's "Cloudbusting"; it reached number four in 1992.

pages.title: N-Joi — Anthem
pages.blurb: Number 45 in October 1990 and number eight when reissued in April 1991.

pages.title: The Shamen — Move Any Mountain
pages.blurb: The Shamen's single that reached number four in summer 1991, weeks after Will Sinnott died during the trip to film its video.

pages.title: The Brain
pages.blurb: A 150-capacity club at 11 Wardour Street, run by Sean McLusky and Mark Wigan, whose Wednesdays were given to live house music.

pages.title: G-Mex
pages.blurb: The Manchester hall where 808 State opened for Happy Mondays in March 1990 and headlined the In Your Face Turbo Rave a year later.

pages.title: Energy – The Live Dance Concept
pages.blurb: A Docklands Arena bill of live dance acts: Adamski, Guru Josh, 808 State, the Shamen, Orbital, Snap!

pages.title: Top of the Pops
pages.blurb: The BBC chart programme, which made dance acts mime in 1990 and sing live over backing tracks from 3 October 1991.

pages.title: The KLF
pages.blurb: Bill Drummond and Jimmy Cauty's group: two UK number ones, Chill Out and The White Room, then a deleted catalogue in May 1992.

pages.title: Bill Drummond
pages.blurb: Zoo Records co-founder, manager of Echo & the Bunnymen and WEA A&R man who formed the JAMs with Jimmy Cauty in 1987.

pages.title: Jimmy Cauty
pages.blurb: Guitarist in Brilliant, co-founder of the Orb and half of the KLF, whose Stockwell squat housed the Trancentral studio.

pages.title: The Orb
pages.blurb: Alex Paterson's ambient house group, begun with Jimmy Cauty in 1988 and shaped in the chill-out room at Land of Oz.

pages.title: KLF Communications
pages.blurb: Drummond and Cauty's own label, first called The Sound of Mu(sic), which deleted its whole catalogue in May 1992.

pages.title: Ambient house
pages.blurb: Beatless or slowed house for chill-out rooms, worked out by the Orb at Heaven in 1989 and by the KLF's Chill Out.

pages.title: The Timelords — Doctorin' the Tardis
pages.blurb: The Doctor Who theme welded to Gary Glitter and the Sweet; one week at UK number one in June 1988.

pages.title: The KLF — What Time Is Love?
pages.blurb: A three-note Oberheim riff issued as a Pure Trance 12-inch in 1988, remade as stadium house in 1990 and as rock in 1992.

pages.title: The KLF — 3 a.m. Eternal
pages.blurb: A 1989 Pure Trance single remade in January 1991 as "Live at the S.S.L.": two weeks at UK number one.

pages.title: The KLF — Chill Out
pages.blurb: A 44-minute ambient collage of an imagined drive along the Gulf Coast, mixed live at Trancentral and released on 5 February 1990.

pages.title: The KLF — The White Room
pages.blurb: The 1991 album built from the stadium house remakes; it entered the UK chart at number three and stayed 46 weeks.

pages.title: The KLF featuring Tammy Wynette — Justified and Ancient
pages.blurb: Tammy Wynette's vocal, recorded in Nashville, took the KLF to number two in Britain and number 11 in the US.

pages.title: The Manual (How to Have a Number One the Easy Way)
pages.blurb: The Timelords' 1988 guide to making a number-one single with no money, written after "Doctorin' the Tardis".

pages.title: The KLF at the Brit Awards, 12 February 1992
pages.blurb: The KLF and Extreme Noise Terror open the ceremony at the Hammersmith Odeon; Drummond fires blanks and the group's exit is announced.

pages.title: K Foundation Burn a Million Quid
pages.blurb: On 23 August 1994 Drummond and Cauty burned £1 million in £50 notes in a boathouse on Jura, witnessed by Jim Reid.

pages.title: Extreme Noise Terror
pages.blurb: Ipswich hardcore band, championed by John Peel, who re-recorded "3 a.m.

pages.title: Keith Flint
pages.blurb: Dancer in The Prodigy from 1990 and its vocalist from "Firestarter" (1996); he died on 4 March 2019.

pages.title: Maxim
pages.blurb: MC and vocalist who joined The Prodigy at their first show in February 1991 and has fronted the band since 2022.

pages.title: Leeroy Thornhill
pages.blurb: Dancer from Rayne, Essex, who started The Prodigy's live act with Keith Flint and left in 2000.

pages.title: Nick Halkes
pages.blurb: Co-founder of XL Recordings who signed The Prodigy in 1990, left to start Positiva in 1993 and later managed the band.

pages.title: Richard Russell
pages.blurb: DJ and producer who joined XL Recordings as an A&R scout in 1991, charted as Kicks Like a Mule and has run it since 1996.

pages.title: The Prodigy — Out of Space
pages.blurb: The 1992 Prodigy single built on a sample of "Chase the Devil", which reached number five in the UK.

pages.title: The Prodigy — Experience
pages.blurb: The debut album, released on XL on 28 September 1992, which peaked at number 12 in the UK.

pages.title: The Prodigy — Music for the Jilted Generation
pages.blurb: The second album, released on 4 July 1994 as the Criminal Justice Bill went through Parliament; it entered the UK chart at number one.

pages.title: The Prodigy — Firestarter
pages.blurb: Keith Flint's first vocal and the band's first UK number one, with a Walter Stern video shot in a disused Underground tunnel.

pages.title: The Prodigy — The Fat of the Land
pages.blurb: The third album, released on 30 June 1997, which reached number one in Britain and the United States.

pages.title: The Prodigy — Smack My Bitch Up
pages.blurb: The 1997 single whose title and Jonas Åkerlund video drew a BBC ban, protests in the United States and two MTV awards.

pages.title: The Prodigy at Glastonbury, 27 June 1997
pages.blurb: The Friday-night Pyramid Stage headline set that Emily Eavis has called the first by a dance band at Glastonbury.

pages.title: Labrynth at the Four Aces
pages.blurb: The rave night at the former Four Aces club in Dalston where The Prodigy played their first PA in February 1991.

pages.title: Roland W-30
pages.blurb: Sampling workstation keyboard with a 16-track sequencer on which Liam Howlett made The Prodigy's demo and sequenced their first two albums.

pages.title: The Chemical Brothers
pages.blurb: Tom Rowlands and Ed Simons, the Sunday Social residents whose albums and audio-visual live show took breakbeat dance music to number one.

pages.title: Fatboy Slim
pages.blurb: Norman Cook, former Housemartins bassist, whose Skint records reached number one and whose 2002 Brighton beach show drew about 250,000 people.

pages.title: Underworld
pages.blurb: Karl Hyde and Rick Smith's group, remade with the DJ Darren Emerson around 1990, whose improvised shows and "Born Slippy .NUXX" reached far beyond clubs.

pages.title: Leftfield
pages.blurb: Neil Barnes and Paul Daley's duo, whose Leftism (1995) spent 136 weeks on the chart and whose sound system shook Brixton Academy's ceiling.

pages.title: Faithless
pages.blurb: Rollo, Sister Bliss and Maxi Jazz's group, formed in 1995, whose "Insomnia" and "God Is a DJ" were top-ten singles.

pages.title: Basement Jaxx
pages.blurb: Felix Buxton and Simon Ratcliffe, named after their Brixton club night; Remedy (1999) reached number four and they won two Brit dance awards.

pages.title: Massive Attack
pages.blurb: The Bristol group that grew out of the Wild Bunch sound system; Brit dance act winners in 1996, with a number one album in Mezzanine.

pages.title: Skint Records
pages.blurb: Damian Harris's Brighton label, begun as an imprint of Loaded Records, which released every Fatboy Slim record.

pages.title: Heavenly Sunday Social
pages.blurb: Heavenly Recordings' thirteen Sunday nights, 7 August to 30 October 1994, in the Albany's basement on Great Portland Street; the Dust Brothers were residents.

pages.title: Big Beat Boutique
pages.blurb: Norman Cook and Damian Harris's Friday night at the Concorde, begun in 1995 or 1996, which by Cook's account gave big beat its name.

pages.title: Big beat
pages.blurb: Loud breakbeats, acid lines and rock and funk samples at 100–140 bpm; a label most of the acts it was pinned on disliked.

pages.title: Big Beach Boutique II
pages.blurb: Fatboy Slim's free show on Brighton beach, planned for about 60,000 people; the BBC reported that a quarter of a million came.

pages.title: The Chemical Brothers — Setting Sun
pages.blurb: The single with Noel Gallagher that gave the Chemical Brothers their first UK number one in October 1996.

pages.title: Underworld — Born Slippy .NUXX
pages.blurb: A 1995 B-side that reached number two in July 1996 after Danny Boyle used it in Trainspotting.

pages.title: Leftfield — Leftism
pages.blurb: Leftfield's first album: number three, 136 weeks on the chart and a Mercury Prize shortlisting in 1995.

pages.title: Fatboy Slim — You've Come a Long Way, Baby
pages.blurb: Released on Skint on 19 October 1998; four weeks at number one and 100 weeks on the UK album chart.

pages.title: Glastonbury Dance Tent / Dance Village / Silver Hayes
pages.blurb: Glastonbury's dance area: a single tent from 1995, the eight-venue Dance Village from 2005 and Silver Hayes from 2013.

pages.title: Glastonbury NME Stage / Other Stage
pages.blurb: Glastonbury's second stage, the NME Stage until 1997, where Orbital headlined in 1994 and electronic acts have often topped the bill since.

pages.title: Orbital at Glastonbury, 25 June 1994
pages.blurb: Orbital's Saturday-night headline set on the NME Stage, shown live on Channel 4 and released in full by London Records in 2026.

pages.title: Orbital — Glastonbury 1994
pages.blurb: The full 1994 NME Stage set, restored from the desk tapes by Mark Ayres and released by London Records in September 2026.

pages.title: The Experimental Sound Field
pages.blurb: Tony Andrews's field at Glastonbury 1992, where Underworld, Darren Emerson and Orbital played through the weekend.

pages.title: Sugarlump
pages.blurb: London sound system that ran an acid house marquee behind a Glastonbury market stall in 1989 and a 24-hour rig in 1992.

pages.title: Lost Vagueness
pages.blurb: Roy Gurvitz's late-night area at Glastonbury, a mock Las Vegas strip of casino, ballroom and chapel that ended in 2007.

pages.title: Trash City
pages.blurb: Late-night Glastonbury area of 2007–09 with Joe Rush as art director, the first home of the NYC Downlow and Arcadia.

pages.title: Shangri-La (Glastonbury)
pages.blurb: The late-night area that replaced Lost Vagueness in Glastonbury's south-east corner in 2008, licensed until 6am.

pages.title: Arcadia
pages.blurb: Pip Rush and Bertie Cole's company, builders of the Afterburner, the 50-tonne Spider (2010) and the Dragonfly (2024) at Glastonbury.

pages.title: Block9
pages.blurb: Gideon Berger and Stephen Gallagher's design company, makers of the NYC Downlow, the London Underground, Genosys and IICON at Glastonbury.

pages.title: NYC Downlow
pages.blurb: Block9's temporary gay club at Glastonbury, first built in 2007 as a ruined New York tenement and co-produced with Horse Meat Disco.

pages.title: Malcolm Haynes
pages.blurb: Glastonbury booker who programmed the Jazz World stage from 1990 and set up the Dance Tent, Dance Village and Silver Hayes.

pages.title: Michael Eavis
pages.blurb: Dairy farmer who founded the Glastonbury Festival at Worthy Farm in 1970 and commissioned its first Dance Tent in 1995.

pages.title: Fairfield Halls
pages.blurb: Park Lane concert hall opened on 2 November 1962; Kraftwerk and Tangerine Dream played it in autumn 1975.

pages.title: The Greyhound, Croydon
pages.blurb: Park Lane venue opposite Fairfield Halls, run by Howard Bossick in the 1970s; Bowie and Roxy Music shared a bill there on 25 June 1972.

pages.title: The Black Sheep Bar
pages.blurb: High Street bar of about 250 where Sgt Pokes and Loefah worked, home of the Dub Sessions and Croydub nights.

pages.title: Swag Records
pages.blurb: Croydon shop run by Liz Edwards, with Terry Francis behind the counter, credited by him with the name tech-house.

pages.title: DJ Hatcha
pages.blurb: Terry Leonard, Big Apple's head buyer and FWD>> resident, who played Skream, Benga and Digital Mystikz's dubplates there and on Rinse FM.

pages.title: Artwork
pages.blurb: Arthur Smith, who ran the studio above Big Apple, started its label with "Red" and co-founded Magnetic Man.

pages.title: Benga
pages.blurb: Adegbenga Adejumo of Croydon, signed to Big Apple at sixteen, who later produced Katy B's "Katy on a Mission".

pages.title: Loefah
pages.blurb: Peter Livingston, from Norwood by his own account, DMZ co-founder, Black Sheep barman and founder of the Swamp 81 label in 2009.

pages.title: Plastician
pages.blurb: Chris Reed of Thornton Heath, pirate-radio, FWD>> and Rinse FM DJ and co-promoter of Croydon's Filthy Dub night.

pages.title: N-Type
pages.blurb: Mark Newton, Big Apple regular, long-serving Rinse FM presenter and founder of the Wheel & Deal label.

pages.title: Magnetic Man
pages.blurb: Skream, Benga and Artwork's live trio, whose 2010 album on Columbia reached number five in Britain.

pages.title: Mad Professor
pages.blurb: Neil Fraser, the dub producer who opened Ariwa Sounds in a Thornton Heath living room in 1979.

pages.title: Saint Etienne
pages.blurb: Bob Stanley and Pete Wiggs's group, whose first single set Neil Young's "Only Love Can Break Your Heart" to a club beat.

pages.title: Katy B — Katy on a Mission
pages.blurb: Benga-produced single on Rinse, released 22 August 2010, which reached number five in Britain.

pages.title: Tangerine Dream — Ricochet
pages.blurb: Virgin album of December 1975, its second part recorded mostly at Fairfield Halls on 23 October.

pages.title: The Rosie (Alex Rosner's mixer)
pages.blurb: Red one-off stereo mixer with level controls and a headphone cue that Alex Rosner built for Francis Grasso at the Haven.

pages.title: Bozak CMA-10-2DL
pages.blurb: Rudy Bozak's six-input rotary stereo mixer with headphone cue, the mixer at Studio 54 and the Paradise Garage.

pages.title: UREI 1620
pages.blurb: UREI's integrated-circuit successor to the Bozak, with six inputs on plug-in cards; the Paradise Garage's mixer by the mid-1980s.

pages.title: Thorens TD-124 / TD-125
pages.blurb: The TD-124 was in Alex Rosner's first club booth; its belt-drive successor of 1968 was the deck of The Loft and the Paradise Garage.

pages.title: Technics SP-10 / SL-1100
pages.blurb: The direct-drive motor unit and the $330 integrated deck that came before the SL-1200; Kool Herc's own decks were SL-1100As.

pages.title: Stanton 681 / 500AL
pages.blurb: Stanton's calibrated 681SE and tougher 500AL, sold to discos for back-cueing; over half of the cartridges named in Billboard's 1978 and 1979 disco polls.

pages.title: Ortofon Concorde
pages.blurb: One-piece cartridge and headshell launched for hi-fi in 1979; the reinforced Concorde Pro of 1984 took it into club booths.

pages.title: Richard Long's DJ crossover (RLA X3000A)
pages.blurb: Richard Long's crossover gave the DJ sub-bass and tweeter controls, as at the Paradise Garage; Rane built the X3000A for him from 1985.

pages.title: The twelve-inch single
pages.blurb: Wider groove spacing gave a louder cut with more bass; promos reached DJs in 1975 and Salsoul sold the format from May 1976.

pages.title: Francis Grasso
pages.blurb: DJ at Salvation II, the Haven and the Sanctuary who slip-cued and beat-mixed records and taught Michael Cappello and Steve D'Acquisto.

pages.title: Tom Moulton
pages.blurb: Mixer whose extended versions for Scepter and others, and a 1974 ten-inch acetate cut with spread grooves, led to the twelve-inch single.

pages.title: Rudy Bozak
pages.blurb: Loudspeaker designer who founded Bozak in 1949 and whose company made the CMA-10-2DL stereo disco mixer.

pages.title: David Mancuso
pages.blurb: Host of The Loft, who played records whole through audiophile equipment, used no DJ mixer and cued by eye.

pages.title: Alan Fierstein (Acoustilog)
pages.blurb: Acoustician who worked on the Paradise Garage's sound with Richard Long and co-wrote their 1980 AES paper on discotheque systems.

pages.title: Billboard International Disco Sourcebook
pages.blurb: Billboard's annual trade directory, whose polls of discos recorded which turntables, cartridges, mixers and headphones the booths used.

pages.title: GLI PMX 7000 / PMX 9000
pages.blurb: GLI's fader mixers with a horizontal crossfader, known as the poor man's Bozak; the PMX 9000 became a favourite of hip-hop DJs.

pages.title: Citronic SMP101 and the British disco console
pages.blurb: Dick Wadman's Wiltshire firm built consoles for the British mobile disco trade and, about 1977, the SMP101, whose crossfader Rane's Rick Jeffs called the earliest he could…

pages.title: Formula Sound PM-80 / PM-90
pages.blurb: Tony Cockell's modular club mixer with EQ on every channel, fitted at the Haçienda in the mid-1980s and reissued in 2005.

pages.title: Melos PMX-2
pages.blurb: The DMC championships' official mixer from 1990 to 1996, specified by Tony Prince with Cutmaster Swift, DJ Pogo and Mysterious K.

pages.title: Vestax PMC-05 Pro
pages.blurb: The two-channel scratch mixer Toshi Nakama developed with Shortkut, Rhettmatic, Q-Bert and Mix Master Mike, with an adjustable crossfader slope.

pages.title: Technics SH-DJ1200 / SH-EX1200
pages.blurb: Technics's scratch mixers: the ¥50,000 SH-DJ1200 with 100,000-operation faders, then the SH-EX1200 with an optical crossfader.

pages.title: Rane TTM 54 / TTM 56
pages.blurb: Rane's turntablist mixers, asked for by New York battle DJs; the TTM 56 of 2001 introduced Rick Jeffs's non-contact magnetic fader.

pages.title: Rane MP 24
pages.blurb: Rane's first DJ mixer, a crossfader desk begun at Richard Long's request, shipped from September 1986 and made until July 2006.

pages.title: Pioneer DJM-500 / DJM-600
pages.blurb: Pioneer's first mixers: four upright channels, built-in effects and an automatic BPM counter, then a sampler on the DJM-600 of 1998.

pages.title: Pioneer EFX-500
pages.blurb: Pioneer's outboard effects unit: tempo-locked beat effects on one side, a jog wheel for jet, zip and wah on the other.

pages.title: Korg Kaoss Pad
pages.blurb: Korg's effects unit played with a finger on an X–Y touch pad, with a phono input and sampling, promoted to DJs from 1999.

pages.title: Allen & Heath Xone:62
pages.blurb: Andy Rigby-Jones's Xone club mixer of 1999, with four-band EQ and two voltage-controlled filters; Fabric was an early adopter.

pages.title: Rane MP 2016 / XP 2016
pages.blurb: Rane's first rotary mixer and its isolator companion, developed from the Bozak design and numbered by mixing up the UREI's 1620.

pages.title: E&S DJR400
pages.blurb: Jerôme Barbé's hand-built portable rotary mixer, conceived with DJ Deep, Kerri Chandler and Joe Claussell; no more than a hundred a year in 2019.

pages.title: Andy Rigby-Jones
pages.blurb: Allen & Heath engineer and former DJ who designed the Xone:62, Xone:92 and Xone:V6, then the Model 1 and MasterSounds' Radius mixers.

pages.title: Denon DN-2000F
pages.blurb: Two-piece rack-mounted twin CD player with pitch bend; £851.05 in 1994, when The Mix called it something of an industry standard.

pages.title: Pioneer CDJ-500
pages.blurb: The deck Pioneer counts as its first CDJ: top-loading, with jog wheel, cue button, loop and Master Tempo; £799 in 1994.

pages.title: Pioneer CDJ-100S
pages.blurb: Slot-loading deck aimed at bedroom DJs, with three jog-wheel effects (Jet, Zip, Wah); sold for about ten years.

pages.title: Pioneer CMX-5000 / CMX-3000
pages.blurb: Pioneer's rack-mounted twin CD players; the CMX-5000's Auto Mix analysed two tracks and blended them, a precursor of sync by Pioneer's account.

pages.title: Pioneer DMP-555
pages.blurb: Short-lived deck that played MP3s from SD cards and had, by Pioneer's account, its first sync button; made for one year and eight months.

pages.title: Denon DN-S5000 / DN-S3500
pages.blurb: Tabletop CD decks with a motor-driven platter and vinyl disc; the DN-S3500 of 2005 had a direct-drive motor.

pages.title: Technics SL-DZ1200
pages.blurb: Technics's CD and SD-card deck with a ten-inch direct-drive platter, listed at $1,199.95; dropped within about four years.

pages.title: Numark CDX / HDX
pages.blurb: CD deck controlled by a real 12-inch record on a high-torque direct-drive platter; the HDX added an 80 GB hard drive.

pages.title: Pioneer DVJ-X1 / DVJ-1000
pages.blurb: DVD decks that scratched, looped and cued video in sync with sound; the DVJ-1000 was announced at $2,999 in 2006.

pages.title: Pioneer CDJ-400
pages.blurb: Compact deck announced in November 2007; by Pioneer's account the first CDJ to play MP3s from a USB stick.

pages.title: Pioneer CDJ-2000 / CDJ-2000 Nexus
pages.blurb: The 2009 deck that moved DJs to USB sticks, with a 6.1-inch screen and Pro DJ Link; the 2012 Nexus added Beat Sync.

pages.title: rekordbox
pages.blurb: Pioneer's music-preparation software, first written with Mixvibes and bundled with the CDJ-2000; analyses tempo, beat grid and waveform.

pages.title: Hedley Jones
pages.blurb: Radio engineer whose 1947 120-watt amplifier and bass-reflex boxes powered Tom the Great Sebastian; he later built for Duke Reid and for Coxsone Dodd's Studio One.

pages.title: Tom the Great Sebastian
pages.blurb: Tom Wong's Kingston sound, from 1950, with Count Machuki on the microphone and Duke Vin selecting.

pages.title: Duke Reid the Trojan
pages.blurb: Former police sergeant Duke Reid's sound, crowned King of Sounds and Blues in the mid-1950s; rival of Coxsone Dodd's Downbeat.

pages.title: Sir Coxsone's Downbeat
pages.blurb: Clement Dodd's Kingston sound, stocked with American rhythm and blues from 1953, the root of Studio One.

pages.title: Tubby's Hometown Hi-Fi
pages.blurb: King Tubby's own sound, built on his amplifiers, known for echo and reverb and for launching U-Roy; police wrecked it in 1975.

pages.title: Duke Vin the Tickler's
pages.blurb: Vincent Forbes's Ladbroke Grove sound, built in 1955 around a £4 amplifier; by BBC News's 2009 report, thought to be the first sound system at Notting Hill Carnival.

pages.title: Count Suckle Sound System
pages.blurb: Wilbert Campbell's rival to Duke Vin, from Ladbroke Grove blues dances to the Roaring Twenties and the Q Club.

pages.title: Sir Coxsone Outernational
pages.blurb: Lloyd Coxsone's London sound, by its own claim first with two 18-inch drivers in a box; dub, dubplates and lovers rock.

pages.title: Saxon Studio International
pages.blurb: Lewisham sound of Musclehead Francis and Denis Rowe; Papa Levi, Tippa Irie, Smiley Culture and fast chat, spread on cassette.

pages.title: Metro (Percival Miller)
pages.blurb: Valve-amplifier builder for Jah Shaka, Jah Tubby's and others, working from north London on 807 and KT88 valves.

pages.title: Sufferah's Hi-Fi
pages.blurb: Ladbroke Grove sound of Dennis Bovell and Matumbi: four 600-watt amplifiers and forty 18-inch drivers, as Melissa Bradshaw describes it.

pages.title: Channel One Sound System
pages.blurb: Mikey Dread and Jah T's east London roots sound, taken on from their father in 1979; at Notting Hill Carnival every year since 1983.

pages.title: Notting Hill Carnival
pages.blurb: West London's August street carnival; sound systems invited in 1973, now more than 30 static systems.

pages.title: Studio 54
pages.blurb: Steve Rubell and Ian Schrager's club in a former CBS studio at 254 West 54th Street, with a Richard Long system.

pages.title: The Levan horn
pages.blurb: Richard Long's sub-bass horn for the Paradise Garage: two 500-watt 18-inch drivers, a 28-square-foot mouth, rated to 30 Hz.

pages.title: Alan Fierstein and Acoustilog
pages.blurb: Acoustician who tuned the Paradise Garage with Richard Long and designed its four-way crossover to Acoustilog's specification.

pages.title: Court Acoustics
pages.blurb: Stephen Court's loudspeaker firm of 1973: studio monitors, rock PAs and the Black Box rig that ran Glastonbury's NME Stage in 1994.

pages.title: DiY Sound System
pages.blurb: Nottingham house collective that went to Glastonbury in 1990 without a rig, built its own, played Castlemorton from its tent and helped fund the communal Kamikaze system.

pages.title: Eskimo Noise
pages.blurb: Neil Johannessen's Elephant and Castle sound company: Nexo and Crown rigs for World Dance, Moondance and Metalheadz at the Blue Note.

pages.title: Britannia Row Productions
pages.blurb: PA hire company formed by Pink Floyd in 1975 and bought out in 1984; flew 50kW of Turbosound Flashlight at Glastonbury in 1994.

pages.title: Skan PA
pages.blurb: Hire company that has run Glastonbury's second stage since 1991, with a Court Black Box rig in 1994 and Turbosound Floodlight stock by 1995.

pages.title: Black Moon Sound System
pages.blurb: Derbyshire free-party system whose rig was seized near Corby in July 1995; SQUALL called it the first rig lost under the 1994 Act, and the legal guide Sound Advice reported it…

pages.title: All Systems and the Kamikaze rig
pages.blurb: Alliance of Midlands and northern sound systems that fought the Criminal Justice Bill and bought a communal rig that could be lost to seizure.

pages.title: Smokescreen Soundsystem
pages.blurb: Sheffield free-party house system, formed about two years after DiY, that moved to Nottingham in 1997 and kept its parties small after 1994.

pages.title: Turbosound TMS-3
pages.blurb: Tri-amped full-range PA cabinet built round a 10-inch cone and the TurboMid device; filed by Turbosound under 1978, current by 1981, over 3,000 in use by 1987 by the company's…

pages.title: Turbosound Flashlight and Floodlight
pages.blurb: Narrow-beam touring system (1989 by Andrews, 1990 by Turbosound) with a 12-inch, 6.5-inch and 1-inch high pack over 21-inch bass, and its wider 50-degree sibling.

pages.title: The Festival System
pages.blurb: Tony Andrews's pre-Turbosound festival PA: double-18 folded-horn bins, twin 10-inch Turbo mids and horn-loaded highs in separate cabinets.

pages.title: Martin Audio 215, 115 and MH212 Philishave
pages.blurb: Dave Martin's shortened RCA W bass horns and his 1978 midrange horn, the stack behind a generation of British hire rigs.

pages.title: The Acton Lane raid
pages.blurb: Easter Sunday raid in which the Territorial Support Group broke through a warehouse wall with a JCB to end a Spiral Tribe party.

pages.title: Police (Disposal of Sound Equipment) Regulations 1995
pages.blurb: Statutory instrument 1995/722: six months after a court forfeits a seized rig it is to be sold, and the proceeds go to the police authority's fund.

pages.title: John Newsham
pages.blurb: Co-founder of Turbosound and Funktion-One with Tony Andrews, and front-of-house engineer for Underworld.

pages.title: Clay Paky Golden Scan
pages.blurb: Moving-mirror scanner with a 575 W or 1,200 W HMI lamp, credited as the first light to use stepper motors.

pages.title: Martin Roboscan 1004
pages.blurb: Scanner from the Danish fog-machine maker Martin, introduced in September 1989 and built for the discotheque market.

pages.title: Sony DTC-1000ES and the backing DAT
pages.blurb: The 16-bit DAT deck that carried a rave act's backing track; the Prodigy played over one, and promoters recorded whole nights to tape.

pages.title: Le Maitre smoke machines
pages.blurb: English effects maker of the Pea Souper, Cloud Nine, Mini Mist and, from 1994, the G300 smoke machine.

pages.title: Argon and krypton display lasers
pages.blurb: Water-cooled ion lasers of up to tens of watts, run by specialist crews and split through fibre heads at the big licensed raves.

pages.title: HSE PM19 and HS(G)95: laser display guidance
pages.blurb: PM19 of December 1980 set separation distances for display lasers; HS(G)95 replaced it in October 1996 and treated audience scanning as high risk.

pages.title: The pirate FM rig
pages.blurb: A £250 transmitter in a box on a tower-block roof, an aerial, and infra-red, microwave and UHF links back to a hidden studio.

pages.title: The DTI's Radio Investigation Service
pages.blurb: The enforcement arm that raided pirate transmitters: 444 raids in 1988, 611 in 1993 and 928 in 1998, by ministers' figures.

pages.title: The tape pack
pages.blurb: Boxed sets of up to twelve cassettes of a rave's DJ sets, sold at £15 to £20; Dreamscape issued a five-pack in summer 1993.

pages.title: BT Voicebank and the party line
pages.blurb: The answerphone service whose message Sunrise updated with directions through the night; premium-rate 0839 lines followed in 1990.

pages.title: Fantazia: The Big Bang
pages.blurb: Ten-hour licensed rave at the SECC for about 12,000, documented cable by cable in Music Technology at a cost of upwards of £250,000.

pages.title: Capital Sound
pages.blurb: Hire company that flew 76 Martin Audio F2 cabinets and 54 Amcron amplifiers for Fantazia's Big Bang in 1993.

pages.title: TX magazine
pages.blurb: Pirate-radio magazine that costed a London station at about £1,500 and described its rooftop transmitters and link chains.

pages.title: Kwaito
pages.blurb: South African house slowed to about 110 bpm, with township slang vocals; the sound of the post-apartheid generation.

pages.title: Brenda Fassie
pages.blurb: Cape Town-born bubblegum singer whose 1983 'Weekend Special' was the fastest-selling record of its time, by SAHO's and the Mail & Guardian's accounts.

pages.title: Oskido
pages.blurb: Johannesburg DJ and producer who sold mix tapes on the street; Far Out and Mixdown credit him and Christos with slowing house into kwaito.

pages.title: Kalawa Jazmee Records
pages.blurb: Kwaito label founded by Oskido, Christos and Don Laka; home of Trompies, Boom Shaka and Brothers of Peace.

pages.title: Boom Shaka
pages.blurb: Kwaito group of Lebo Mathosa, Thembi Seete, Theo Nhlengethwa and Junior Sokhela, famous for a kwaito national anthem at the 1997 SAMAs.

pages.title: House Afrika Records
pages.blurb: Label that grew out of Christos and Tim White's Megatrax record shop; Vinny Da Vinci became a co-owner.

pages.title: YFM
pages.blurb: Johannesburg youth radio station, on air from 1997 with a less-talk, more-tunes format, that rode the wave of kwaito and house.

pages.title: Black Coffee
pages.blurb: Nkosinathi Maphumulo, Durban house DJ and producer whose label Soulistic Music released Culoe De Song and Zakes Bantwini.

pages.title: DJ Mujava — Township Funk
pages.blurb: Minimal house record from Atteridgeville, co-produced by DJ Spoko and snapped up by Warp; the sound its buyers called bacardi house.

pages.title: DJ Lag
pages.blurb: Clermont gqom producer whose Goon Club Allstars EPs and 2016 tour helped take the sound abroad; co-producer of Beyoncé's 'My Power'.

pages.title: Rudeboyz
pages.blurb: KwaMashu gqom group whose 2015 EP on Goon Club Allstars was many listeners' first taste of the sound.

pages.title: Babes Wodumo — Wololo
pages.blurb: Gqom single produced by Distruction Boyz; gqom's first mainstream hit in DJ Mag's words, and featured in Black Panther in 2018.

pages.title: Distruction Boyz
pages.blurb: Durban duo Que and Goldmax, producers of Babes Wodumo's 'Wololo', makers of 'Omunye' and of the 2017 album 'Gqom Is the Future'.

pages.title: Gqom Oh!
pages.blurb: Label started by the Rome-based DJ Nan Kolè, with Lerato Phiri's help in reaching the artists; it compiled 'The Sound of Durban' in 2016 and issued 'The Originators' EP in 2018.

pages.title: Kuduro
pages.blurb: Fast Angolan dance music and dance style born in Luanda's discotheques and musseques, spread by minibus taxis and burned CDs.

pages.title: Tony Amado
pages.blurb: Angolan dancer and MC who claims to have founded kuduro and released "Amba Kuduro Mamá" in 1996.

pages.title: Buraka Som Sistema
pages.blurb: Lisbon group named for Buraca, who took kuduro to clubs worldwide with M.I.A.

pages.title: Enchufada
pages.blurb: Lisbon label founded in 2006 by Buraka Som Sistema to release their records and kuduro-related club music.

pages.title: Príncipe Discos
pages.blurb: Lisbon label that releases batida from the city's outer neighbourhoods and runs the monthly Noite Príncipe night.

pages.title: Batida
pages.blurb: Stripped, percussive Lisbon club music from Afro-Portuguese estates, built on kuduro, kizomba, funaná and tarraxinha.

pages.title: DJ Marfox
pages.blurb: Lisbon DJ and producer whose Eu Sei Quem Sou (2011) launched Príncipe Discos; later released on Warp.

pages.title: Nídia
pages.blurb: Producer from Vale da Amoreira whose 2017 album Nídia é Má, Nídia é Fudida made Rolling Stone's electronic top twenty.

pages.title: Noite Príncipe
pages.blurb: Príncipe's monthly night at Musicbox in Cais do Sodré, which brought bairro DJs to a central club sound system.

pages.title: DJ Marlboro
pages.blurb: Rio DJ who brought Miami bass to the bailes, released Funk Brasil in 1989 and built the Big Mix company.

pages.title: DJ Marlboro — Funk Brasil
pages.blurb: DJ Marlboro's 1989 LP, which Billboard Brasil says sped the bailes' move from imported records to songs composed in Rio.

pages.title: Furacão 2000
pages.blurb: Rio sound system and producer, merged from Som 2000 and Guarani 2000, behind the Tornado Muito Nervoso compilations and Gaiola das Popozudas.

pages.title: Tamborzão
pages.blurb: The Afro-Brazilian drum pattern that RBMA Daily and Sounds and Colours credit to DJ Luciano Oliveira in 1998; it dominated Rio funk until about 2010.

pages.title: Proibidão
pages.blurb: The explicit, 'forbidden' strand of funk carioca; RBMA Daily names Rap das Armas (1995) as the first song officially called proibido.

pages.title: Funk ostentação
pages.blurb: São Paulo funk about cars, brands and money, dating from Bonde da Juju in 2008 and spread by KondZilla's videos.

pages.title: DJ Rennan da Penha
pages.blurb: Founder of Baile da Gaiola, jailed from April to November 2019 and acquitted by the STJ in June 2023.

pages.title: Paraisópolis, 1 December 2019
pages.blurb: Nine people aged 14 to 23 died during a military police operation at the Baile da DZ7.

pages.title: Mamba Negra
pages.blurb: Party collective founded in May 2013 by Cashu and Laura Diaz, staging nights in abandoned buildings across São Paulo.

pages.title: D-Edge
pages.blurb: Club founded by Renato Ratier in Campo Grande in 2000, opened in Barra Funda, São Paulo, on 28 April 2003.

pages.title: Hernán Cattáneo
pages.blurb: Argentine progressive house DJ, resident at Clubland Pachá from 1996 and founder of the Sudbeat label.

pages.title: ZZK Records
pages.blurb: Label of digital cumbia that grew out of the Zizek club nights begun by El G, DJ Nim and Villa Diamante.

pages.title: N.A.A.F.I
pages.blurb: Mexico City party crew and label founded by Tomás Davó and Alberto Bustamante, first night July 2010.

pages.title: MDLBeast
pages.blurb: Saudi music company formed in 2019 that runs Soundstorm, XP Music Futures, Balad Beast and a record label, with government and private funding.

pages.title: XP Music Futures
pages.blurb: MDLBeast's music-industry conference, first held at Jax in Riyadh on 13–15 December 2021, the three days before Soundstorm.

pages.title: Cosmicat
pages.blurb: Nouf Sufyani, a Jeddah DJ and producer who trained as a dentist, played her first gig in 2018 and released the Dilemma EP in 2020.

pages.title: Dish Dash
pages.blurb: Jeddah brothers Hassan and Abbas Ghazzawi, who came up through private and compound parties and have played Soundstorm since 2019.

pages.title: Vinyl Mode
pages.blurb: Mohannad Nassar, a Jeddah DJ since 2005; The National called him the first local artist to headline Soundstorm's Big Beast stage, in December 2021.

pages.title: Baloo
pages.blurb: Ahmad Alammary, a Riyadh house DJ since 1997, head of Gabu Records and chief creative officer of MDLBeast.

pages.title: Riyadh
pages.blurb: Saudi capital where a small private-party circuit of the 1990s gave way after 2019 to Soundstorm at Banban and the XP conference at Jax.

pages.title: Jeddah
pages.blurb: Red Sea port, home of Cosmicat, Dish Dash and Vinyl Mode; site of the January 2017 Mohammed Abdo concert and of Balad Beast.

pages.title: Dubai
pages.blurb: Gulf city whose clubs sit in licensed hotels: the Lodge and Cyclone in 1997, Peppermint and Trilogy in the 2000s, WHITE at Meydan from 2013.

pages.title: WHITE Dubai
pages.blurb: Club at Meydan run by Addmind, holding about 2,000, with a top-20 DJ Mag placing; a seated dinner venue under Covid rules by November 2020.

pages.title: Analog Room
pages.blurb: Dubai club night founded by the Iranian promoter Mehdi Ansari, which booked only local performers for a year and brought Mutek to the city.

pages.title: Soundscapes
pages.blurb: Bahraini pop-up party series founded in 2015, with no table service or sponsors, drawing 500 people or more by 2019.

pages.title: Kalibr+
pages.blurb: Kuwaiti label and loose collective with more than 200 tracks released by July 2020, working where public shows are hard to stage.

pages.title: Escape from Samsara
pages.blurb: Hard trance night at the Fridge in Brixton, started by Tim Samsara and a partner, Richard: monthly from September 1995, every Friday from May 1997 to 2002, with reunions from 2006.

pages.title: Megatripolis
pages.blurb: Fraser Clark's Thursday club at Heaven: trance and ambient rooms, market stalls and a talk room where McKenna, Ginsberg and Leary appeared.

pages.title: Megadog
pages.blurb: Monthly all-nighter at the Rocket on Holloway Road and a touring show of live electronic acts, DJs, lights and circus, grown from Club Dog.

pages.title: Club Dog
pages.blurb: Weekly Friday of psychedelic bands, films and light shows in Wood Green and then at the Sir George Robey, Finsbury Park; the root of Megadog.

pages.title: Whirl-Y-Gig
pages.blurb: All-ages world and dance club begun by Ros Madden in 1981 and run since the mid-1980s by DJ Monkey Pilot and Mary Sutcliffe.

pages.title: Fraser Clark
pages.blurb: Founder of Encyclopedia Psychedelica, champion of the 'zippie' and founder of Megatripolis; he died on 21 January 2009.

pages.title: Michael Dog
pages.blurb: DJ and promoter who with Bob Dog ran Club Dog, Megadog and the Planet Dog label.

pages.title: Monkey Pilot
pages.blurb: Richard Sutcliffe, Whirl-Y-Gig's DJ since 1983 and an early Club Dog resident, whose sound system travelled in a hearse.

pages.title: Planet Dog
pages.blurb: Megadog's label, home of Eat Static, Banco de Gaia, Timeshard and Children of the Bong; its catalogue went into receivership in 1999.

pages.title: Megadog Midi Circus
pages.blurb: Megadog's summer 1993 tour of Orbital, the Drum Club and Aphex Twin, which Michael Dog calls Britain's first live electronic music tour.

pages.title: Lab 4
pages.blurb: Hard trance live act of Les Elston and Adam Newman, regulars at Escape from Samsara; their first album, Neurocide, came out in 1999.

pages.title: Mixmaster Morris
pages.blurb: Ambient DJ who played Megatripolis's first night, often played all night in its Sound Shaft room and toured with the Midi Circus.

pages.title: The Rocket
pages.blurb: Holloway Road venue that housed Megadog's monthly all-nighter and a Return to the Source residency.

pages.title: Cyberdog
pages.blurb: Camden clubwear business begun by Terry Davy and Spiros Vlahos as a market stall playing psychedelic trance.

pages.title: Transient Records
pages.blurb: London trance label set up by Disco Volante; it released Otherworld's compilation Dance, Trance & Magic Plants in 1997.

pages.title: Happy Days
pages.blurb: Timi Ram Jam's Sunday afterparty for Ministry of Sound clubbers, which moved from a pub to the Frog & Nightgown and the Arches.

pages.title: Twice as Nice
pages.blurb: Garage night where DJ Spoony was resident for more than seven years; it banned trainers, jeans and baseball caps and in time installed a metal detector to screen for guns.

pages.title: Tuff Jam
pages.blurb: DJ and production duo Matt Jam Lamont and Karl Tuff Enuff Brown, Kiss presenters from 1997 to 2000 and central figures in underground garage.

pages.title: Dreem Teem
pages.blurb: DJ Spoony, Mikee B and Timmi Magic, who met on the pirate London Underground, took garage to Kiss and Galaxy FM and joined BBC Radio 1 in January 2000.

pages.title: Todd Edwards
pages.blurb: New Jersey producer whose chopped, triplet-swung vocal style was pitched up by London DJs and became a blueprint for UK garage.

pages.title: Ayia Napa
pages.blurb: Cypriot resort whose clubs, from Black & White in 1985, became the summer home of UK garage until restrictions in 2002.

pages.title: So Solid Crew
pages.blurb: South London collective of up to 30 members whose "21 Seconds" reached number one in August 2001 and drew a political and police backlash.

pages.title: Ms Dynamite
pages.blurb: MC and singer who began over garage beats at seventeen and won the 2002 Mercury Prize for A Little Deeper.

pages.title: MJ Cole — Sincere
pages.blurb: Matt Coleman's Metrix Recordings 2-step record, made in a Twickenham bedroom on an Atari ST and an MPC3000XL.

pages.title: Pay As U Go
pages.blurb: Rinse FM garage crew of Wiley, Maxwell D, Carl and DJ Target, from which Roll Deep grew; their "Champagne Dance" reached number 13.

pages.title: Wiley
pages.blurb: Rinse FM MC and producer behind "Eskimo" and eskibeat, a founding member of Pay As U Go, and later of Roll Deep.

pages.title: Dizzee Rascal
pages.blurb: Bow MC and producer whose Boy in da Corner (2003) won the Mercury Prize when he was 19, then crossed to pop number ones.

pages.title: Lord of the Mics
pages.blurb: Jammer's filmed MC clash series, begun in his basement with Wiley against Kano and released on DVD.

pages.title: Boy Better Know
pages.blurb: Independent label and crew founded by brothers Skepta and Jme Adenuga in north London.

pages.title: Skepta
pages.blurb: MC and producer whose Konnichiwa (2016) reached number two and won the Mercury Prize.

pages.title: Stormzy
pages.blurb: MC whose Gang Signs & Prayer (2017) was, as The FADER reported, the first independently released grime album to top the chart, and who headlined Glastonbury in 2019.

pages.title: Plastic People
pages.blurb: The small Shoreditch club on Curtain Road, with a much-praised sound system, that housed FWD>> and closed in January 2015.

pages.title: FWD>>
pages.blurb: The night begun at the Velvet Rooms in Soho in 2001 by Sarah Lockhart and Ammunition, later at Plastic People in Shoreditch.

pages.title: DMZ
pages.blurb: Mala, Coki, Loefah and Sgt Pokes's night in Third Base and Mass, the club in St Matthew's Church, Brixton.

pages.title: Digital Mystikz
pages.blurb: Mala and Coki, the Brixton-based producers who ran DMZ and made Anti War Dub.

pages.title: Skream
pages.blurb: Croydon producer whose Midnight Request Line and remix work took dubstep to the charts, and a founder of Magnetic Man.

pages.title: Kode9
pages.blurb: Steve Goodman, who founded Hyperdub and hosted the FWD>> show on Rinse FM.

pages.title: Burial
pages.blurb: South London producer William Bevan, Hyperdub's first signing, whose Untrue was nominated for the Mercury Prize in 2008.

pages.title: Hyperdub
pages.blurb: Kode9's label, begun as a webzine, home to Burial, Cooly G, Ikonika and Laurel Halo.

pages.title: Dubstep Warz
pages.blurb: Mary Anne Hobbs's BBC Radio 1 Breezeblock special that took dubstep to a national audience.

pages.title: Niche
pages.blurb: Steve Baxendale's Sidney Street club, the birthplace of bassline, raided in 2005 and closed for good by 2011.

pages.title: Bassline
pages.blurb: Speed-garage-derived sound from Sheffield's Niche, reaching number two in 2007 with T2's Heartbroken and revived in the 2020s.

pages.title: UK funky
pages.blurb: Roughly 130 bpm London sound spread by Rinse FM and Deja Vu, with the Crazy Cousinz remix of Do You Mind as its defining record.

pages.title: Hessle Audio
pages.blurb: Label of Ben UFO, Pangaea and Pearson Sound, central to the post-dubstep years.

pages.title: Night Slugs
pages.blurb: Club night and label begun by Bok Bok and L-Vis 1990 at the Redstar, Camberwell, in March 2008.

pages.title: Dub War
pages.blurb: Dave Q and Joe Nice's night, the first dubstep night in the United States, begun in a Bed-Stuy basement.

pages.title: 2 Live Crew
pages.blurb: Miami group whose 1989 album As Nasty as They Wanna Be was ruled obscene in 1990 and cleared on appeal in 1992.

pages.title: Luther Campbell (Uncle Luke)
pages.blurb: Promoter, manager and Luke Records founder who ran Pac Jam and the Ghetto Style DJs.

pages.title: Mr. Mixx
pages.blurb: 2 Live Crew's DJ and producer, who bought a Roland TR-808 in a pawnshop for $300 around 1984.

pages.title: Pac Jam
pages.blurb: Luke Campbell's teen club in Miami, later the base of Luke Skyywalker Records.

pages.title: 2 Live Crew — Throw the D
pages.blurb: January 1986 single that set a blueprint for later Miami bass records.

pages.title: 2 Live Crew — As Nasty as They Wanna Be
pages.blurb: Platinum album of 7 February 1989, ruled obscene in 1990 and cleared on appeal in 1992.

pages.title: DJ Magic Mike
pages.blurb: Orlando DJ and producer of car audio bass records, whose Royal Posse debut went platinum in 1989.

pages.title: Miami bass
pages.blurb: Booty-shaking party rap built on 808 drums and a long kick, from South Florida.

pages.title: New Orleans bounce
pages.blurb: Call-and-response party rap built on the Triggerman beat, sampled from the Showboys' Drag Rap.

pages.title: Big Freedia
pages.blurb: Bounce performer who began as a backup dancer and singer in Katey Red's shows around 1998 and appeared on Beyoncé's Break My Soul.

pages.title: Katey Red
pages.blurb: Bounce artist born in the Melpomene projects, credited with starting the style the press called sissy bounce.

pages.title: Dance Mania
pages.blurb: Ray Barney's Chicago label, grown from a record distributor, that issued the first ghetto house records and carried them to Europe.

pages.title: Ray Barney
pages.blurb: Chicago distributor and founder of Dance Mania, who took in the tracks the city's South and West Side DJs brought to his office.

pages.title: DJ Deeon
pages.blurb: South Side ghetto house pioneer who sold mixtapes from his sister's building, recorded for Dance Mania and died in July 2023, aged 56.

pages.title: DJ Funk
pages.blurb: Charles Chambers, who funded his first record by selling his waterbed and car, and is credited with the phrase ghetto house.

pages.title: RP Boo
pages.blurb: Kavain Space, Chicago producer and House-O-Matics DJ whose 1997 Dance Mania white label 'Baby Come On' is usually called the first footwork track.

pages.title: DJ Rashad
pages.blurb: Teklife co-founder whose Hyperdub album Double Cup (2013) brought footwork to a wide audience; he died on 26 April 2014.

pages.title: Teklife
pages.blurb: Footwork crew founded by DJ Rashad and DJ Spinn as Ghettoteknitianz, with members from Chicago to London and Belgrade, and a label from 2015.

pages.title: Planet Mu
pages.blurb: Mike Paradinas's label, which issued DJ Nate, DJ Roc and the Bangs & Works compilations from 2010.

pages.title: DJ Rashad — Double Cup
pages.blurb: Hyperdub album released in October 2013, made over seven or eight months in Chicago and San Francisco, and reissued by Partisan for its tenth anniversary.

pages.title: Footwork
pages.blurb: Chicago dance-battle music at about 155–160bpm, grown from ghetto house and juke, danced in circles and built on chopped vocal samples.

pages.title: DJ Assault
pages.blurb: Craig Adams, Detroit booty-music DJ and producer behind 'Ass N Titties', who toured Britain on Mo' Wax's Booty Wax label in 2000.

pages.title: DJ Godfather
pages.blurb: Brian Jeffries, who ran Databass and Twilight 76 and played in Germany, Puerto Rico and Brazil in the late 1990s.

pages.title: The Outcast
pages.blurb: Motorcycle club that held about 2,500 people from 2 a.m.

pages.title: Disco D
pages.blurb: David Shayman, Ann Arbor producer credited with shortening ghettotechno to ghettotech, who later moved to New York.

pages.title: Scottie B
pages.blurb: Baltimore DJ and producer, co-founder of Unruly Records and a pioneer of Baltimore club.

pages.title: Unruly Records
pages.blurb: Baltimore club label founded by Scottie B, Shawn Caesar and Karizma, which averaged eight to ten releases a year, mostly 12-inch EPs.

pages.title: The Paradox
pages.blurb: Wayne Davis's warehouse club on Russell Street, home of Baltimore club for 25 years.

pages.title: K-Swift
pages.blurb: 92Q radio host who took Baltimore club to commercial radio; died in July 2008 aged 29.

pages.title: Stonewall Inn
pages.blurb: The Greenwich Village bar where dancing was allowed and whose raid on 28 June 1969 set off the riots that began the gay liberation marches.

pages.title: Continental Baths
pages.blurb: Steve Ostrow's bathhouse in the Ansonia basement, where Bette Midler sang and Larry Levan and Frankie Knuckles learned to DJ.

pages.title: Michael Fesco
pages.blurb: Broadway chorus boy who opened the Ice Palace in Cherry Grove in 1970, created its Sunday Tea and ran the Flamingo.

pages.title: Ice Palace (Cherry Grove)
pages.blurb: Michael Fesco's foil-walled club in Cherry Grove, modelled on the Sanctuary, which replaced the jukebox with a DJ in 1970.

pages.title: Flamingo (New York)
pages.blurb: Michael Fesco's members-only gay club at 599 Broadway, home of the Black Party, which lost its members to the Saint.

pages.title: Robbie Leslie
pages.blurb: DJ at the Sandpiper on Fire Island from 1977, at 12 West, and from 1980 a resident at the Saint.

pages.title: Crystal LaBeija
pages.blurb: Ball pioneer whose walk-out from a 1967 drag pageant led to the first annual House of LaBeija Ball in 1972 and the start of the house system.

pages.title: Willi Ninja
pages.blurb: Founder of the House of Ninja, known as the godfather of voguing, who appeared in Paris Is Burning and Malcolm McLaren's "Deep in Vogue".

pages.title: Masters at Work — The Ha Dance
pages.blurb: The house record built on a shouted "ha" from Trading Places, with a crash on the fourth beat that signals ballroom dancers to pose; reworked by Vjuan Allure, Angel X and MikeQ.

pages.title: The Saint
pages.blurb: Bruce Mailman's members-only club in the former Fillmore East, under a planetarium dome, whose membership the AIDS epidemic emptied.

pages.title: Patrick Cowley
pages.blurb: San Francisco synthesiser producer, a pioneer of hi-NRG and Sylvester's collaborator, who died of AIDS on 12 November 1982, aged 32.

pages.title: Sylvester
pages.blurb: Singer of "You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real)" who left his royalties to two AIDS charities and died on 16 December 1988.

pages.title: Bronski Beat
pages.blurb: Jimmy Somerville, Steve Bronski and Larry Steinbachek, whose 1984 hit "Smalltown Boy" reached number three in Britain.

pages.title: Section 28
pages.blurb: Clause barring councils from promoting homosexuality, law from 24 May 1988 until repeal in Scotland (2000) and England and Wales (2003).

pages.title: Horse Meat Disco
pages.blurb: Disco party begun on New Year's Day 2004 at Dukes in Vauxhall by Hillard, Howard, Stanton and Panzetta; four Strut compilations.

pages.title: Royal Vauxhall Tavern
pages.blurb: Vauxhall pub and queer venue, Grade II listed on 8 September 2015 after the RVT Future campaign.

pages.title: Dalston Superstore
pages.blurb: Bar-club opened in May 2009 by Dan Beaumont and Matt Tucker; its basement grew Body Movements and Mighty Hoopla.

pages.title: Flesh at the Haçienda
pages.blurb: Paul Cons and Lucy Scher's monthly gay night from late October 1991, eight years after the club's short-lived Gay Mondays, with DJ Paulette in the Pussy Parlour.

pages.title: Vague
pages.blurb: Leeds night from Suzy Mason and Paul Fryer, at the Warehouse, billed as mixed; Pete Tong recorded an Essential Mix there.

pages.title: Homoelectric
pages.blurb: Luke Una's queer night and, with Homobloc, the party that filled Mayfield Depot with about 10,000 on 9 November 2019.

pages.title: Adonis
pages.blurb: Queer rave started by Shay Malt in Tottenham, with Hannah Holland and Grace Sands as residents and a vibe-based door.

pages.title: SchwuZ
pages.blurb: Berlin's gay centre turned club, proclaimed on 26 June 1977; home to the first CSD march and Siegessäule, later in Neukölln.

pages.title: Metropol (Berlin)
pages.blurb: Studio 54-inspired Schöneberg disco on Nollendorfplatz that turned increasingly gay from around 1980 and gave Westbam a residency.

pages.title: Le Palace
pages.blurb: Fabrice Emaer's theatre-club at 8 rue du Faubourg-Montmartre, opened 1 March 1978 with Grace Jones and a door that mixed Paris on purpose.

pages.title: The iT
pages.blurb: Manfred Langer's Amstelstraat club in the old Be-Bop cinema, which he set out to make the biggest and hottest gay disco in the Netherlands.

pages.title: Cocktail d'Amore
pages.blurb: Sex-positive Italo, disco and house party started by Discodromo and Berghain's Boris, with a darkroom floor called the Cosmic Hole.

pages.title: Herrensauna
pages.blurb: Hard techno party founded by Nicolas Endlicher and Cem Dukkha, two DJs from Vienna; about 5,000 came to its September 2021 return.

pages.title: Horoom Nights
pages.blurb: Vetted, free queer party at Bassiani, created with the Equality Movement; later got its own dance floor.

pages.title: Pxssy Palace
pages.blurb: London queer collective known for tiered ticketing, a trained support team and calling its spaces 'intentional' rather than 'safe'.

pages.title: Laurence Malice
pages.blurb: Promoter who opened Trade at Turnmills in 1990, then founded Egg in King's Cross in 2003.

pages.title: Egg London
pages.blurb: King's Cross club in a Victorian warehouse, opened by Laurence Malice in May 2003 with a 24-hour weekend licence; refitted in 2024.

pages.title: Daz Saund
pages.blurb: Original Trade resident from 1990 to 1993 and early hard house remixer, later of Black & Brown with Trevor Rockcliffe.

pages.title: Hard house
pages.blurb: UK style of about 150 bpm shaped at Trade and spread by labels such as Tidy Trax and nights such as Frantic and Storm.

pages.title: Trade Lite
pages.blurb: Second, lighter room at Trade, from about 6am, proposed by the Sharp Boys for funkier house.

pages.title: Fire, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: Multi-room club in the South Lambeth Road railway arches, home to Orange, A:M, Beyond and Later, and a weekend that ran into Monday.

pages.title: The Hoist
pages.blurb: Leather and dress-code club in the Vauxhall arches that closed in December 2016 after 21 years.

pages.title: The Eagle, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: Kennington Lane pub-club, called Dukes when Horse Meat Disco arrived on New Year's Day 2004; Duckie held daytime parties there from August 2022.

pages.title: Duckie
pages.blurb: Club and cabaret night founded in 1995 by Simon Casson and friends; at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern until July 2022, then by day at the Eagle, and from March 2026 back as Duckie…

pages.title: Orange (Orange Nation)
pages.blurb: Sunday night that began at Fire in Vauxhall in 2003 and gave its name to the promoter behind the club's long weekend.

pages.title: Above the Stag Theatre, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: LGBTQ+ theatre in a Vauxhall railway arch that announced on 7 August 2022 that it had closed, citing its finances and Network Rail safety work.

pages.title: Market Tavern, Nine Elms
pages.blurb: Porters' pub at New Covent Garden Market with a late licence; from 1983 it billed itself south London's first gay pub open to 2am.

pages.title: Chariots, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: The last of the Chariots gay saunas, billed as Europe's largest; shut in March 2020 and went into liquidation in January 2021.

pages.title: Barcode, Vauxhall
pages.blurb: Gay bar in Vauxhall that closed at the end of May 2015, a month short of its tenth birthday.

pages.title: Bloc South
pages.blurb: Wayne Shires's club on the former Club 65 site in the Vauxhall Triangle, given a 5am licence by Lambeth in January 2017.

pages.title: Tom Stephan
pages.blurb: DJ at Wayne Shires's Substation and Crash, later co-running East Bloc in Shoreditch and its Blocheads all-nighters.

pages.title: The Readers Wifes
pages.blurb: Mark Wood and Mark Johnston, Duckie's resident DJs, who played records without beatmixing at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern.

pages.title: Paul O'Grady
pages.blurb: Entertainer whose drag character Lily Savage held an eight-year residency at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern.

pages.title: Junior Vasquez
pages.blurb: DJ who opened the Sound Factory in 1989 and played its nights, with later residencies at the Tunnel, ArenA and Twilo.

pages.title: The Roxy (New York)
pages.blurb: 515 West 18th Street roller rink turned club; its Saturday gay night, from 1990, closed with a 14-hour party in March 2007.

pages.title: Body & Soul (New York)
pages.blurb: Sunday-afternoon party at Vinyl run by François Kevorkian and John Davis, with Danny Krivit and Joe Claussell, for a mixed crowd.

pages.title: The Black Party
pages.blurb: The Saint at Large's annual leather and fetish marathon, at Roseland for 24 years, then warehouses, and back in 2024 and 2025.

pages.title: Papi Juice
pages.blurb: Party and art collective founded by Oscar Nñ and Adam Rhodes for queer and transgender people of colour; first night held in a 72-person bar.

pages.title: The Carry Nation
pages.blurb: Party formed by Will Automagic and Nita Aviance, named for the temperance campaigner; a monthly at Good Room in Brooklyn.

pages.title: New York Cabaret Law
pages.blurb: The 1926 licensing rule restricting dancing in bars, revived under Giuliani and repealed in October 2017 after a campaign by Discwoman's co-founder and others.

pages.title: Trocadero Transfer
pages.blurb: Dick Collier's club at 520 Fourth Street with a Graebar system, where Bobby Viteritti played from 1977 to 1981.

pages.title: The EndUp
pages.blurb: Former hotel at Sixth and Harrison where the Sunday tea dance and 6 am Church party fed a weekend that ran close to 50 hours.

pages.title: I-Beam
pages.blurb: Gay disco and later rock venue at 1748 Haight Street, with Michael Garrett as main DJ from 1980 to 1992; closed after neighbour noise complaints.

pages.title: The Stud (San Francisco)
pages.blurb: South of Market dance bar, collectively owned from 2016, that closed in 2020 and reopened at 1123 Folsom Street in 2024.

pages.title: Honey Soundsystem
pages.blurb: Party crew and label founded by Jacob Sperber and Ken Woodard, curators of Patrick Cowley's archive and of Tea With Honey and Deviants.

pages.title: Jewel's Catch One
pages.blurb: Jewel Thais-Williams's Black LGBTQ disco at 4067 West Pico Boulevard; closed July 2015 and designated a Historic-Cultural Monument in 2024.

pages.title: Circus Disco
pages.blurb: Latinx-centred gay club at 6655 Santa Monica Boulevard, Hollywood, founded by Gene LaPietra and Ed Lemos; demolished in spring 2016.

pages.title: A Club Called Rhonda
pages.blurb: House and disco night begun by Loren Granic and Gregory Alexander, which grew from Guatelinda to Los Globos with a mixed, queer-friendly crowd.

pages.title: Mustache Mondays
pages.blurb: Monday party founded by Nacho Nava and Josh Peace at Crash Mansion; mixed DJs with performance art and built followings for Kelela and Kingdom.

pages.title: Dugan's Bistro
pages.blurb: Primarily gay Chicago disco where Lou DiVito was resident; demolished for a car park in 1982.

pages.title: Carol's Speakeasy
pages.blurb: Members-only gay club on North Wells Street where Frankie Knuckles had Fridays in 1979; its 1985 raid led to an ACLU suit.

pages.title: Queen! at Smartbar
pages.blurb: Sunday queer night at Smartbar founded by Michael Serafini and Garrett David, with drag hosts booked as carefully as DJs.

pages.title: Warsaw Ballroom
pages.blurb: South Beach gay club at Collins Avenue and Espanola Way, run from 1989 by Andrew Delaplaine.

pages.title: White Party Miami
pages.blurb: AIDS benefit that began as one formal evening for 1,600 guests and grew into a week of circuit-party events.

pages.title: Backstreet
pages.blurb: Midtown Atlanta's 24-hour gay club on Peachtree Street, run by the Vara family; the city refused to renew its 24-hour licence in 2003 and it closed in 2004.

pages.title: Komrads
pages.blurb: Club at 1 Isabella Street, near Yonge and Wellesley, with a steel dance floor; for a time Toronto's only permanent after-hours club.

pages.title: Circuit party
pages.blurb: Multi-day gay dance weekends run as charity benefits, from the Fire Island Morning Party to Black & Blue.

pages.title: Manto
pages.blurb: Glass-fronted Canal Street bar opened just before Christmas 1990 by Carol Ainscow and Peter Dalton; it closed in October 2013.

pages.title: Paradise Factory
pages.blurb: Peter Dalton's Princess Street house club, a little apart from Canal Street, remembered in reunion parties until 2014.

pages.title: Nightingale Club
pages.blurb: Birmingham gay club begun in a Camp Hill restaurant bought for £600 in 1967 or 1968; on Kent Street since 1999.

pages.title: Matinée Group
pages.blurb: Barcelona promoter run by Manolo Soria, from El Divino in Ibiza and Space to Circuit Festival.

pages.title: Home of La Troya
pages.blurb: Brasilio de Oliveira's gay night, from Privilege and Amnesia to Wednesdays at Space.

pages.title: Disco Anfora
pages.blurb: Dalt Vila club that Travelgay called the island's only exclusively gay club for more than thirty years; the same listing now marks it closed.

pages.title: Muccassassina
pages.blurb: Weekly Friday party begun in October 1990 to fund the Mario Mieli association's HIV work; now at Qube.

pages.title: Plastic
pages.blurb: Milan's queer and underground club, opened 23 December 1980 and closed in June 2025.

pages.title: Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras
pages.blurb: Began as a June 1978 march on Oxford Street; its parties grew to 15,000 by 1989.

pages.title: Sleaze Ball
pages.blurb: Mardi Gras fundraiser launched in 1982 at Paddington Town Hall, a Hi-NRG and disco all-nighter that later moved to the Hordern Pavilion.

pages.title: Hordern Pavilion
pages.blurb: Agricultural hall that hosted RAT raves and Mardi Gras parties, with crowds above 6,000.

pages.title: RAT (Recreational Arts Team)
pages.blurb: The Recreational Arts Team, behind CelebRAT '88 at the Hordern and 28 Hordern parties in 1989.

pages.title: Midnight Shift
pages.blurb: Club at 85–91 Oxford Street, known for its Hellfire Club night; it announced its closure for 1 October 2017.

pages.title: Shinjuku Ni-chōme
pages.blurb: Tokyo's gay district, with more than 300 venues in five blocks according to a 2026 guide.

pages.title: WAIFU
pages.blurb: Queer and femme collective formed in 2019 after a trans woman was refused entry to a Ni-chōme party.

pages.title: Pervert
pages.blurb: Roving queer techno party begun in April 2017 by Alberto Herbel and Robin Garcia, with a dark room at every night.

pages.title: Simon Nkoli
pages.blurb: Activist at the front of the Johannesburg Pride march of 13 October 1990, which Daily Maverick calls Africa's first.

pages.title: Commodore Amiga
pages.blurb: Home computer whose Paula chip played four channels of 8-bit sound and made the tracker, and much early hardcore, possible.

pages.title: Ultimate Soundtracker
pages.blurb: Karsten Obarski's Amiga program of 1987, which Xavier Borderie calls the first tracker to use samples, and the origin of the MOD file.

pages.title: NoiseTracker and ProTracker
pages.blurb: Scene rewrites of Soundtracker that became the Amiga standard for hardcore, jungle and gabber producers.

pages.title: OctaMED
pages.blurb: Teijo Kinnunen's Amiga tracker, with eight channels and MIDI; Aphrodite, Bizzy B and DJ Zinc are among the producers credited with using it.

pages.title: Scream Tracker
pages.blurb: PC tracker by PSI of Future Crew, whose S3M format added channels and a volume column.

pages.title: FastTracker 2
pages.blurb: Shareware PC tracker by Mr H and Vogue of Triton; its XM format allowed 32 channels and envelopes.

pages.title: Impulse Tracker
pages.blurb: Jeffrey Lim's PC tracker, with resonant filters and New Note Actions, the rival of FastTracker 2.

pages.title: Jeskola Buzz
pages.blurb: Windows modular studio that kept a tracker as its sequencer; development stalled and restarted after its creator lost the source code.

pages.title: Renoise
pages.blurb: Commercial tracker built from Arguru's NoiseTrekker code, with plug-in and ReWire support.

pages.title: Urban Shakedown
pages.blurb: Gavin King, Claudio Giussani and Michael Hearne, who made hardcore on two hand-synced Amiga 500s.

pages.title: Polyend Tracker
pages.blurb: Polyend's self-contained, USB-powered hardware tracker of 2020, with the functions of a software tracker.

pages.title: Steinberg Pro-24
pages.blurb: Werner Kracht's 24-channel MIDI sequencer for the Atari ST, the forerunner of Cubase.

pages.title: Digidesign Pro Tools
pages.blurb: Digidesign's four-track Mac system of 1991, $6,000 complete, modelled on analogue studio workflow.

pages.title: Logic Pro
pages.blurb: Sequencer from C-Lab's Creator and Notator through Emagic, bought by Apple in July 2002, $199.99 from 2011.

pages.title: GarageBand
pages.blurb: Apple's entry-level studio, announced by Steve Jobs on 6 January 2004 and developed under Gerhard Lengeling.

pages.title: VST (Virtual Studio Technology)
pages.blurb: Steinberg's plug-in standard: effects in 1996, instruments with VST 2.0 in 1999, VST 3 with Cubase 4 in 2006 (SDK 2008), open under the MIT licence in 2025.

pages.title: Steinberg Neon
pages.blurb: A simple subtractive synth shipped in Cubase VST 3.7 with VST 2.0 in 1999; Plugin Boutique and CDM call it the first VST instrument.

pages.title: Native Instruments
pages.blurb: Berlin software maker behind Generator, Reaktor, Absynth, Massive, Traktor and Maschine, begun by Stephan Schmitt and Volker Hinz.

pages.title: Native Instruments Generator / Reaktor
pages.blurb: A modular environment for building instruments and effects; Generator was shown in 1996 and became Reaktor 2.0 in 1999.

pages.title: Native Instruments Absynth
pages.blurb: Brian Clevinger's synth, first released in 2000, retired by Native Instruments in 2022 and revived as Absynth 6 at the end of 2025.

pages.title: Native Instruments Massive
pages.blurb: Mike Daliot's wavetable bass synth, slow to sell at first; by Native Instruments' own account its success came in dubstep.

pages.title: Xfer Serum
pages.blurb: Steve Duda's wavetable synth, released September 2014; Serum 2 followed in March 2025 as a free update for owners.

pages.title: LennarDigital Sylenth1
pages.blurb: A CPU-light virtual analogue synth that Dance Music Northwest called the first pick of trance and EDM producers in 2017.

pages.title: reFX Nexus and Vanguard
pages.blurb: Preset-led synths for dance producers; Vanguard (2004) was programmed by Markus Krause of Tone2, with presets by Manuel Schleis.

pages.title: Waves L1 Ultramaximizer
pages.blurb: A Pro Tools TDM look-ahead limiter that became a go-to tool of the loudness war.

pages.title: Antares Auto-Tune
pages.blurb: Released in 1997 as a subtle pitch corrector; a retune speed of zero turned it into a vocal effect.

pages.title: Steve Duda
pages.blurb: Programmer and multi-instrumentalist on Nine Inch Nails' The Fragile, half of BSOD with deadmau5, and the maker of Serum.

pages.title: The log drum
pages.blurb: Amapiano's bass sound; NKC (Mixmag) traces it to FL Studio's Fruity DX10 preset; DJ Maphorisa and Kabza De Small credit MDU aka TRP.

pages.title: MFR Souls
pages.blurb: Katlehong duo of Maero and Force Reloaded who say they pioneered amapiano; 'Amanikiniki' set off a nationwide TikTok dance craze in 2020.

pages.title: Kabza De Small
pages.blurb: Pretoria DJ and producer, half of Scorpion Kings; Rolling Stone called him a foundational figure in amapiano.

pages.title: DJ Maphorisa
pages.blurb: Producer Rolling Stone calls partly responsible for Drake's 'One Dance'; formed Scorpion Kings with Kabza De Small in 2019.

pages.title: Scorpion Kings
pages.blurb: Kabza De Small and DJ Maphorisa's duo, formed in 2019; their EP came out that July and 'Emcimbini' followed in early 2020.

pages.title: Kelvin Momo
pages.blurb: Soweto producer whose jazz, deep-house and lounge sound Masterpiece named 'private school' amapiano; Beatport's top-selling amapiano artist of 2024.

pages.title: Major League DJz
pages.blurb: Twins Banele and Bandile Mbere, whose rooftop Balcony Mix streams spread amapiano in lockdown; sold out O2 Academy Brixton in 2022.

pages.title: Tyla
pages.blurb: Johannesburg-born singer whose 'Water' reached No. 4 in the UK and No. 7 in the US; she called 'Getting Late' pop-piano.

pages.title: Tyla — Water
