pages.blurb: Amapiano-infused Afro pop single (grammy.com); UK No. 4 in October 2023; won the first Grammy for best African music performance in 2024.

pages.title: TitoM and Yuppe — Tshwala Bam
pages.blurb: Released 23 February 2024, with vocals by S.N.E and EeQue; a house-party dance clip made it a TikTok hit.

pages.title: Focalistic — Ke Star
pages.blurb: Lockdown-era single with Vigro Deep; its 2021 remix with Davido took it abroad.

pages.title: Phazon
pages.blurb: New York design and installation company of which Steve Dash was a principal, maker of the PDS subs; systems for Twilo, Vinyl, Cream, Home and crobar.

pages.title: Steve Dash
pages.blurb: Club sound designer and Phazon principal; by Mix's 2000 account, thirty years of club systems including Twilo and crobar.

pages.title: Dave Parry
pages.blurb: Lighting and sound engineer who redesigned Ministry of Sound's rig and designed fabric's installation and vibrating floor in 1999.

pages.title: fabric's Room One floor
pages.blurb: Tactile dance floor on Bodysonic transducers, 450 by the London Museum's count, rebuilt in 2025 on 36 Powersoft Movers and tuned with Deaf Rave.

pages.title: Ministry of Sound's Box system
pages.blurb: Room-built system: £500,000 in 1991, Martin Audio from the mid-2000s, Dolby Atmos trial in 2016, KV2 Audio from 2026.

pages.title: KV2 Audio
pages.blurb: Loudspeaker maker with a factory in Czechia; its SL412 and VHD subs replaced Martin Audio in Ministry of Sound's Box in a refit from 7 January 2026, by KV2's announcement.

pages.title: Studt-Akustik
pages.blurb: Peter Studt's Dresden hi-fi company; fitted Panorama Bar with a four-point linear array and six more subwoofers in 2017.

pages.title: Ade Fakile
pages.blurb: Founder of Plastic People, who ran its sound and its Balance nights; his ear traced to his father's public sound work in Ibadan.

pages.title: Robert Johnson
pages.blurb: Club in a former rowing club at Nordring 131, Offenbach, owned by Ata of Playhouse by DJ Mag's 2009 account; praised by DJs for its sound.

pages.title: Output
pages.blurb: Williamsburg club on Wythe Avenue with a Funktion-One rig including prototypes; closed at the start of 2019, after John Digweed's set on 31 December 2018.

pages.title: crobar Miami
pages.blurb: South Beach club whose 2000 system, by Steve Dash, used JBL components, 14-inch PDS subs and over 40,000 watts.

pages.title: Precious Hall
pages.blurb: Sapporo's oldest operating club by RA's 2016 account; a room inspired by David Mancuso that James Murphy cites as an inspiration for Despacio.

pages.title: STAX
pages.blurb: Danny Tenaglia's Brooklyn party, planned for 15 April 2023 on ten stacks: the Phazon system from Vinyl and Gary Stewart's GS-WAVE prototype.

pages.title: Brilliant Corners
pages.blurb: Dalston bar run by Amit and Aneesh Patel, playing jazz, disco and electronic records through Klipschorns.

pages.title: L-Acoustics
pages.blurb: Christian Heil's French loudspeaker maker, whose V-DOSC line source of 1992 and K1 of 2008 reshaped festival sound.

pages.title: L-Acoustics V-DOSC
pages.blurb: Line-source array developed in 1992 from Heil's Wavefront Sculpture theory, coupling a column of boxes into one wavefront.

pages.title: Meyer Sound
pages.blurb: John and Helen Meyer's Californian firm: self-powered systems from the MSL-4 (1994), the PSW-6 cardioid sub (1998), the M3D array (2001).

pages.title: d&b audiotechnik
pages.blurb: German loudspeaker maker founded by Jürgen Daubert and Rolf Belz; its Cardioid Subwoofer Array arrived in 2004, the J-Series in 2006.

pages.title: Valve Sound System
pages.blurb: Dillinja and Lemon D's drum and bass rig, a '96K' system that needed three trucks on tour.

pages.title: Iration Steppas
pages.blurb: Mark Iration's Leeds dub system, resident at SubDub, which moved from dubplates to DAT and to Powersoft amplification.

pages.title: Sinai Sound System
pages.blurb: Huw Williams's system, begun with three bass boxes after an apprenticeship with Iration Steppas; about fifty by 2018.

pages.title: SubDub
pages.blurb: Leeds bass night with Iration Steppas as resident system; its crew put together the first Outlook festival in 2008.

pages.title: Aba Shanti-I
pages.blurb: Dub and roots system that has played Notting Hill Carnival for nearly thirty years, at East Row and Southern Row.

pages.title: Noise Council Code of Practice on Environmental Noise Control at Concerts
pages.blurb: The 'Pop Code': 65 or 75 dB(A) over 15 minutes at 1 m from a façade; inaudible indoors after 11pm.

pages.title: Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005
pages.blurb: Workplace noise rules applied to bars and nightclubs from 6 April 2008: action at 80 and 85 dB(A), limit 87 dB(A).

pages.title: WHO Global Standard for Safe Listening Venues and Events
pages.blurb: WHO's six features for venues: 100 dB average over 15 minutes, monitoring, acoustics, earplugs, quiet zones, trained staff.

pages.title: Night & Day Café
pages.blurb: Northern Quarter venue whose 2021 noise abatement notice was upheld but varied in 2024, keeping weekend DJ nights to 3am.

pages.title: Berlin's club noise protection fund
pages.blurb: €1 million pledged in December 2017 for soundproofing clubs, outdoor barriers and neighbours' windows.

pages.title: Serato Scratch Live
pages.blurb: Timecode-vinyl DJ system from Serato, sold with Rane's USB interfaces from 2004; worked only with Rane hardware.

pages.title: Native Instruments Traktor
pages.blurb: Native Instruments' DJ software, first released in 2000; the engine of Traktor Final Scratch, Traktor Scratch and the Kontrol controllers.

pages.title: Native Instruments Traktor Scratch
pages.blurb: Native Instruments' own timecode system with the Audio 8 DJ, announced January 2007 at $669; the subject of N2IT's June 2007 claim, which ended with a licence in April 2008.

pages.title: Rane TTM 57SL
pages.blurb: Rane's scratch mixer with Scratch Live functions built in, claimed by Rane as the first of its kind (2006).

pages.title: Allen & Heath Xone:3D
pages.blurb: Four-channel DJ mixer, USB sound card and MIDI surface in one box; Hawtin and Liebing consulted; £1,645 in 2006.

pages.title: Vestax VCI-100
pages.blurb: Laptop-sized two-deck MIDI controller with Traktor LE, announced March 2007; the base for DJ TechTools' 2009 Special Edition.

pages.title: Numark NS7
pages.blurb: Controller with motor-driven seven-inch vinyl platters, shown at winter NAMM 2008 for Serato Itch.

pages.title: Native Instruments Traktor Kontrol S4
pages.blurb: Four-deck Traktor controller with built-in 24-bit sound card and sample decks, announced August 2010 at $999.

pages.title: Pioneer DDJ-T1 and DDJ-S1
pages.blurb: Pioneer's Traktor and Serato Itch controllers, announced 11 January 2011 at £899 and £1,099.

pages.title: Native Instruments Stems
pages.blurb: Open four-part audio file format for DJs, announced 30 March 2015 and on sale from 3 August 2015.

pages.title: Mark-Jan Bastian
pages.blurb: Dutch inventor of Final Scratch at N2IT, visited by John Acquaviva while still a teenager, by DJ Mag's account.

pages.title: Ean Golden
pages.blurb: DJ and founder of DJ TechTools, who released the VCI-100 Special Edition with Vestax in 2009.

pages.title: Dennis Ferrer
pages.blurb: DJ and producer who, in a 2012 Attack interview, called DJs' use of the sync button lazy.

pages.title: Pioneer DJ CDJ-2000NXS2
pages.blurb: Pioneer DJ's last flagship with a disc slot, announced January 2016 at €2,299; added FLAC and ALAC playback.

pages.title: Pioneer DJ CDJ-3000
pages.blurb: Flagship player of September 2020 with no CD drive: nine-inch touchscreen, MPU processor, Key Shift; $2,299 / £2,169 at launch.

pages.title: AlphaTheta CDJ-3000X
pages.blurb: AlphaTheta-branded successor of September 2025: 10.1-inch screen, Wi-Fi, Beatport and TIDAL streaming, USB-C, no SD slot.

pages.title: AlphaTheta Euphonia
pages.blurb: Four-channel rotary mixer with Rupert Neve Designs transformer circuit; the first AlphaTheta-branded product, March 2024, $3,799 / £3,249.

pages.title: AlphaTheta XDJ-AZ
pages.blurb: Four-deck all-in-one standalone DJ system, October 2024, £2,799, laid out after the CDJ-3000 and DJM-A9.

pages.title: Denon DJ Prime and Engine DJ
pages.blurb: Denon DJ's standalone players and mixers from NAMM 2017 (SC5000 Prime, $1,899), with streaming from 2020 and stems from 2024.

pages.title: Technics SL-1200MK7
pages.blurb: DJ turntable of 2019 with a coreless direct-drive motor and reverse play, following the SL-1200G revival of 2016.

pages.title: MWM Phase
pages.blurb: Wireless timecode: remotes on the turntable spindle replace control vinyl; on sale from April 2019 at $450 and up.

pages.title: Stem separation in DJ software
pages.blurb: Machine-learning splitting of finished tracks: djay Pro and VirtualDJ (June 2020), Serato (2022), rekordbox (2023), Traktor Pro 4 (2024).

pages.title: Algoriddim djay Pro
pages.blurb: DJ app whose Neural Mix separated drums, vocals and harmonic parts on the fly from June 2020; supports Apple Music streaming.

pages.title: DJ with Apple Music
pages.blurb: Apple Music streaming inside Serato, rekordbox, Engine DJ and djay from March 2025; terms limit it to non-commercial use.

pages.title: Adam Smith and Marcus Lyall
pages.blurb: Show directors of the Chemical Brothers since 2009; Smith has made the duo's visuals since their first gig in 1995.

pages.title: Isles of Wonder: the London 2012 opening ceremony
pages.blurb: Danny Boyle's Olympic opening ceremony of 27 July 2012, its music directed by Underworld's Rick Smith.

pages.title: Justice
pages.blurb: Gaspard Augé and Xavier de Rosnay, the Ed Banger duo whose 2008 tour stood them before a wall of Marshall amplifiers.

pages.title: Soulwax / 2manydjs
pages.blurb: Stephen and David Dewaele's rock band and DJ act; the Radio Soulwax tour ran 2005–08 and Despacio followed in 2013.

pages.title: LCD Soundsystem
pages.blurb: James Murphy's band, which played a three-hour farewell at Madison Square Garden on 2 April 2011.

pages.title: Rudimental
pages.blurb: East London drum and bass collective whose "Feel the Love" (2012) and Home (2013) both went to number one.

pages.title: Disclosure
pages.blurb: Guy and Howard Lawrence, whose first two albums, Settle (2013) and Caracal (2015), both went to number one.

pages.title: Fred again..
pages.blurb: Producer Frederick Gibson; played Glastonbury's Other Stage in 2023 and headlined Reading and Leeds in August 2024.

pages.title: Four Tet
pages.blurb: Kieran Hebden, who headlined Glastonbury's Woodsies in 2025 and held his own Finsbury Park All Dayer each summer from 2022.

pages.title: Bicep
pages.blurb: Belfast-born duo whose Isles reached number two in 2021; they sold out the Royal Albert Hall for 26 November 2026.

pages.title: Overmono
pages.blurb: The Welsh brothers Tom and Ed Russell, whose Good Lies (2023) reached 11 and Pure Devotion (2026) reached 12 on the Official Albums Chart.

pages.title: Jersey club
pages.blurb: Newark's fast, bouncy offshoot of Baltimore club, first called Brick City club, built on triplet kicks, chopped vocals and the bed squeak.

pages.title: Philly club (party music)
pages.blurb: Philadelphia's take on Baltimore club, called party music locally; VICE in 2015 heard it at up to 150 bpm, with sirens, danced in Tang ciphers.

pages.title: DJ Tameil
pages.blurb: Newark DJ who brought Baltimore club records north, released the Dat Butt EP in 2001 and chopped the bed squeak.

pages.title: Brick Bandits
pages.blurb: Newark crew founded by Tim Dolla and Mike V, later joined by DJ Tameil, with chapters in Philadelphia and Chicago.

pages.title: Tim Dolla
pages.blurb: Brick Bandits co-founder and producer of "Swing Dat Shyt"; his death was reported in July 2022.

pages.title: DJ Sliink
pages.blurb: Newark producer who joined the Brick Bandits in 2010 and signed to Skrillex's OWSLA.

pages.title: UNIIQU3
pages.blurb: Newark producer, DJ and party-thrower who started Vixen, a street team of girls, and by the Guardian's 2021 account ran PBNJ, a club night.

pages.title: DJ Jayhood
pages.blurb: Jersey club producer of "Hit It to the Beat" and an outspoken voice on credit for the scene's sound and dances.

pages.title: Cookiee Kawaii
pages.blurb: Irvington artist whose 2020 track "Vibe (If I Back It Up)", SoundCloud says, tied Jersey club to viral dance videos.

pages.title: DJ Smallz 732
pages.blurb: Jersey club producer behind the 2014 "We Are Young" remix and co-producer of Nicki Minaj's "Everybody".

pages.title: DJ Sega
pages.blurb: North Philadelphia DJ and producer, a quasi-folk hero at the Jamz roller rink by 2009 (XLR8R), Mad Decent signing in 2007, maker of New Jack Philly.

pages.title: MCVertt
pages.blurb: Newark producer who co-produced Lil Uzi Vert's "Just Wanna Rock" and produced seven songs on Bandmanrill's Club Godfather.

pages.title: Bandmanrill
pages.blurb: Newark rapper whose "Heartbroken" (2020), built on T2's UK bassline hit, exploded on TikTok and led to a Warner Records deal; he calls his music Jersey rap, not drill.

pages.title: Lil Uzi Vert — Just Wanna Rock
pages.blurb: Jersey club single co-produced by MCVertt; it reached No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 dated 11 February 2023.

pages.title: Cookiee Kawaii — Vibe (If I Back It Up)
pages.blurb: Jersey club track of 2020 that, SoundCloud says, tied the sound to viral dance videos.

pages.title: Max (Max/MSP)
pages.blurb: Visual patching environment begun by Miller Puckette at IRCAM, sold by Opcode from 1989–90, audio added as MSP in 1997.

pages.title: Cycling '74
pages.blurb: David Zicarelli's company that develops Max; bought by Ableton in June 2017.

pages.title: Pure Data
pages.blurb: Miller Puckette's free, open-source patching environment, continuing the tradition of Max.

pages.title: SuperCollider
pages.blurb: James McCartney's programming language and sound server for synthesis, free under the GPL since 2002.

pages.title: Autechre
pages.blurb: Sean Booth and Rob Brown, the Warp duo whose Confield (2001) came largely out of Max experiments; by 2016 Booth said he used only Max/MSP.

pages.title: Robert Henke (Monolake)
pages.blurb: Monolake producer and Ableton co-founder who prototyped Live's effects and his Monodeck controller in Max.

pages.title: Algorave
pages.blurb: Club nights of live-coded dance music; a Live AlgoRave was held in London on 17 March 2012.

pages.title: TOPLAP
pages.blurb: Live-coding organisation formed in a Hamburg bar; its manifesto asks performers to show their screens.

pages.title: TidalCycles
pages.blurb: Alex McLean's Haskell pattern language for live coding, played through SuperCollider; ported as Strudel from 2022.

pages.title: Sonic Pi
pages.blurb: Sam Aaron's free live-coding program, made at Cambridge with the Raspberry Pi Foundation for school lessons.

pages.title: Zero-G Datafile sample CDs
pages.blurb: Ed Stratton's breakbeat and sound CDs, published by Time+Space and sold at £49.95 each in 1992.

pages.title: Loopmasters
pages.blurb: Matt Pelling's online sound-pack shop, parent of Plugin Boutique and Loopcloud; bought by Beatport in December 2020.

pages.title: Splice
pages.blurb: Sample subscription service founded by Steve Martocci and Matt Aimonetti; Splice Sounds launched in 2015.

pages.title: BeatStars
pages.blurb: Beat marketplace founded by Abe Batshon, where producers lease type beats; home of the "Old Town Road" beat.

pages.title: Suno
pages.blurb: AI song generator sued by major labels in June 2024; Warner settled in 2025, Sony and Universal sued again in 2026.

pages.title: Electric Daisy Carnival UK
pages.blurb: Insomniac and Cream's British EDC at the National Bowl in Milton Keynes; over 50,000 at the first, by Insomniac's count.

pages.title: Bloc
pages.blurb: Alex Benson and George Hull's holiday-camp electronic weekender; collapsed at the London Pleasure Gardens in July 2012.

pages.title: Secret Garden Party
pages.blurb: Freddie Fellowes's Cambridgeshire party, where The Loop opened public drug checking in 2016; returned in 2022.

pages.title: Q-dance
pages.blurb: Dutch hardstyle promoter co-founded by Wouter Tavecchio and by 2024 part of ID&T; ran Qlimax until 2024, and Defqon.1.

pages.title: Qlimax
pages.blurb: Q-dance's indoor hardstyle show at the GelreDome in Arnhem; the last, "The Final Prophecy", was held on 16 November 2024.

pages.title: ID&T
pages.blurb: Dutch promoter of Thunderdome and Mysteryland, co-founded by Duncan Stutterheim; sold to SFX in 2013 and to Superstruct in 2021.

pages.title: I Love Techno
pages.blurb: Ghent's techno night, from the Vooruit in 1995 to Flanders Expo crowds of over 35,000; moved to Montpellier in 2015.

pages.title: Drug checking in Zürich (Streetwork and DIZ)
pages.blurb: The city's mobile drug checking from 2001 and fixed testing at the Drogeninformationszentrum from 2006; a stand at the Street Parade.

pages.title: DIMS (Drug Information and Monitoring System)
pages.blurb: Dutch drug-testing network of 32 addiction-care organisations, coordinated by the Trimbos Institute, which issues national Red Alerts.

pages.title: Ferropolis
pages.blurb: Open-air museum of five lignite-mining machines on the Gremminer See, framing a 25,000-capacity arena; Melt's home from 1999 to 2024.

pages.title: Exit
pages.blurb: Born in the 2000 student protests against Milošević, held at the Petrovaradin Fortress from 2001; left Serbia after 2025, return for July 2027 announced.

pages.title: Kazantip
pages.blurb: A weeks-long Crimean beach 'republic' founded by Nikita Marshunok; moved to Anaklia, Georgia, in 2014 after Russia annexed Crimea from Ukraine.

pages.title: Ultra Europe
pages.blurb: Joe Bašić's Croatian edition of Ultra, at Split's Poljud stadium from 2013 and later at Park mladeži.

pages.title: Insomniac
pages.blurb: Pasquale Rotella's Los Angeles promoter behind EDC, Nocturnal Wonderland and Electric Forest; in partnership with Live Nation from 2013.

pages.title: Pasquale Rotella
pages.blurb: Founder of Insomniac in 1993; took over the Electric Daisy Carnival name and moved the festival to Las Vegas in 2011.

pages.title: EDC Mexico
pages.blurb: Insomniac and OCESA's edition at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, Mexico City, from 2014; more than 250,000 in 2025 by Electronic Groove's count.

pages.title: Gary Richards
pages.blurb: Los Angeles promoter who founded HARD, whose first event was on New Year's Eve 2007.

pages.title: Alain Mongeau
pages.blurb: Founder of Mutek, launched in 2000 while he was director of new-media programming at Ex-Centris in Montreal.

pages.title: Paxahau
pages.blurb: Detroit rave producer founded by Jason Huvaere; took over Movement at Hart Plaza in 2006.

pages.title: Wire
pages.blurb: Takkyu Ishino's all-night indoor techno rave, at Yokohama Arena except for two years at Saitama Super Arena (2002–03), inspired by Germany's Mayday; Wire13 in 2013 was the last…

pages.title: Takkyu Ishino
pages.blurb: Denki Groove member and techno DJ who founded the Wire raves in 1999 after Germany's Mayday.

pages.title: The Labyrinth
pages.blurb: Mindgames' techno weekend, its line-up revealed only on arrival in 2018, with a Funktion-One rig in 2019; Wada Tōge 2001, Naeba Greenland 2009–18, Minakami from 2019.

pages.title: Ultra Korea
pages.blurb: The first Ultra event in Asia, opened in Seoul in 2012.

pages.title: Earthcore
pages.blurb: Spiro Boursine's Victorian bush doof, begun at Toolangi in 1993, on hiatus until 2013 and last held in 2017.

pages.title: AfrikaBurn
pages.blurb: Burning Man's South African offshoot in the Tankwa Karoo, from about 1,000 people in 2007 to 10,728 ticket holders in 2025, by its own counts.

pages.title: Ultra South Africa
pages.blurb: Ultra's licensed edition in Cape Town and Johannesburg; more than 40,000 in 2014, by Dancing Astronaut.

pages.title: Tomorrowland Brasil
pages.blurb: Tomorrowland's Brazilian edition at Parque Maeda, Itu: 180,000 tickets in 2015; a storm cancelled its Friday in 2023.

pages.title: Superstruct Entertainment
pages.blurb: Festival group founded with Providence money in 2017 and led by James Barton; bought by KKR in 2024, with CVC investing alongside.

pages.title: Live Nation
pages.blurb: Concert promoter whose British festivals had a combined capacity of 880,000 in 2025, including three of the four largest, by the AIF's count.

pages.title: SFX Entertainment / LiveStyle
pages.blurb: Robert Sillerman's dance-event roll-up, bankrupt in 2016 and renamed LiveStyle; sold ID&T to Superstruct in 2021.

pages.title: Association of Independent Festivals
pages.blurb: British trade body for independent festivals; counts the festivals lost each year and ran the first full sector count in 2025.

pages.title: Cercle
pages.blurb: Derek Barbolla's streamed DJ sets, from his Paris flat and then heritage sites, beginning with the Eiffel Tower in 2016; appealed to viewers for support in 2026.

pages.title: The Purple Guide
pages.blurb: Britain's guide to health, safety and welfare at music events, first published by the HSE (in 1992, by the AIF's account); run by the Events Industry Forum since 2012.

pages.title: UK Live Events Reinsurance Scheme
pages.blurb: Government-backed cover of over £750 million for events cancelled by new Covid restrictions, September 2021 to September 2022.

pages.title: Burning Man
pages.blurb: Week-long participant-built city in Nevada's Black Rock Desert, begun on Baker Beach in 1986; 78,850 people in 2019.

pages.title: Larry Harvey
pages.blurb: Co-founder of Burning Man, who burned the first figure on Baker Beach with Jerry James in 1986; died 28 April 2018.

pages.title: San Francisco Cacophony Society
pages.blurb: Prank and adventure group whose members Kevin Evans, John Law and P Segal took the Man to the Black Rock Desert in 1990.

pages.title: Terbo Ted
pages.blurb: Oakland rave DJ who, with Craig Ellenwood, brought the first sound system to Burning Man in 1992.

pages.title: Opulent Temple
pages.blurb: Burning Man sound camp from 2003, with a flame-throwing DJ booth; its big-name guests were not paid, Syd Gris said in 2014.

pages.title: Camp Question Mark
pages.blurb: Burning Man bass camp at 2:00 running PK Sound rigs for peak crowds of 10,000 to 15,000, by Mixmag's account.

pages.title: Robot Heart
pages.blurb: Art car built on a 1972 Leland double-decker bus, on the playa since 2008; its camp numbered 90 to 100 people in 2024.

pages.title: Mayan Warrior
pages.blurb: Pablo González Vargas's Mexico City art car, at Burning Man from 2012; destroyed by fire in 2023 and rebuilt for 2024.

pages.title: PK Sound
pages.blurb: Loudspeaker maker founded by Jeremy Bridge and Eroca Colins, directors of Shambhala's Village stage, whose rigs ran all but one of its main stages, by EDM Maniac's account.

pages.title: ANKORS
pages.blurb: Kootenay harm-reduction charity that ran Shambhala's drug-checking tent from 2003; over 2,000 checks in 2017.

pages.title: Cxema
pages.blurb: Slava Lepsheev's rave series, begun April 2014, held in skateparks, garages and film-studio pavilions; holding daytime parties by March 2026, CNN reported.

pages.title: ∄ (K41)
pages.blurb: Techno club in a former brewery at Kyrylivska 41, Podil; a shelter in 2022, later a non-profit raising money for the front.

pages.title: Otel'
pages.blurb: Club in the ribbon factory's old boiler house, opened April 2014; where Cxema's first party was held, by the Kyiv Post's and Don't Take Fake's accounts; a volunteer base and…

pages.title: Xlib
pages.blurb: Basement club on Kyrylivska Street in Podil, among Kyiv's first unglamorous electronic rooms by LB.ua's account.

pages.title: Torba Party
pages.blurb: Vitalii Ulitskyi's party series: fifteen nights of house, jungle and video at Flamingo, New York and the House of Cinema.

pages.title: Nastia
pages.blurb: DJ from Luhansk region; Kazantip resident from 2006; Strichka began around her birthday party in 2014; founder of the labels Propaganda and TECHNO Records.

pages.title: Vakula
pages.blurb: House and techno producer from Konotop; records on Shevchenko, Dekmantel, Firecracker and ARMA; his labels included Leleka and Bandura.

pages.title: Stanislav Tolkachev
pages.blurb: Dnipro-raised techno producer working with modular synthesisers; revived Rudiment for wartime charity compilations.

pages.title: Etapp Kyle
pages.blurb: Techno producer from Chernivtsi region, known through Klockworks; released Nolove on Ostgut Ton in 2020.

pages.title: Repair Together
pages.blurb: Volunteer group holding clean-up raves to clear and rebuild villages such as Yahidne after Russian occupation, by summer 2022.

pages.title: Vakula — You've Never Been to Konotop
pages.blurb: Firecracker's 2013 collection of Vakula's 2009–2012 work, named after his home town.

pages.title: Yellow Magic Orchestra
pages.blurb: Haruomi Hosono, Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi's band, early users of the MC-8 sequencer, the TR-808 and sampling on Technodelic.

pages.title: Gold
pages.blurb: Tokyo's bubble-era mega club in a converted seven-storey warehouse on the Shibaura canal; Larry Levan and François K played its Harmony Tour.

pages.title: Maniac Love
pages.blurb: Aoyama basement techno club opened in November 1993, home of the Sublime party and an after-hours with free coffee.

pages.title: Sublime Records
pages.blurb: Tokyo label founded in spring 1994 by Manabu Yamazaki after his Maniac Love parties; first releases by Ken Ishii and Susumu Yokota.

pages.title: Susumu Yokota
pages.blurb: Tokyo producer of The Frankfurt-Tokyo Connection on Harthouse and Acid Mt. Fuji on Sublime, later an ambient composer on his own Skintone label.

pages.title: Fumiya Tanaka
pages.blurb: Kyoto-born DJ who founded Torema Records in 1993, ran Distortion at Yellow and the long-running Chaos parties, and records for Perlon.

pages.title: Denki Groove
pages.blurb: Takkyu Ishino's band, whose first album came out in 1989 and whose single "Niji" was released in Germany by MFS in 1994.

pages.title: Satoshi Tomiie
pages.blurb: Tokyo producer who made "Tears" (1989) with Frankie Knuckles and Robert Owens; later ran SAW Recordings with Hector Romero.

pages.title: Soichi Terada
pages.blurb: Founder of Far East Recording in 1989 and composer for the Ape Escape games, rediscovered through Rush Hour's Sounds from the Far East (2015).

pages.title: Soichi Terada — Sounds from the Far East
pages.blurb: Rush Hour's compilation of Far East Recording house tracks, curated by Hunee, which brought Terada an international audience.

pages.title: ageHa
pages.blurb: Tokyo's largest nightclub for two decades, in Studio Coast on the Shin-Kiba waterfront, with a poolside terrace; closed on 30 January 2022.

pages.title: Future Terror
pages.blurb: DJ Nobu's techno and house party, started in Chiba in 2001 to book his friends and later moved to Tokyo; Haruka joined later.

pages.title: DJ Nobu
pages.blurb: DJ from Kamogawa in Chiba, out of hardcore punk, who runs Future Terror and the label Bitta.

pages.title: Contact
pages.blurb: Dogenzaka club run by Global Hearts beside Vision; closed on 17 September 2022 when its building was demolished for redevelopment.

pages.title: Vent
pages.blurb: Basement club in the Festa Omotesando building, Minami-Aoyama, opened in September 2016 with its dance room separate from the bar.

pages.title: Zouk
pages.blurb: Lincoln Cheng's club in three 1919 warehouses on Jiak Kim Street from 1991; Genting Hong Kong took over in 2015; Clarke Quay from 2016.

pages.title: Cakeshop
pages.blurb: Itaewon basement opened in September 2012 by Gabriel Joseph and Samuel Swanson; Seoul's room for bass, grime, gqom and baile funk.

pages.title: vurt.
pages.blurb: Techno club beneath a karaoke bar in Hapjeong, founded in 2014 under the slogan Ancient Future.

pages.title: Yaeji
pages.blurb: Queens-born producer and DJ raised partly in South Korea; Godmode EPs in 2017, then What We Drew and With a Hammer on XL.

pages.title: Park Hye Jin
pages.blurb: Former Pistil resident who sings, raps and produces house; How Can I came out on Ninja Tune in 2020.
Producer Lee Hohyeong, whose ppongjjak album Ppong (2022) won four Korean Music Awards; producer for NewJeans.

pages.title: Bhavishyavani Future Soundz
pages.blurb: Mumbai collective whose founders included Ashim Ahluwalia, Mukul Deora and Tejas Mangeshkar; parties from 13 May 1999.

pages.title: Blue Frog
pages.blurb: Live music and club venue in a converted mill compound; about 200 shows a year; closed on 28 August 2016 over rising rents.

pages.title: Boxout.fm
pages.blurb: Delhi online station launched in April 2017; closed its studio in 2021 and ended broadcasts for a streaming site in 2022.

pages.title: Headquarters
pages.blurb: House and techno room at 66 Boat Quay from the crew behind The Council; opened May 2016, closed by choice on 30 May 2026.

pages.title: Savage
pages.blurb: House and techno club in Tây Hồ, opened 2016; moved after noise complaints, reopening in the former Angolan embassy in June 2020.

pages.title: The Observatory
pages.blurb: Club co-owned by Dan Bi Mong across three sites for nearly thirteen years; announced its closure for the end of October 2026.

pages.title: Stadium
pages.blurb: Four-floor club on Jalan Hayam Wuruk with room for about 5,000; closed by the city in May 2014.

pages.title: Funkot
pages.blurb: Funky kota, city funk: hard, fast house with dangdut; the Jakarta Post points to Barakatak and DJ Jockie Saputra, early 1990s.

pages.title: Budots
pages.blurb: Davao street-dance music at 140 bpm on Amen breaks and trance basslines; Mixmag credits DJ Love as its chief originator.

pages.title: CzechTek
pages.blurb: The Czech free tekno teknival begun by Spiral Tribe and the Mutoid Waste Company; riot police broke it up at Mlýnec in 2005.

pages.title: Parada Wolności
pages.blurb: Łódź's Freedom Parade, run by the New Alcatraz crew; about 80,000 took part in 2002, RMF24 reported, before a new mayor banned it, as DJ Mag tells it.

pages.title: Instytut
pages.blurb: Warsaw techno nights begun by Groove Control in 2000 at the Instytut Energetyki with Claude Young; later a festival at Modlin.

pages.title: Smolna
pages.blurb: Techno club in a city-centre townhouse at ulica Smolna 38, listed by In Your Pocket as open Friday and Saturday 23:00–08:00, with a no-photo policy.

pages.title: Recognition
pages.blurb: Jacek Sienkiewicz's Warsaw techno label, founded in 1999.

pages.title: U.Club (Subclub)
pages.blurb: Tibor Holoda's club in a communist-era nuclear bunker under Bratislava Castle, home of Slovakia's stark techno; U.Club until 2003, the space closed as Subclub in 2019.

pages.title: Lärm
pages.blurb: Techno-only room for about 200 behind the Fogasház ruin pub in Budapest's District VII, opened in March 2014 by Gábor Manek.

pages.title: [a:rpia:r]
pages.blurb: The label of Rhadoo, Petre Inspirescu and Raresh, formed in 2006 or 2007 in XLR8R's account; the foreign music press calls the sound Ro-minimal.

pages.title: Rhadoo
pages.blurb: Bucharest DJ and producer, born in Galați in 1975; one of the RPR trio, whose label is [a:rpia:r].

pages.title: Club Guesthouse
pages.blurb: Bucharest club begun in 2010 at Traian 42, an incubator of the city's minimal scene; it moved downtown in 2020.

pages.title: Klub Industrija
pages.blurb: Basement club for about 800 under a central Belgrade bookshop that kept techno going through war, sanctions and the 1999 bombing.

pages.title: Drugstore
pages.blurb: Techno club in a former Belgrade slaughterhouse, opened in 2012; it stayed closed on 24 January 2025 for the general strike in support of the student-led protests.

pages.title: Klub K4
pages.blurb: Basement club at Kersnikova 4, formally established in 1989, an early Ljubljana techno venue, where Umek and Valentino Kanzyani started.

pages.title: Umek
pages.blurb: Slovenian techno DJ and producer, born in Ljubljana in 1976, who founded the label 1605 in 2007.

pages.title: Kablys
pages.blurb: Arts venue in Vilnius's 1956 railway workers' Palace of Culture, home to what Lithuanian Music Link calls the country's first raves, with a club from 2013.

pages.title: Yalta
pages.blurb: Sofia venue opened in 1959 that, by its own account, became the first place in Bulgaria dedicated to electronic music soon after 1989.

pages.title: The Shelter
pages.blurb: Club in a former bomb shelter on Yongfu Road, co-founded by Gareth (Gaz) Williams and Gary Wang; Resident Advisor reported in October 2016 that its licence could not be renewed,…

pages.title: SVBKVLT
pages.blurb: Shanghai label launched in 2013 as one of Gareth (Gaz) Williams's ventures; Hyph11E, 33EMYBW, Gooooose and others.

pages.title: Genome 6.66 Mbp
pages.blurb: Label and party crew founded by Tavi Lee and Kilo Vee, formed by the Shelter circle; first compilation 2016.

pages.title: Do Hits
pages.blurb: Party begun at School Bar in 2011 by Sulumi, Howie Lee, Guzz and Billy Starman; a label from June 2015.

pages.title: Tzusing
pages.blurb: Producer born in Kota Kinabalu; Shelter parties, 東方不敗 on L.I.E.S.

pages.title: Howie Lee
pages.blurb: Beijing-born producer in the Do Hits crew; Homeless EP (Do Hits, 2017).

pages.title: Hyph11E
pages.blurb: Producer from Hebei, in Shanghai since 2015; Aperture (SVBKVLT, 2020); a track on Genome's first compilation (2016).

pages.title: 33EMYBW
pages.blurb: Shanghai producer of Arthropods (2019) and Amalgamate (2026) on SVBKVLT; co-founded Duck Fight Goose in 2009.

pages.title: Lantern
pages.blurb: Weng Weng's techno club near the Workers' Stadium; shut in August 2020 for the stadium's redevelopment.

pages.title: Zhao Dai
pages.blurb: Beijing techno club opened in 2017; shut eight months by the 2022 lockdown, reopened December 2022.

pages.title: .TAG
pages.blurb: Club on the 21st floor of a Chengdu tower (the Poly Center, per the Goethe-Institut); announced its last party for 17 August 2025 after a 2am closing rule.

pages.title: Oil
pages.blurb: Futian club opened November 2017 with a Danley Sound Labs system; eighth anniversary in November 2025.

pages.title: XXX
pages.blurb: Club and gallery, run as a private venue, from Sheung Wan to Tai Kok Tsui; closed on 10 February 2018 after seven years.

pages.title: Korner
pages.blurb: Club outside The Wall in Gongguan; DJ Mag calls it the birthplace of Taipei's current clubs.

pages.title: Pawnshop
pages.blurb: Three-room Da'an club with Funktion-One, opened December 2019 by the people behind Korner; closed about three months by Covid rules in 2021.

pages.title: Meuko! Meuko!
pages.blurb: Taipei artist mixing noise, gabber and hardcore since 2015; 鬼島 Ghost Island (Danse Noire, 2018).

pages.title: Mahraganat
pages.blurb: Cairo's wedding-born electronic shaabi, made on cheap software with autotuned MCs; banned from stages by Egypt's musicians' syndicate in 2020.

pages.title: 100Copies
pages.blurb: Mahmoud Refat's Cairo label and studio, issuing 100 CDs a release; it brought mahraganat artists into the studio and onto stages.

pages.title: Islam Chipsy
pages.blurb: Cairo wedding keyboard player who, with drummers as EEK, toured Britain in 2014 and released Kahraba on Nashazphone.

pages.title: DJ Figo
pages.blurb: Salam City producer whom Groove and Afropop credit as mahraganat's first producer or creator.

pages.title: Hassan Shakosh
pages.blurb: Mahraganat singer whose 'Bint El Giran' passed 100 million YouTube views by February 2020 and preceded the syndicate's ban.

pages.title: Cairo Jazz Club
pages.blurb: Mohandiseen live-music club opened in 2001 by three musician and artist partners, with no cover charge.

pages.title: B018
pages.blurb: Naji Gebran's club, moved in 1998 to Bernard Khoury's sunken building at Karantina with a retracting circular roof.

pages.title: The Grand Factory
pages.blurb: Factory People's Beirut club, damaged in the 2020 port explosion and reopened in 2023.

pages.title: AHM
pages.blurb: Open-air Beirut club, about 90 per cent damaged in the 2020 blast, rebuilt with Carl Gerges and reopened on 12 July 2024.

pages.title: The Ballroom Blitz
pages.blurb: Three-room club in an old textile factory near Beirut's port, with a small Gold Room for experimental music.

pages.title: Jazar Crew
pages.blurb: Haifa collective of five friends, throwing parties from 2011, who played Boiler Room's first Palestine broadcast in 2018.

pages.title: Kabareet
pages.blurb: Palestinian-run Haifa club, home to Jazar Crew's parties, which closed for good in September 2024.

pages.title: Club 2019
pages.blurb: Junkyard club at Maslak run by Ceylan Çaplı and Mehmet Cavcı; its team launched the techno station Radio 2019.

pages.title: Babylon
pages.blurb: Live-music club opened in Asmalımescit in 1999 with John Lurie and the Lounge Lizards on the bill; moved to Bomontiada in 2015.

pages.title: MiniMüzikhol
pages.blurb: Unsigned 150-capacity room in Cihangir, described by Dekmantel as the spiritual successor to (((Godet))).

pages.title: Kafes
pages.blurb: Open-air beach club on the Black Sea at Kilyos, where Solomun drew about 6,000 in 2017 (Mixmag).

pages.title: Deena Abdelwahed
pages.blurb: Tunisian producer and DJ, raised in Doha, who played Tunis's Le Plug before moving to France; her album Khonnar came out on InFiné in 2018.

pages.title: Arabstazy
pages.blurb: Live project and compilation series from Mettani's label Shouka; Under Frustration Vol. 1 (2018) gathered producers from Tunisia, Egypt and beyond.

pages.title: Moroko Loko
pages.blurb: Amine K's underground party series, started in 2009 against the clubs' commercial music, later holding poolside parties in Marrakech.

pages.title: Amine K
pages.blurb: Self-taught Moroccan DJ with a master's in market finance, founder of Moroko Loko in 2009 (Le Matin).

pages.title: Maâlem Mahmoud Guinia
pages.blurb: Gnawa master who recorded Marhaba (Eglo, 2015) with Floating Points and James Holden after a 2014 Marrakech residency.

pages.title: Maâlem Mahmoud Guinia, Floating Points and James Holden — Marhaba
pages.blurb: Eglo 12-inch: Guinia with Floating Points on one side and with James Holden on the other.

pages.title: Guedra Guedra
pages.blurb: Abdellah M Hassak, producer and field recordist whose album Vexillology (2021) sets gnawa polyrhythms and bendir against footwork and sub-bass.

pages.title: The Joshua Light Show
pages.blurb: Joshua White's light show, house show at the Fillmore East from 8 March 1968 to 27 June 1971, projected from behind a 20-by-30-foot screen.

pages.title: Mark Boyle and Joan Hills
pages.blurb: Scottish artists whose liquid light shows lit UFO on Tottenham Court Road and toured with Soft Machine and Jimi Hendrix in 1968.

pages.title: The Exploding Plastic Inevitable
pages.blurb: Warhol's multimedia shows with the Velvet Underground at the Dom on St Marks Place: film and slide projection, strobes and mirrored balls.

pages.title: UFO Club, London
pages.blurb: Hoppy Hopkins's club on Tottenham Court Road, where Mark Boyle and Joan Hills projected liquids from a scaffolding tower behind the crowd.

pages.title: Fillmore East
pages.blurb: Bill Graham's hall at 105 Second Avenue, home of the Joshua Light Show; the building later housed the Saint.

pages.title: Laserium
pages.blurb: Ivan Dryer's laser concerts, first staged at Griffith Observatory in late 1973; ran there 28 years and in 46 cities.

pages.title: Clay Paky
pages.blurb: Pasquale Quadri's Italian lighting firm, founded 28 August 1976: oil wheels, the Astrodisco (1982), Astroraggi (1983) and Golden Scan (1987).

pages.title: The mirror ball
pages.blurb: Described in an electricians' union paper in 1897, patented as a 'myriad reflector' in 1924, mass-made by Omega of Louisville from the 1950s.

pages.title: 2001 Odyssey
pages.blurb: Bay Ridge disco at 802 64th Street, Brooklyn, where Saturday Night Fever's lit dance floor was built for the film.

pages.title: Ben Kelly
pages.blurb: Designer of the Haçienda (1982): blue-grey walls, diagonal-striped columns, bollards and cat's eyes marking the dance floor.

pages.title: Claude Bessy
pages.blurb: The Haçienda's first video operator, cutting VHS montages of found film for the club's two stage-side screens.

pages.title: Coldcut
pages.blurb: Matt Black and Jonathan More: Kiss FM's Solid Steel, Ninja Tune's founders, and pioneers of the audiovisual DJ set with Hex.

pages.title: Hex
pages.blurb: Coldcut with Robert Pepperell and Miles Visman: Hardwire's computer-made videos, Top Banana, Global Chaos on CDTV and live video mixing.

pages.title: Hexstatic
pages.blurb: Stuart Warren-Hill and Robin Brunson, Hex's successors: 'Timber' with Coldcut, then Rewind (2000) and Master-View (2004).

pages.title: VJamm
pages.blurb: Matt Black and Camart's real-time audiovisual sampler, written for Coldcut's 1997 tour; VJamm3 sold by Ninja Tune by 2006.

pages.title: Coldcut and Hexstatic — Timber
pages.blurb: Built from Greenpeace logging footage, every sound cut with its picture; released as a single in January 1998 with five videos.

pages.title: Coldcut — Let Us Play!
pages.blurb: Ninja Tune, 8 September 1997, with Hex's CD-ROM of playtools; given by the artists to the Centre Pompidou in 2002.

pages.title: Hex — Global Chaos
pages.blurb: Commodore CDTV disc of November 1992 combining rave visuals, techno and ambient tracks and the game Top Banana.

pages.title: The Duvet Brothers
pages.blurb: Rik Lander and Peter Boyd Maclean, scratch-video makers who showed at the Fridge's video lounge in August 1984.

pages.title: Scratch video
pages.blurb: British video art cut from taped television on home VCRs, first shown in clubs, then at the ICA.

pages.title: Stakker
pages.blurb: Mark McLean and Colin Scott's video team, for whose film Brian Dougans made 'Stakker Humanoid'; their Eurotechno video followed in 1989.

pages.title: Vegetable Vision
pages.blurb: Adam Smith and Noah Clark's 16mm and slide visuals for clubs and raves, and the Chemical Brothers' shows from 1995.

pages.title: The Light Surgeons
pages.blurb: Christopher Thomas Allen's audiovisual studio, incorporated in London in 1995, with Andy Flywheel's 16mm film loops.

pages.title: Tomato
pages.blurb: Soho design group whose members included Underworld's Karl Hyde and Rick Smith; made the band's sleeves and videos.

pages.title: Telepathic Fish
pages.blurb: Ambient parties co-run by Kevin Foakes, one in a Brixton squat in summer 1993 with Matt Black on video.

pages.title: Ninja Tune
pages.blurb: Coldcut's label, founded in 1990 on their first tour of Japan; Stealth club nights at the Blue Note, Hoxton, from December 1995.

pages.title: ArKaos
pages.blurb: Belgian VJ software built as a visual sampler of video loops; US$335 in 2004; later GrandVJ and MediaMaster; bought by inMusic in 2020.

pages.title: Resolume
pages.blurb: VJ software from The Hague by Edwin de Koning and Bart van der Ploeg, begun in 1998; version 2.0 in 2004.

pages.title: VDMX
pages.blurb: Vidvox's Mac VJ software, begun by Johnny DeKam as a Max project; US$250 in 2004.

pages.title: Modul8
pages.blurb: GarageCube's OpenGL video compositor for Mac OS X by Yves Schmid and Boris Edelstein; first released 2004, version 2 in 2005.

pages.title: Edirol V-4
pages.blurb: Four-input VJ video mixer with T-bar, 200 effects and BPM sync, US$1,195 in 2004; succeeded by the V-8.

pages.title: Eclectic Method
pages.blurb: Audiovisual remix act of Jonny Wilson, Geoff Gamlen and Ian Edgar, mixing film clips and acapellas on Pioneer DVJ decks.

pages.title: Addictive TV
pages.blurb: Graham Daniels's AV company: Transambient on Channel 4 and DVD (1999–2002), then live AV with Mark Vidler from 2005.

pages.title: D-Fuse
pages.blurb: Mike Faulkner's audiovisual collective, from VJing and design; visuals for Beck and the book VJ: Audiovisual Art and VJ Culture (2007).

pages.title: AntiVJ
pages.blurb: Visual label of Joanie Lemercier, Yannick Jacquet, Olivier Ratsi and Romain Tardy (name 2006, group 2008), taking projection onto buildings and sets.

pages.title: Ninja Jamm
pages.blurb: Ninja Tune and Seeper's free iOS remix app of 11 April 2013, with Matt Black as creative director.

pages.title: Daft Punk's pyramid: Alive 2006/2007
pages.blurb: The LED and video-mapped pyramid Martin Phillips designed for Daft Punk, first seen in Coachella's Sahara tent on 29 April 2006.

pages.title: Martin Phillips
pages.blurb: Designer of Daft Punk's Alive pyramid and its lighting; his production company is Bionic League.

pages.title: 1024 architecture
pages.blurb: François Wunschel and Pierre Schneider's Paris collective, which built Etienne de Crécy's projection-mapped cube in 2007.

pages.title: deadmau5 (Joel Zimmerman)
pages.blurb: Producer whose LED cubes, from 2010 to Cube v3, made the stage a structure he stood on and programmed himself in TouchDesigner.

pages.title: Amon Tobin
pages.blurb: Ninja Tune producer who played ISAM Live from inside a projection-mapped stack of boxes, from Mutek 2011.

pages.title: Amon Tobin — ISAM Live
pages.blurb: Projection-mapped set by Vita Motus, V Squared Labs, Blasthaus and Leviathan; premiered at the Metropolis, Montreal, on 1 June 2011.

pages.title: Plastikman Live (2010)
pages.blurb: Richie Hawtin's 2010 show, opened at Time Warp on 27 March, with Ali Demirel's TouchDesigner visuals driven by Ableton Live.

pages.title: Ali Demirel
pages.blurb: Richie Hawtin's visual artist, who built the Plastikman Live content and interface with Derivative in 2010.

pages.title: TouchDesigner
pages.blurb: Derivative's real-time visual programming environment, used for Plastikman, ISAM Live and deadmau5's Cube v3.

pages.title: United Visual Artists
pages.blurb: Chris Bird, Matt Clark and Ash Nehru's studio, formed after lighting Massive Attack's 2003 tour; Nehru wrote its d3 software.

pages.title: Notch
pages.blurb: Real-time visual effects and rendering engine from 10bit FX, whose scenes run inside media servers on tours.

pages.title: Eric Prydz — EPIC and HOLO
pages.blurb: Prydz's shows with holograms on Holo-Gauze: EPIC 5.0 in Victoria Park (2017), the HOLO tour (2018) and EPIC: Holosphere (2019).

pages.title: Sphere, Las Vegas
pages.blurb: A $2.3 billion venue with 160,000 square feet of immersive picture inside, opened by U2 on 29 September 2023.

pages.title: Anyma (Matteo Milleri)
pages.blurb: Tale Of Us's Matteo Milleri as a solo audiovisual act: Sphere's first electronic residency, then the ÆDEN show of 2026.

pages.title: Anyma — The End of Genesys at Sphere
pages.blurb: Twelve nights at Sphere, 27 December 2024 to 2 March 2025; the first six sold more than 100,000 tickets in 24 hours.

pages.title: Ariel Figueroa
pages.blurb: Lighting operator at Tracks, the Sound Factory, Vinyl and Cielo, who played the board beside Larry Levan, Junior Vasquez and others.

pages.title: Robert Henke — Lumière
pages.blurb: Henke's laser and sound piece: three white lasers at Unsound in 2013, coloured diodes from Lumière II (2015), Lumière III in 2017.

pages.title: Ryoji Ikeda
pages.blurb: Artist and composer whose spectra put 49 searchlights over London for seven nights in August 2014.

pages.title: Ryoji Ikeda — spectra (London, 2014)
pages.blurb: Grid of 49 searchlights in Victoria Tower Gardens, 4–11 August 2014, for the First World War centenary; produced by Artangel.

pages.title: Christopher Bauder
pages.blurb: Berlin light artist who made SKALAR with Kangding Ray, 65 kinetic mirrors at Kraftwerk for CTM 2018, and Deep Web with Robert Henke.

pages.title: MFO (Marcel Weber)
pages.blurb: Visual artist and scenographer, a club VJ from the early 2000s, later director of light and visuals for Berlin's Atonal.

pages.title: Trauma Bar und Kino
pages.blurb: Berlin club whose visual designer Veslemøy Rustad Holseter lights techno nights in red and white and trains new light technicians.

pages.title: Karhard
pages.blurb: Berlin design studio that converted the Friedrichshain power station into Berghain in 2004.

pages.title: Nitemind
pages.blurb: Michael Potvin's lighting studio: light shows and installations for festivals and venues, including Sustain-Release, and amber light for a song in Kelela's concert at Berghain.

pages.title: Amber's, Manchester
pages.blurb: 1,000-capacity club on Oxford Road that opened with a total filming ban and a sticker on every phone camera.

pages.title: Rost, Glasgow
pages.blurb: Glasgow club, opened in March 2019, that asks guests to let staff sticker their phone cameras.

pages.title: The camera sticker
pages.blurb: The club rule, spread from Berlin, of covering phone cameras at the door; Berghain, FOLD, Rost and Amber's among those using it.

pages.title: Chris Binks
pages.blurb: Lighting designer who ran fabric's desk from its opening in 1999, after club shows at Bagley's, the Hanover Grand and the Cross.

pages.title: Loud Noise
pages.blurb: Lisa Loud and Nancy Noise's midweek night, which lasted only a few months; Lisa Loud describes two women running a night as groundbreaking.

pages.title: Feline
pages.blurb: Storm's 2007 night at Herbal for women in drum and bass.

pages.title: Jive Turkey
pages.blurb: Winston Hazel and Parrot's Friday night in Sheffield, listed with Occasions as the city's soul-into-bleep nights of 1985 to 1990.

pages.title: Sabresonic
pages.blurb: Andrew Weatherall's Friday techno night at Happy Jax under London Bridge, where the Chemical Brothers played their first live gig.

pages.title: Bubblegum
pages.blurb: The sound of South African pop in the 1980s, labelled "bubblegum"; most of its makers rejected the word and preferred "disco".

pages.title: Gqom
pages.blurb: Made at home in Durban's townships on pirated software, passed round on phones and USB sticks and played in minibus taxis: programmed drums, usually without the four-on-the-floor…

pages.title: Baile funk
pages.blurb: Rio DJs took Miami bass records, sped them up and put Portuguese on top: a dance music that became central to Brazilian pop and was policed as a crime problem for decades.

pages.title: Digital cumbia
pages.blurb: Cumbia reworked with laptops, the sound of the Zizek parties in Buenos Aires and of ZZK Records.

pages.title: Otherworld
pages.blurb: Trance promotion that had the first Friday of the month at the Fridge in Brixton in the mid-1990s, with Lol and Yazz as residents; its compilation Dance, Trance & Magic Plants…

pages.title: Science Fiction
pages.blurb: Night with Sid Shanti that had the last Friday of the month at the Fridge in Brixton, moving to Cloud 9 in Vauxhall in May 1997.

pages.title: Pendragon
pages.blurb: Trance crew whose usual base was the Theatre Factory, a warehouse on Tyssen Street in Dalston; it sometimes took the Fridge's fifth Friday and helped with Escape from Samsara's…

pages.title: X-ClaimNation Co-op
pages.blurb: Night that opened at the Fridge in Brixton at the end of May 1995, with Megatripolis-style stalls for massage, face painting and smart drinks.

pages.title: Grime
pages.blurb: A darker, more instrumental garage with space left for MCs, made by teenagers on pirate radio and in bedroom studios on east London estates; journalists named it from the grimy…

pages.title: Dubstep
pages.blurb: The dark, stripped-down end of UK garage: 2-step's shuffled, syncopated drums kept, the diva vocals and house chords thrown away, leaving sub-bass and space.

pages.title: Brostep
pages.blurb: A lurching, aggressive variant of dubstep, in Spin's words: where traditional dubstep emphasises sub-bass, brostep leans on the middle register.

pages.title: Ghetto house
pages.blurb: The faster, cruder music Chicago's South and West Sides made for themselves on Dance Mania, while the city's deep house went abroad.

pages.title: Ghettotech
pages.blurb: Detroit's other dance music: Miami bass and electro at 140 to 150bpm, played on radio mix shows and danced as the jit.

pages.title: Baltimore club
pages.blurb: House records from Chicago and New York cut up on the spot in Baltimore: a vocal chopped to a chant, a drum break from 1970s funk and a stuttering kick, at about 130 beats per…

pages.title: Hi-NRG
pages.blurb: The uptempo, synthesiser-driven strain of disco, its lineage running back to Donna Summer's "I Feel Love" (1977) and Giorgio Moroder's basslines.

pages.title: Asylum and Pyramid at Heaven
pages.blurb: Kevin Millins's Thursday at Heaven from 14 April 1983 with Colin Faver and Mark Moore; by 1985 it had become Pyramid, which the Museum of London counts among the first clubs in…

pages.title: Fruit Machine
pages.blurb: Heaven's Wednesday night in the 1990s, hosted by Miss Kimberley.

pages.title: Inferno
pages.blurb: Techno night founded by the DJ and artist Lewis G. Burton in 2015, by 2023 held at Colour Factory in Hackney Wick.

pages.title: Batty Bass
pages.blurb: Hannah Holland's night, later a label, started in east London around 2006.

pages.title: Xanadu
pages.blurb: Laurence Malice's Saturday night at Turnmills early in 1990, run with the promoter Robert Pereno; it lasted five or six months, and Trade followed that October.

pages.title: Speed Queen
pages.blurb: Leeds Saturday that started at the Warehouse, moved to Stinky's Peep House, where about 350 came to a terrace and a giant bed, and returned to the Warehouse in 2003 before…

pages.title: Amapiano
pages.blurb: A South African offshoot of house made of kwaito, deep house, jazz and lounge, played at a slow, rolling tempo; the word is isiZulu for "the pianos".

pages.title: Hardstyle
pages.blurb: The Dutch hard dance that took shape around 2000, grown from gabber with hard trance and hard house in it: a distorted kick at about 150 bpm, made for Q-dance's arena nights and…

pages.title: Disco
pages.blurb: Began in 1970 as a private party in a Manhattan loft, for Black, Latino and gay New Yorkers; it gave dance music the four-to-the-floor, the remix and the twelve-inch single.

pages.title: Dub
pages.blurb: In 1968 an engineer cutting a dubplate left the vocal off by accident; instrumental "versions" became the B-sides of Jamaican 45s, and Britain became a new centre of dub in the…

pages.title: Juke
pages.blurb: The updated name for ghetto house, in Time Out Chicago's words; DJ Puncho and Gant-Man coined the word with their 1997 track "Juke It", and by 2002 it had stuck.

pages.title: EDM
pages.blurb: The one new name the American music business gave house, trance and dubstep in the boom years; the Billboard writer Kerri Mason dated the change to 2009.

pages.title: Electro house and big room
pages.blurb: The festival main-stage house of the EDM years: electro house's heavy, distorted basslines from the mid-2000s, then big room's long build-ups and kick-heavy drops at Ultra and…

pages.title: Singeli
pages.blurb: Dar es Salaam's street-party music, built from looped and sped-up taarab and mchiriku at 200 bpm and faster; Nyege Nyege Tapes' Sounds of Sisso took it abroad in 2017.

pages.title: Love Muscle
pages.blurb: The Fridge's Saturday from September 1992: uplifting house, go-go dancers and stage shows, with Yvette the Conqueror as hostess; it ended at the Fridge in 2004 and was later…

pages.title: Daisy Chain
pages.blurb: One of the nights Andrew Czezowski and Susan Carrington created at the Fridge in Brixton, running from 1987 to 1990.

pages.title: Trash
pages.blurb: Erol Alkan's Monday night at The End, indie into electro, the night that made his name.

pages.title: The Gallery
pages.blurb: Friday trance and hard house night run by Lock n Load, at Turnmills in Clerkenwell and on Fridays at Ministry of Sound; Lottie was made a resident in 1996.

pages.title: Knowledge at the SW1 Club
pages.blurb: Friday techno night at the SW1 Club in Victoria with Colin Dale, Colin Faver and Dave Angel: purist techno before Final Frontier.

pages.title: Full Circle
pages.blurb: Phil Perry's Sunday-afternoon Balearic session at the Greyhound in Colnbrook.

pages.title: Roast
pages.blurb: Monthly jungle rave at Linford Film Studios in Battersea with Jumpin' Jack Frost, named with Jungle Fever and Telepathy as the raves of the scene.

pages.title: Innovation
pages.blurb: Micky Finn's drum and bass event, among the big raves of the jungle years, held on Fridays at Ministry of Sound.

pages.title: Bedrock (club night)
pages.blurb: John Digweed and Nick Muir's Bedrock as a night: monthly at Heaven in London and at The Beach in Brighton from 2000 to 2005.

pages.title: FABRICLIVE
pages.blurb: fabric's Friday: begun as a monthly of drum and bass, hip hop and breaks, with James Lavelle in the 3–5am slot, it grew into a survey of British beats where grime and dubstep…

pages.title: Playaz
pages.blurb: DJ Hype's Playaz as a night: its drum and bass residency inside fabric's FABRICLIVE Fridays, halved with the bass nights after 2016.

pages.title: WetYourSelf!
pages.blurb: Sunday night of underground house and techno at fabric from February 2009, with Peter Pixzel, Jacob Husley, Carlos Ryan and Lamine.

pages.title: Peach
pages.blurb: Graham Gold's night at Camden Palace from 1993 to 2004; Peach also had Fridays of trance at Bagley's in King's Cross.

pages.title: Nude
pages.blurb: Mike Pickering's Friday at the Haçienda, established by early 1986 with Little Martin Prendergast and later Graeme Park: salsa, electro and northern soul at first, then the first…

pages.title: Hot at the Haçienda
pages.blurb: Mike Pickering and Jon Dasilva's Wednesday at the Haçienda from July 1988, opened with palm trees, beach balls and a 20-foot swimming pool, replacing Paul Cons's Zumbar.

pages.title: Temperance Club
pages.blurb: Dave Haslam's Thursday at the Haçienda, from 1986 to October 1990, mixing hip hop, rock and house.

pages.title: Zumbar
pages.blurb: Paul Cons's Wednesday cabaret-and-house night at the Haçienda, replaced by Hot in summer 1988.

pages.title: Freak at the Haçienda
pages.blurb: The Saturday running at the Haçienda's close: the club's last night, on 28 June 1997, was a Freak, with Dave Haslam, Miles Hollway and Elliot Eastwick.

pages.title: Bugged Out
pages.blurb: Manchester techno night of 1994, at Sankeys Soap in Ancoats on Fridays, that became a brand and later came to Amnesia in Ibiza.

pages.title: Polysexual
pages.blurb: Sunday night at Godskitchen's CODE in Digbeth, with Fergie as a resident in the early 2000s; it took the Nitrogen Room at AIR and programmed a room at Godskitchen's Last Dance.

pages.title: Babooshka
pages.blurb: Saturday night at Godskitchen's CODE in Digbeth, which programmed a room at Godskitchen's Last Dance.

pages.title: Atomic Jam
pages.blurb: Birmingham's big techno room: monthly in the main room of the Que Club from 1995, and back in the reopened Q Club for its 13th birthday on 22 November 2008.

pages.title: Subculture
pages.blurb: Slam's Saturday at the Sub Club since 9 April 1994, with Harri and Domenic as residents: the longest-running weekly in the UK.

pages.title: Klubnacht
pages.blurb: The long weekend at Berghain: it opens on Saturday night and on most weekends runs until late on Monday morning, with residents including Marcel Dettmann, Ben Klock, Steffi, Nick…

pages.title: Snax
pages.blurb: Norbert Thormann and Michael Teufele's party, begun in 1994 in the Reichsbahnbunker on Albrechtstraße in Mitte; it led them to Ostgut in 1998 and Berghain in 2004, and still…

pages.title: Dubmission
pages.blurb: E-Werk's Saturday house-and-trance night, where Paul van Dyk was resident and out of which came his 'For an Angel'.

pages.title: Wake Up
pages.blurb: Laurent Garnier's Thursday night at the Rex Club from 21 May 1992, which brought Derrick May, Carl Craig, Jeff Mills and the founders of techno and house to Paris, often for the…

pages.title: Bass Culture
pages.blurb: D'Julz's monthly residency at the Rex Club from 1997, the longest-standing in the club's history; it marked twenty years in 2017 and played the old room's last party on 27 May…

pages.title: Flower Power
pages.blurb: Pacha's 1960s night, started in 1980 or 1981 and still running, with Piti Urgell; the Guardian calls it the club's earliest themed party.

pages.title: Pyramid at Amnesia
pages.blurb: The night that took Cocoon's Mondays at Amnesia in 2018, opening with Villalobos on the Terrace and Ben Klock in the Club room; in 2026 it held Sundays from 14 June to 4 October.

pages.title: Music Is Revolution
pages.blurb: Carl Cox's Tuesday residency at Space, sixteen summers from 2001; its 2016 season was The Final Chapter and the last night was 20 September 2016.

pages.title: La Espuma
pages.blurb: Amnesia's weekly foam party under that name: Sundays in 2005 to pop, hip-hop and reggaeton, Saturdays shared with Foam & Diamonds by 2015, Wednesdays in the Club room by 2018.

pages.title: Judgement Sundays
pages.blurb: Judge Jules's Sunday night at Eden in San Antonio, one of the Ibiza residencies of the trance years.

pages.title: Mister Saturday Night
pages.blurb: Justin Carter and Eamon Harkin's party and label, which opened Nowadays in Ridgewood, Queens, in June 2015 and raised $100,000 on Kickstarter for its sound system.

pages.title: Mister Sunday
pages.blurb: Justin Carter and Eamon Harkin's daytime Sunday party, moved from Industry City to Nowadays in April 2016.

pages.title: Subliminal Sessions
pages.blurb: Erick Morillo's midweek night, which moved to Centro-Fly after it was evicted from Champs; a Subliminal Night late in 1999 brought in Danny Tenaglia, Derrick Carter and Tony…

pages.title: Next Generation
pages.blurb: The Music Institute's Friday: the techno night, meant to be as young, fast and aggressive as possible, with Derrick May and D-Wynn after Kevin Saunderson.

pages.title: A.R.T. at Yellow
pages.blurb: K.U.D.O.'s Friday at Yellow in Tokyo, renamed Zero from 1994.

pages.title: Biyoshi Night
pages.blurb: Yellow's Monday from 1994 to 1999, the hairdressers' night.

pages.title: Savage!
pages.blurb: Hip-hop night at Yellow hosted by DJ Muro and DJ Kensei, from 1997.
